issues.title: Turner Duckworth dips Maker's Mark's new identity in red wax
issues.summary: Five years after its last refresh, the Kentucky bourbon has gone back to the London agency for a global identity pressed, quite literally, from the very farm it comes from. If you love your bourbon as...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Five years after its last refresh, the Kentucky bourbon has gone back to the London agency for a global identity pressed, quite literally, from the very farm it comes from.

If you love your bourbon as much as I do, then you'll know every bottle of Maker's Mark is still dipped in red wax by hand. It's a slow and messy process any creative can appreciate, especially in a year when Cambridge Dictionary named 'human' its word of 2026.

So it makes sense that the brand's new global identity would go down the same route. Turner Duckworth London has taken stalks of soft red winter wheat, rings of American oak and plants native to Star Hill Farm, the distillery's home in Loretto, Kentucky, and dipped and pressed each one into that same red wax. What came out of that is a set of fresh marks that sit at the heart of the brand. There's also an updated colour palette, new photography and custom typography that pays homage to the brand's family roots.

Sound familiar? That's because Turner Duckworth has been here before. We covered its first Maker's Mark identity in 2021, when the agency built a system around a graphic version of the famous drip. Five years later, the drawing has made way for the real thing. Why illustrate wax when you've got access to vats of it?

The typography has its own story, too. It's inspired by the handwriting of Margie Samuels, who founded Maker's Mark with her husband, Bill Samuels Sr, and who came up with the bottle, label and wax in the first place. It is Margie's wit that the brand has always traded on. Well, I never.

Now for a little history lesson. Bill famously burned the family's 170-year-old recipe to start afresh and come up with a more balanced bourbon. The couple chose Loretto for its proximity to water and grain growers. And Margie decided that every bottle must be hand-dipped – a strategy that literally made its mark. Maker's Mark calls this streak 'Perfectly Unreasonable', the name of its brand platform, and the new identity is designed to carry this idea consistently worldwide, in what the brand describes as a "modern, more minimal way".

"In a world increasingly driven by speed and automation, we still believe some things are worth making slowly, by hand," says Chloe Lloyd-Jones, vice president of global brand marketing, Maker's Mark. "We returned to Star Hill Farm, working with natural materials from the land and our signature red wax to create a visual identity that reflects the 'Perfectly Unreasonable' spirit behind our bourbon. The result gives us a powerful way to tell our story around the world, while creating experiences that feel personal and relevant in each market."

"My grandparents weren't thinking about 'branding' when they created Maker's Mark. They cared about a hand-made process in service to flavour and design that honours that vision," adds Rob Samuels, eighth-generation whisky maker and managing director. "That deeply personal approach created some of the most recognisable symbols in bourbon. This new and exceptional work brings that same intention forward, honouring what they created and ensuring Maker's Mark feels as personal and distinctive today as it did from the start."

The identity was launched on 17 November and is rolling out across digital, social, advertising and retail, as well as events and experiences. Parts of it have already appeared at events in the US and China and in out-of-home campaigns in Australia and the UK, with more markets to follow throughout 2027.

issues.title: &Walsh takes a bite out of the moon for Insomnia Cookies
issues.summary: Jessica Walsh and her team have given the late-night bakery's identity a refresh, and it's based on the very thing it's promised since it launched in 2003: a warm cookie at any hour. Milk and cookies...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Jessica Walsh and her team have given the late-night bakery's identity a refresh, and it's based on the very thing it's promised since it launched in 2003: a warm cookie at any hour.

Milk and cookies is very much an American thing. I've never once been tempted to sneak down the stairs in the dead of night and snack on something delicious. It's just not in our culture. Nigella Lawson might, god bless her. I can picture her now in her silk dressing gown, the goddess that she is. But late-night treats are not for me. Seeing the new identity for Insomnia Cookies, though, might tempt me otherwise.

The heart of &Walsh's rebrand is a logo that looks good enough to eat, and it pays homage to the whole premise. Insomnia Cookies is a late-night bakery that Seth Berkowitz started from his University of Pennsylvania dorm room in 2003. It now has more than 375 bakeries across the US, Canada and the UK. Its original identity had a cookie moon. Genius. &Walsh has thankfully kept that but swapped the drawing for the real deal: a photograph of a melted chocolate chunk cookie, half-eaten into the shape of a crescent. Anyone suddenly think of "Half mooooon!" or is that just me?

Yes, it's a brave move, a photographic logo. Any designer will tell you they're awkward at small sizes and damn fussy in print, yet here we are. But have no fear, dear readers – &Walsh has a vector version in reserve for exactly those moments. Everywhere else, though, the cookie is on full show.

So why didn't they start from scratch? One would assume the importance of heritage, certainly. By Insomnia's own account, it created the warm cookie delivery category, and &Walsh set out to recommit to that rather than reinvent it. So whilst everyone else is chasing trends, the new strategy focuses on a single promise: 'Always Warm'. Gosh, my mouth is watering just thinking about it.

That brand promise suits Insomnia's purpose – turning up at your door at any unreasonable hour with something straight from the oven. It's why the agency didn't overcomplicate things or try and be clever. When you look at this refreshed logo, you get that instant promise. It's confident without trying too hard.

Around the moon is a system built on the hours Insomnia operates. There's a nice late-night purple palette (Premier Inn, anyone?), along with a run of cookie-dough browns. Typography by Julio Zukerman is rounded and chunky. Illustration is also by Julio and Simran Meshram. And there's a refreshed tone of voice throughout.

The new identity has been rolled out across campaigns, digital, newsletters, print and packaging, including pizza-style boxes that regulars will be familiar with.

Then there's Insomnia's menu, which rotates constantly. And every limited-time offer is another opportunity for the brand to show off its new look. To keep it all feeling like one brand, &Walsh designed a tiered system: most launches share the same warm, appetising photography and art direction, while a select few campaigns get a more graphic approach.

What's really interesting is the sheer volume of the work. Over six months, &Walsh produced more than five photography and video shoots to cover 12 campaigns, from the core range of cookies to seasonal specials. OK, now I want to know about seasonal specials. Photography was by Henry Hargreaves, while Charlotte Omnes and Daniella Khan handled food styling. Motion design is by Pedro Magalhães, Igor Fajardo and Marco Del Pra, and moving elements can be seen across the refresh. It looks so good you can almost see the heat coming off the freshly baked cookies.

"Every decision in this rebrand, the photo moon cookie, the photography, the rounded type, the colours, was built toward the same feeling: warm, late night and confident," says Carolina Vazquez, art director at &Walsh. "The goal was to make the brand feel fresh without losing what's always made it Insomnia."

Given how much I'll be playing GTA 6 over the coming weeks, I reckon I could be persuaded to enjoy a late-night cookie.

issues.title: It's official: creatives are using AI daily, but most aren't making extra money from it
issues.summary: Envato's second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don't always tell the client. But whether they're using it well remains an open question....
issues.author: Tom May
issues.content_html:
Envato's second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don't always tell the client. But whether they're using it well remains an open question.

This time last year, many creatives were rushing to adopt AI tools, but nervously. Twelve months later, things have changed a lot. That's according to Beyond the Hype: The State of AI in Creative Work, the second annual report from Envato, the creative asset and AI toolkit owned by Shutterstock.

Based on a survey of 1,033 creatives across 103 countries and territories, the report reveals what creatives are actually doing with AI. And two big things immediately grabbed my attention. Firstly, more than half of AI users have used it on key client work without telling their client. And secondly, while AI may save you time, most creatives aren't seeing that turn into actual money.

To unpack these findings and more, I spoke to Hichame Assi, president of Shutterstock, which includes Envato.

Why ask?

Envato first ran the survey in 2025, and Hichame says the reason was simple. The public conversation about AI didn't match what he was seeing from the working creatives who use Envato. "At face value, the narrative was all hype or doom," he recalls. "Yet in our community, creatives were quietly working AI into client jobs." So last year, Envato asked creatives how they were using it.

One finding from that first survey stayed with Hichame in particular. "Almost half were using AI every day, but only about a third felt really prepared for it. That gap felt worth keeping an eye on, so we came back to see what had changed."

So what has changed in the last 12 months? Well, quite a lot actually. For a start, today 87% of creatives use AI at work at least occasionally, and 58% use it every day.

"AI is now part of the daily routine for most creatives," says Hichame. "Daily use rose from 49% to 58%, and agentic tools, which we didn't even ask about last year, are now used regularly by more than a third of AI users. At the same time, active avoidance has grown from 3% to 8%, so not everyone is on board yet."

But while most creatives are using AI to help them in their work, that doesn't mean that AI is doing their work, at least not all of it.

The survey split people's creative work into six stages, from research and admin to editing. At five of the six stages, "directing [AI] closely" was the most common approach. The percentage of creatives who let AI work "with little input" never went above 11%, and at some stages, it dropped to 4%. As for generating assets, only 7% took a hands-off approach.

The fall of the prompt

For Hichame, the biggest surprise in this year's data concerned the skill that, only a year ago, everyone seemed to agree was essential: prompting.

"Last year, our respondents named prompting as a skills gap and predicted 'prompt engineer' as a new job," he recalls. "This year, though, creatives ranked it last of eight factors, at 19%." Taste and judgement came first, at 53%. Craft came second, at 49%, followed by the strength of the idea, at 39%.

So what's going on? Perhaps this is just a sign that models have got much better at understanding natural language and visual references. Consequently, the time when precise prompts were all-important is long gone.

"The tools are going to keep getting easier and more accessible, so knowing how to use them won't be what sets creatives apart," says Jessica Walsh, founder of New York studio &Walsh and one of the experts interviewed for the report. What will, in her view, is "being able to recognise great work when you see it [which is] not something you can prompt, or learn overnight."

A lack of rules

One thing that surprised me personally is that nearly six in 10 creatives who work in teams say they have no written AI policy. Even in organisations of 250 or more people, four in 10 say they've been given nothing in writing. As Hichame puts it: "The tools moved fast, and the rules didn't. Most are working it out as they go." Which brings us to a thorny question: should creatives disclose whether they've used AI in their work?

In practice, it seems, this has become a matter of personal judgement. More than half of AI users (53%) have used it on key client work without telling the client, and most don't see that as a problem. Only 7% felt uncomfortable staying quiet.

Hichame notes, though, that when there are rules in place, "creatives are more open with clients, with 47% always disclosing AI use, compared with 38% where there's no policy." Age can play a part, too: while only 40% of creatives always tell clients when they've used AI, that rises to 53% among those aged 50 and over.

What humans are for

One of the most commonly cited concerns about AI is that its output is bland and lacks soul. Yet when creatives discard AI-generated concepts, that's rarely the real reason. According to the report, one third (34%) do so because the concepts missed the brief or vision, and a similar number (32%) do so because of errors or low quality, such as garbled logos or glitchy video. Only 5% drop them because they lack feeling or soul.

What's just as interesting is what creatives keep. "The typical creative generates three to five AI concepts and keeps about two," notes Hichame. "Three in four keep half or fewer of their concepts." That, as he sees it, shows how important human creativity remains in the creative process. "Quality control is where humans make the difference," he says. "Knowing what the brief needs, seeing where an output falls short and choosing what makes the cut are judgement calls.

"Generating 10 options is easy," he adds. "Knowing which one is right is the skill, and it's one that creatives build over years."

Where's the money?

Here's another interesting question the report poses: is AI making creatives richer? The answer is: mostly not, or at least not yet.

"Half of creatives who use AI say it makes them faster," says Hichame. "But of those, only one in four report any financial upside. Another one in five earn about the same for less effort. For the rest, they gain time, not money."

This isn't, though, because people are cutting their rates: quite the reverse. "Of the freelancers and agency owners we asked, 40% raised their rates this year and only 6% cut them," he says. More to the point, more than a quarter of AI users (28%) now offer services they couldn't before, and 26% of those whose rates moved credited new services.

The conclusion in Hichame's mind is clear. "Getting better results from AI is the skill creatives most want to learn, at 45%, while creative direction sits near the bottom at 18%," he notes. Yet in the survey, the creatives who have raised their rates credited speed, reputation and creative direction ahead of AI skills. "This suggests people are chasing the skill the market isn't paying for, and ignoring the ones it is."

His advice? "Take the hours AI gives back and put them where clients pay," he says. "That means turning work around faster, investing in your own name and point of view, so your work is recognisable as yours, and sharpening your direction. Because three in four creatives already discard at least half of what AI produces, and that judgement is what sets you apart."

issues.title: Julie Legrand finds poetry in coffee pots, shells and other things you see every day
issues.summary: The French illustrator and screen printer turns objects from her kitchen and studio into bold, smudged, characteristically simple images. Julie Legrand's portfolio is full of things you've seen a thou...
issues.author: Ayla Angelos
issues.content_html:
The French illustrator and screen printer turns objects from her kitchen and studio into bold, smudged, characteristically simple images.

Julie Legrand's portfolio is full of things you've seen a thousand times and probably never stopped to really look at, let alone draw them. There's a moka pot drawn in a wobbly black line, a large-scale sunshine-yellow coffee pot on chocolatey brown, a hand holding a shell among pale blue crabs and whelks, and roses in all sorts of guises, from a yellow bloom with 'ROSA' scrawled underneath in her own lettering to a tomato-red one floating on cobalt blue. A few simple shapes, a handful of colours and the odd paper dot from a hole punch are all it takes to make a kitchen staple feel like a star. And it's all so cheerful and homely that we want to put the kettle on, and maybe pin a few of these to the fridge.

The illustrator and screen printer comes from the south of France. "I grew up in the mountains of the Hérault hinterland," she says, before studying illustration in Épinal, eastern France, and later printmaking in Galicia, Spain. Those roots led her to work with traditional techniques, and are perhaps a key reason why rural life and seaside imagery turn up again and again in her work.

When asked where she finds inspiration, she says: "Primarily from everyday life: objects I find in my kitchen or my studio." That's the sort of stuff we all have lying around at home. Her themes are always "rooted in the intimate and the mundane," and she adds: "I try to convey the memories and poetry associated with them." Since moving to Sète, the sea has crept into her work, including its plant life, mineral forms and inhabitants. "I like to interpret the landscape through the elements and forms that compose it, rather than by representing the landscape itself."

Once she has her inspiration in check, she moves on to her process. "I exhaust forms," she explains, "meaning I choose an object or subject and explore its variations, sometimes over the course of months." That explains why a coffee pot and rose each show up in so many guises. She starts with photos, sketches, and drawings she's happy with, then works in collage or with pens, pencils, rulers, and lettering templates, before digitising and editing. The handcrafted feel matters enormously to her, so the paper textures from her collages and the marks and smudges on her drawings all make it through. "Cleaning up a scan is the opposite of my approach," she says – and we're glad.

Recently, Julie created a pair of collages for the Slow Down Studio open call, featuring a stem of nodding bell-shaped flowers and a cream rose, both on brown. "It perfectly sums up what I enjoy doing right now: flowers, a subject I find delightful, combined with my signature stylistic approach," she says. And what is that approach, you might ask? Well: "simple, synthetic forms, a limited colour palette, including brown (my favourite colour), a mix of angles and curves and those small paper circles from my hole punch (one of my favourite tools)." Those little dots scatter around the edges like confetti, and she deliberately avoids over-editing the colours or saturation so the original scan's "authentic, handmade quality" can shine through.

As for what she hopes people take away from her work, Julie is refreshingly relaxed about it. "There isn't really a message, other than raising my audience's awareness of the poetry found in simple things," she says. She thinks the people who connect with her work appreciate its materiality and "see themselves reflected in the universal motifs I choose to depict."

Plenty is in the works for Julie, including a personal piece for an upcoming exhibition in Sète, plus fairs and markets in London, Marseille, Milan and Valencia in the coming months. She's also about to start a screen-printed book with the Berlin-based studio Le Raclet. And while we have you, she'd like us to know she's "looking to expand my commission work as much as possible (take note!)", with branding projects and press work at the top of her wishlist. "That would be amazing," she says.

issues.title: How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design
issues.summary: From retractable saunas to immersive ice rooms, the German company is exploring how engineering, materials, and technology can reshape traditional wellness rituals
issues.author: Bianca Weeko Martin
issues.content_html:
The sauna is Finnish. The company reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

At Klafs headquarters, where the company’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he says, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the company describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden bench.

Blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

From the heat of the sauna, the tour moves into an altogether different climate. I retreat into the cool blue light of a Frimas ice steam room, where a glowing central ice fountain grows delicate, flower-like formations.

Around the corner, a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of the ice steam shower. The cooling phase of a hot-and-cold bathing ritual isn’t where most people want to linger, but these spaces make a compelling case for slowing down. Rather than treating cold exposure as something to endure, KLAFS creates immersive environments that make it part of the experience.

Klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Then there’s the foam. I also discovered foam steam baths, which replace the intensity of a traditional aufguss with a more playful, tactile experience. Steam rooms equipped for foam treatments can be integrated into hotel and spa programming as scheduled group experiences. The suds, reminiscent of childhood bubble baths and the elaborate foam sculptures they inspired, bring out a part of my inner child I had long since stowed away. Espuro, Klafs’s proprietary foam essence, is formulated with plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds, which the company says help care for skin exposed to heat.

Designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photography
courtesy of Klafs.

Beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. The retractable S1 sauna expands from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna, addressing the spatial constraints that often keep one out of the home. The design-led S11, a collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, pairs delicate washi paper and multicolor light panels with smooth, sinuous lines.

Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Long established in Germany, Klafs has been expanding into the American market since its acquisition by Kohler in 2024. The premium Altea fitness club in my city, for instance, features Klafs installations, including the Sanarium and Polaris Ice Room. Yet what stays with me after the visit isn’t a particular product. It’s the willingness to question what a sauna, steam room, or cooling space can be. At Klafs, even the most familiar wellness rituals seem open to reinvention.

Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

issues.title: Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide
issues.summary: From clever everyday objects to sculptural statement pieces, explore our favorite gifts for every budget and design sensibility.
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Good design makes a gift memorable, whether it’s a small object that solves an everyday problem or a sculptural piece worthy of display. And while great design doesn’t necessarily come with a hefty price tag, it does require a little thought.

For our 2026 holiday gift guides, we’ve gathered an eclectic mix of finds that celebrate creativity, craftsmanship, and unexpected details. From affordable stocking stuffers to considered splurges, these are gifts that bring something interesting to the table (or desk, shelf, or wherever they end up).

Explore our complete collection of 2026 gift guides below, and check back as we add more throughout the season.

Gifts for Every Budget

A good gift doesn’t have to be expensive, but it should feel considered. Our budget-friendly guides focus on products that deliver personality, functionality, and thoughtful design at a range of price points.

The Best Gifts Under $25 (That Don’t Look or Feel Cheap)

Small price tags, big design appeal. From playful accessories to practical little discoveries, these affordable finds prove that creativity and good design don’t have to cost a fortune.

The Best Gifts Under $100 for Design Enthusiasts

A little more room in the budget opens up plenty of interesting possibilities. Discover sculptural home accessories, clever everyday essentials, and unexpected objects that make the most of every dollar.

Gifts for Every Personality

Some people are easy to shop for. Others have very particular tastes. These guides take cues from how people live, work, and play, with gifts that reflect their interests and design sensibilities.

The Best Gifts for Minimalists Who Appreciate Good Design

For those who prefer fewer, better things, the details matter. These understated finds favor considered materials, clean silhouettes, and clever functionality, proving that simplicity doesn’t have to be boring.

The Best Tech Gifts for Design Enthusiasts

Technology can be practical, playful, and surprisingly good-looking. From inventive gadgets to thoughtfully designed digital essentials, these picks bring a little more personality to the world of tech.

More Good Gifts Are on the Way

We’re not done yet! We’ll be adding more gift guides throughout the holiday season, so bookmark this page and check back for fresh finds, unexpected discoveries, and a little more gifting inspiration.

issues.title: Tiffany & Co. Brings a Century of American Beauty to Crystal Bridges
issues.summary: From a 27-carat Arkansas diamond to intricate orchid brooches, Nature Adorned explores the relationship between nature, jewelry, and fine art.
issues.author: Misha Agostinelli
issues.content_html:
In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

The Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the company’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

An 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the company’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

Installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

“This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” says Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”

Inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

George Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

George Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s New Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

While Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the company’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”

Jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination is on view through Mar. 29, 2027, at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

issues.title: Carsten Höller’s Monumental Slides Bring Play to Mexico City
issues.summary: Four towering, functional slides connect different parts of Antara, where Sordo Madaleno’s latest expansion brings architecture, contemporary art, and public space together
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a new way to move between them.

The slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”

The installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A new 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

Art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a new location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

For SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he says. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”

The expansion also introduces more than 80 new retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

The new public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

issues.title: CAN combines eclectic references for eccentric revamp of London house
issues.summary: Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House-Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN. The post CAN combines eclectic references for eccentric revamp of London house appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Lizzie Crook
issues.content_html:
Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House-Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.

Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.

Drawings and exterior photos

    Drawings and exterior photos

    Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.

    Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons.

    “The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients' diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.

    “This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”

    Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.

    The resultant design inspired the project's name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.

    “We reject the idea that a project needs to be driven by a single, homogeneous idea or material,” said Barnes.

    “Instead, we celebrate the complexity, diversity and even contradiction inherent in our clients’ tastes and design references," he continued.

    "We see these different influences not as competing ideas, but as an opportunity to create something individual and ultimately more meaningful.”

    The focal point of the project is its highly unique rear elevation, with features including two towers of engineering drainage tubes, which break through a red-steel canopy that extends over the patio.

    Interior photos

      Interior photos

      Meanwhile, bright blue and red fibre-cement panels decorate its elevation, alongside portions of textured raked render and exposed concrete, punctured by irregular shapes.

      Details also include a metal sawtooth roof at first-floor level, alongside a bright yellow screen facing the neighbouring property to prevent overlooking.

      Finally, at ground level, a full-width set of doors open onto a patio with a winding perimeter, referencing the designs of Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx.

      "It brings together a mix of materials, forms and ideas drawn from the huge range of references the clients shared with us,” said Barnes. “I think it captures the character and personalities of the clients brilliantly.”

      Inside, the back half of the ground floor has been rearranged to maximise its connection to the rear garden. This is where the new open-plan kitchen, dining and living space is positioned.

      Meanwhile, at the front of the ground floor, the studio has created a secondary dining area and living space, and a children's playroom in the original lounge.

      Above, a void on the north side of the first floor has been filled to add a main bedroom suite, complete with an ensuite and roof terrace. Another bedroom has also been added.

      The roof terrace has a walk-on, diamond-shaped skylight, which sits directly above the dining table.

      Interior finishes echo the eclecticism of the exterior, with a bold mix of colours, materials and textures. This includes exposed steel joists and trusses, and a colourful timber kitchen with contrasting black tiles.

      Walls of ceramic tiles on the ground floorhave shell-like forms, handmade by Fabiane Lee-Perrella with glazing that shifts from pink to blue hues.

      A microcement floor runs throughout the ground floor and incorporates pebble inlay that evokes a river and is a nod to the water feature at SESC Pompéia.

      CAN hopes the project will highlight the importance of challenging the “established or standard way of doing things in a particular city or context”.

      “We think it's important to look beyond the usual architectural references and draw inspiration from unexpected places, whether that be sculpture, set design, or even infrastructure,” Barnes said.

      “These disciplines can offer entirely different ways of thinking about space, material and form. Ultimately, it's about exposing clients to these different ways of doing things.”

      Read:

      CAN adds fake mountain to Edwardian house in south London

      CAN, known fully as Critical Architecture Network, was founded by Barnes in 2016. Its previous projects include the equally bold house extensions Druid Grove and Mountain View.

issues.title: Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
issues.summary: They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo's pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades. In this interview for Dezeen’s 20x20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, […] The post Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo'
issues.author: Rima Sabina Aouf
issues.content_html:
They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo's pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20x20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20x20 series, launched to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we've seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a big impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a new wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier's Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

"Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” said Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful."

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play

Quickly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” said Abascal.

“And also how to plan for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all users.

“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” said Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a company after that.”

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she said.

“Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

Arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

“We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo said. “We analyse what's the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” said Abascal.

The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

“I’m the bad cop,” he says with a smile.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

“I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” said Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it's things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”

“And it's not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

“I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” said Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”

Lanza Atelier’s slate currently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on bird migration and pregnancy. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year plan – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

Read:

Ten stand-out projects by Serpentine Pavilion architect Lanza Atelier

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.

Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.

“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” said Abascal.

“I feel a sense of doing nothing,” said Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”

Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

“Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” said Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a big issue and will be forever for these big cities.”

There is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

issues.title: Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"
issues.summary: Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London's Design Museum. The post Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design" appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Jennifer Hahn
issues.content_html:
Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London's Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

"It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work," she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

"I was like: 'Oh, there hasn't been anything like that in the UK that I'm aware of,'" explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum's project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh says, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

"If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible," she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

"It's not like Black people weren't making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define," Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko's curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a "powerful place from which to examine the issues that will dominate the next century".

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

"I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again," Prempeh explained. "It's not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns."

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins's monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya's viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition's final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who's brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There's also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the "lack of curiosity around Blackness" – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

"I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative," she said.

The post Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design" appeared first on Dezeen.

issues.title: "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"
issues.summary: Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House highlights the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy. The post "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions" appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Aaron Betsky
issues.content_html:
Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong's buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta's just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks

There's only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

Read:

Five striking Snøhetta buildings that you can walk all over

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don't mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

The architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

Read:

"Getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they actually want to live is quite another"

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same issues that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can't easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

To be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many users, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma's Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers

That leaves only a deeper issue, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an "open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart" for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once said, "all conditioned space is conditional" and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Designand president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

Dezeen In Depth

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

The post "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions" appeared first on Dezeen.
