issues.title: Muse’s Matt Bellamy wants an AI guitar – but still calls for human-made art and live performance
issues.summary: An AI robot recently featured on their current UK tour The post Muse’s Matt Bellamy wants an AI guitar – but still calls for human-made art and live performance appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Damian Jones
issues.content_html:
Muse‘s Matt Bellamy has admitted that he would like his very own AI guitar.

READ MORE: Matt Bellamy on rediscovering his own muse: “I can’t live without music – that feeling came back to me on this album”

The band, who are constantly embracing futuristic technology, brought ‘The Wow! Signal‘ to The O2 in London for two nights earlier this week and with it an AI robot manning a sound desk adjusting controls as well as singing vocals on a reimagined version of ‘Kill Or Be Killed’, ‘JFK’ and delivering the now iconic drill sergeant speech intro to ‘Psycho’.

Speaking in a new interview with Guitar.com, Muse’s frontman spoke about the prospect of an AI guitar.

“I like the idea of trying to integrate AI components into guitars, where you can prompt a guitar to sound a certain way… I’d like to explore that,” he said. “I like the idea of trying to integrate some of that into guitar, so you can essentially talk to your guitar and tell it how you want it to sound. I’m not quite sure the tech’s there yet, but we’ll see!”

Bellamy added: “I’ve got a big bank of synthesisers, and it can sometimes take hours and hours to get a sound out of it – whereas the prompting synthesiser thing is interesting. The sound quality isn’t as good, but the interface is great, you know?”

“I like the idea of prompting something, but then something analogue happens – that’s interesting to me. I think that’s probably a long way to go before we get that into a guitar, but the idea of it is interesting.”

Despite that he went on to say that human-made art and live performance is something that will continue to be important in the future.

“I’m not that worried about AI music because I can already see a change with my kids,” he explained. “[The next generation is] gravitating towards the real so much more now, because half of what they see on their feeds is AI.

“So, for that reason, I think live music is going to be trending upwards, with real musicians playing. I think that’s what we’re going to be craving more than anything else, because it’s the only thing we know is real.”

Bellamy recently spoke to NME about his relationship with music and how it influenced their new album.

“That’s the thing with this album. I went through difficult personal life things this past year, so making this album reminded me of making music when I was a kid in my teenage years, back when music was everything. ‘I can’t live without music’ – that feeling came back to me on this album. Music became a lifeline again, a catharsis, the thing that I held on to, to hold on to my identity.”

He added: “In those early years, you didn’t have any success, you didn’t have any guaranteed tours happening or anything. It was just, ‘This is who I am, this is who I want to be, this is what I need to do to express myself…’

“Then you go through that success period. For the last 10 to 15 years, my life has generally been very good. Nice family, kids, blah, blah, blah. I’ve been through a few minor difficulties here and there, but generally speaking, music didn’t always become what I had to do; it was just what I chose to do. This has been an important album for me, both emotionally speaking with what it’s about, but it also reminded me again of why I got into music. It’s a little bit of a surprising late-stage renaissance.”

Elsewhere, Muse recently broke out the live debut of their Ellie Goulding collab ‘Hush’ during their second night at The O2.

While Goulding didn’t make a guest appearance on the night, she did appear on the screens, singing along to the song while looking straight into the camera, as Bellamy duetted with her playback vocals.

Muse’s UK and European 2026 arena tour continues with more shows in Milan tonight (November 20), Düsseldorf, La Defense, Amsterdam, Zürich and Montpellier. January 2027 will see the band call at Lisbon, Floirac, Madrid and Valencia, and over the summer they will go on to headline BST Hyde Park, Roundhay in Leeds and Cardiff’s Blackweir Fields. Visit here for tickets and more information.

‘The Wow!’ Signal’ was recently given a glowing four-star review from NME and praised as the trio’s “best album in 20 years”.

“In rekindling their own purpose, the Teignmouth trio have delivered undoubtedly their most consistent and satisfying album since ‘Black Holes & Revelations’ – doubling up as either a knowing gift to the fans or at least a response to any concerns that Muse had long disappeared too far up their own supermassive blackholes,” it read. “Look up to the sky with a sigh of relief or a simple ‘wow’.”

issues.title: The College Kids Who Drove a Duck Across the Americas
issues.summary: In 1961, nine young Americans set out to promote international friendship. Their adventures survive in a remarkable collection of letters. The post The College Kids Who Drove a Duck Across the Americas appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: April White
issues.content_html:
The DUKW was designed for war. The gray metal vehicle had six wheels, a rudder, and a propeller, an unlikely cross between a Jimmy deuce-and-a-half—as the standard GMC military truck was known—and a bulky metal scow. Between 1942 and 1945, more than 21,000 DUKWs came off the assembly lines in Michigan and Missouri. Called “ducks” by just about everyone, these land-water hybrids would carry troops and supplies to the beaches of Sicily and Normandy and countless other battle sites through World War II. Later they delivered the same cargo to the shores of Incheon, changing the tide of the Korean War.

And then in the summer of 1961, an aging DUKW from an Akron scrapyard became an unlikely symbol of peace in the midst of the Cold War.

“What I learn from this trip will make me appreciate life (especially with you) more.”

It was an adventure only a couple of college kids could dream up—a yearlong road trip across the Americas in a vehicle that had broken down five times on the drive from Ohio back home to New York. But “adventure was only part—a small part—of this trip,” Dan Twomey, one of nine men who participated in what they called Operation Americas, told a local newspaper. (The contingent also included his twin brother, Tom.)

For Twomey, who documented the odyssey in letters to his girlfriend Rosemarie Feuerbach, now shared by Drew University via JSTOR, the purpose was much bigger. The adventure was both a goodwill mission and a personal quest.

To the newspapers, Twomey explained that the goal was “friendship and understanding”—“meeting ordinary people, listening to their ideas and perhaps putting across the true American story was and is the sole purpose of this whole thing.”

“I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.” Click on the letter to take a closer look. “I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.” Click on the letter to take a closer look.

But to Feuerbach, Twomey confessed from Panama during a particularly challenging stretch of the trip that the “noble” reasons “really don’t mean as much.” “What I learn from this trip will make me appreciate life (especially with you) more,” he wrote. “I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.”

Their journey kicked off in August 1961 with a media tour, including an interview on Today. Over the next several months, the men and their DUKW—which was christened El Pato Valiente (“The Valiant Duck”) and painted with a cheerful Donald Duck in a mortarboard—would cross the United States, zigzag through Mexico, and ping-pong around Central America before finding themselves seemingly stuck in Panama.

Along the way, the men spent much of their time visiting college campuses, where they played guitar, performed silly skits, and challenged students on the basketball court. But Twomey credited most of the trip’s successes—and most of its troubles—to the DUKW itself.

“One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look.

Everywhere they went, the odd vehicle attracted curiosity. In Mexico City, the sight of a boat with wheels caused a traffic collision: “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!” In Juchitán, Mexico, it attracted a mob. As the men navigated the DUKW through the rough, narrow back streets of the community’s poor neighborhoods, “we had a crowd of about 50 people following us,” Twomey wrote to Feuerbach. When they stopped at a basketball court for an impromptu game, “In about 10 minutes there was a crowd of two to three hundred watching. Many of the people cheered for us.” (The DUKW crew lost 38–34.) By the time they reached Guatemala in mid-October 1961, Twomey reported that “people, crowds, unusual happenings are so commonplace, I feel like I’m repeating myself.”

“We had a crowd of about 50 people following us.” Click on the letter to take a closer look. “We had a crowd of about 50 people following us.” Click on the letter to take a closer look.

Maintenance on the DUKW was also unfortunately commonplace. In the first two weeks of the trip alone, there was a brake issue in New Jersey, a flat tire in Indiana, and a busted fan belt in St. Louis. But the real trouble came just before Christmas, one hundred miles from Panama City, when a busted motor required the US Army to step in, towing the immobile vehicle to the Canal Zone.

The men, the machine, and their mascot, a German shepherd named Robin who had joined the crew in Texas, would stay much longer than they intended in Panama. They needed to raise more money, first to fix El Pato Valiente and then for boat passage to South America, bypassing the impenetrable Darién Gap. In theory their duck could swim, but they’d been warned the waters would be too rough. Eventually, though, the men became impatient and decided to set off across the Caribbean to the northern coast of Colombia.

Their planned five-day voyage was doomed almost from the beginning. “For the first few hours everything went o.k.,” Twomey wrote. “Then the rudder cable broke.” The men had to steer by hand as waves washed over the DUKW, swamping the new motor and washing the survival gear overboard. Everyone was seasick, even Robin. They continued to limp along for a couple of days. “Then it happened,” Twomey wrote.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

“A loud noise told us something had gone wrong (broken) with our propeller,” he wrote. They beached the DUKW on an island off the coast of Panama, where it would stay for a week—delaying the men still further, but attracting ever more publicity to their travels. It even caught the attention of President Kennedy, who assured one frantic parent that the US government would help her stranded son, despite the administration’s previous misgivings about the trip. With help, the men eventually made their way to Colombia, spending another five months touring South America before returning to the United States.

More than 50 years later, Matt Twomey told the story of this more-than-an-adventure in a documentary titled Duck Diaries: A Cold War Quest for Friendship Across the Americas. In interviews and images, the film brings to life the amazing stories in the Drew University archives. And it provides a lovely coda to the tale: the filmmaker is the son of Dan Twomey and Rosemarie Feuerbach, who married a year after Dan’s return. When Dan Twomey passed away in 2024, his obituary noted that his time on the DUKW and the couple’s correspondence through Operation Americas had, as Twomey had hoped in 1962, “set the tone for a life full of adventures and global interest and inquiry.”

issues.title: The Stories That Make Thanksgiving
issues.summary: Turkey or Tofurkey? Stuffing or dressing? Whatever’s on your table, these Thanksgiving stories will satisfy your curiosity. The post The Stories That Make Thanksgiving appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: The Editors
issues.content_html:
Americans are getting ready to celebrate Thanksgiving, the middle entry in the Halloween-Thanksgiving-Winter holidays trifecta. Plate up with some table talk about the origins of the holiday, the reason we eat turkey, and what really makes people so sleepy after the annual meal. Extra fixings: all stories contain free links to the supporting academic research on JSTOR. Happy Thanksgiving!

How Thanksgiving took shape

Quakers Against Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 24, 2025 In colonial America, government “thanksgivings” blurred faith and politics. For Quakers, rejecting them was an act of religious conviction.

Why the Pilgrims Were Actually Able to Survive

Peter C. Mancall November 28, 2019 If you were reading Bradford's version of events, you might think that the survival of the Pilgrims' settlements was often in danger.

Thanksgiving Has Been Reinvented Many Times

Matthew Wills November 1, 2019 From colonial times to the nineteenth century, Thanksgiving was very different from the holiday we know now.

The Modern Invention of Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 26, 2014 Thanksgiving as we know it was deliberately invented in the nineteenth century.

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade: A History in Pictures

The Editors November 12, 2021 In 1927, the parade replaced live animals with helium balloons designed by puppeteer Tony Sarg.

Indigenous histories and living traditions

Translating Corn

Matthew Wills November 22, 2023 To most of the world, “corn” is “maize,” a word that comes from the Taíno mahizwas. Not for British colonists in North America, though.

Returning Corn, Beans, and Squash to Native American Farms

Christina Gish Hill November 24, 2020 Returning the “three sisters” to Native American farms nourishes people, land, and cultures.

How (Not) to Teach Kids about Native Cultures

Livia Gershon November 23, 2020 Even well-intentioned books for children can romanticize (or demonize) Native Americans. But better materials exist.

From turkey to tofu

Let’s Talk Turkey

Matthew Wills November 26, 2014 First of all, why the name "turkey?"

The Great American Turkey

Livia Gershon November 27, 2024 The turkey was semi-domesticated and kept in pens in the American Southwest some 2,000 years ago—but not for the reason you think.

Seven Things You Might Not Know About Cranberries

Matthew Wills November 21, 2018 They're red, tart, and mostly eaten at Thanksgiving. Love them or hate them, here are seven things you might not have known about the humble cranberry.

Vegetarian Thanksgiving Dates Back to the 1900s

Lina Zeldovich November 25, 2019 Tofu Turkey was created in 1990, but some Americans celebrated Thanksgiving with veggie dishes over a century ago.

The Real Joy of Mock Food

Livia Gershon November 8, 2019 "Wow, this really kind of tastes like turkey.”

Beyond the meal

Thanksgiving Is a Feast of Things Forgotten

Sarah McColl November 22, 2016 Thanksgiving is a feast so complex and semiotically dense that things are very often forgotten and rarely go according to plan.

What Does Thanksgiving Look Like in Prison?

Morgan Godvin November 23, 2021 Our American Prison Newspapers collection provides a peek at Thanksgiving celebrations in prisons throughout the decades.

Why Does Eating Food Make You Sleepy?

James MacDonald November 25, 2015 Your turkey is not to blame.

Synesthetic Adjectives Will Make You Eat Your Words

Chi Luu November 23, 2016 Fragrant. Sweet. Tangy. Certain synesthetic adjectives actually trigger cognitive simulations of eating.

It’s Time to Reinvent Food Waste!

Lori Miller Kase November 13, 2018 Startups worldwide convert refuse into energy, biomaterials, and more food.

A moment of gratitude

Eight Poems of Gratitude

The Editors November 23, 2020 Let us pause now and give thanks.

issues.title: The Great American Beer Wars
issues.summary: In the late nineteenth century, rival breweries slashed prices in a ruthless fight to dominate America's booming beer industry. The post The Great American Beer Wars appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Matthew Wills
issues.content_html:
Since wet grains ferment naturally in the presence of airborne yeasts, various forms of beer were likely discovered by multiple agriculturalists across the early farming regions of the world. The earliest archeological evidence of fermentation dates back 13,000 years. For thousands of years, beer was an artisanal product made at home, one that was sometimes safer to drink than the local water. Then the Industrial Revolution transformed beer into a mass-produced beverage.

German immigrants were largely responsible for bringing beer culture to the US. Anheuser-Busch, Pabst, Schlitz, Coors, and Yuengling, for instance, were all founded by German Americans. These giants of the industry today (minus Schlitz) emerged victorious from the wild and foamy “beer wars” of the late nineteenth century.

In one locally notorious case, a construction worker’s rented room collapsed from all the hoarded cheap beer he was storing against an inevitable price increase.

Historian Braden Neihart explores that ferocious competition in a case study of Rock Island, Illinois.

“Brewers fought constantly for market share on multiple fronts, through price dropping and undercutting each other with little concern for the immediate fallout. The end goal was survival, and the casualties along the way were the cost of sustaining business.”

In 1886, Rock Island’s three major local breweries produced a total of 80,000 barrels of beer. This was enough, Neihart figures, for an astonishing 800 beers per resident annually. Because this was well-above-average, the brewers were clearly finding additional markets in nearby towns like Moline as well as in Bettendorf and Davenport across the Mississippi in Iowa.

“Brewers operated within a fiercely capitalist market, restrained by few rules and characterized by high risk,” writes Neihart, noting that the competition was both homegrown and from big beer cities like Peoria, Chicago, and Milwaukee.

Locally, the Rock Island Brewing Company (RIBC) ended up buying its competitors, Atlantic Brewery, City Brewery, Rock Island Brewery, and Junge’s Bottling Works, by 1894. But then, in early 1895, Milwaukee-based Schlitz Brewing Company started rolling its barrels into town. On the road to becoming the nation’s largest beer producer, Schlitz dropped the price of its barrels from $6 to $4. The RIBC was forced to follow suit, though the price was ruinous for the company. The RIBC counterattacked with an advertising campaign to “Sustain Home Industry” and support local unions, which helped it weather the onslaught.

More to Explore

“Brewed with Blood”: The Coors Beercott of the 1970s

H.M.A. Leow June 12, 2026 An unusual coalition transformed a labor dispute into one of the longest-running consumer protests in US history.

Drinkers, on the other hand, celebrated; in one locally notorious case, a construction worker’s rented room collapsed from all the hoarded cheap beer he was storing against an inevitable price increase.

Another strategy was to challenge a competitor’s ingredients and hence impugn their purity. German immigrant brewers came with the tradition of the centuries-old Reinheitsgebot “purity order.” This stated that “beer” was to be made from water, barley, and hops. As a form of time-honored branding, this meant that if you added anything else, you could be called out for faking it.

Challenging the purity of ingredients still goes on, as Neihart notes. Anheuser-Busch spent $30 million during the 2019 Super Bowl boasting that its Bud Light was made from rice while Molson Coors’ products, Miller Lite and Coors Lite, were made from corn syrup. Molson Coors subsequently took Anheuser-Busch to court. The Court of Appeals, which hopefully didn’t have to do a taste test, said the companies were free to list each other’s ingredients.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

But back to the turn-of-the-twentieth-century strife and competition. It all came to a sudden end with the onset of Prohibition in January 1920. The Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution prohibited the “manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors.” The law crippled America’s robust beer industry and culture. Local brewers like the RIBC were driven out of business, but large factory producers had the wherewithal to pivot to legal “near-beers” and “soft drinks.”

The re-legalization of beer in 1933 left the field to the beer factories that had survived the dry years. Local beer-making didn’t really recover until the 1970s, when craft beer and the microbrewery movement began. These were in many ways a protest against the bland quaffs sold by the major players. More recent years have seen the rise of “nanobrewers”—very small operations producing beer for sale—because, like all those millennia ago, you can still brew beer at home.

issues.title: How WW2 pushed the world to the brink
issues.summary: Jonathan Fennell explores the social origins of a global catastrophe, revealing how ordinary people's hopes, fears and relationships helped shape the conflict that transformed the modern world
issues.author: Elinor Evans
issues.content_html:
In the 1930s, how did a world that many considered civilised collapse into barbarity? And how did ordinary people's hopes and fears across the globe help to drive the world towards catastrophe?

Drawing on a trove of wartime letters and reports on morale from across international archives, historian Jonathan Fennell offers a remarkable new perspective on the Second World War. In today's episode, he explains to Elinor Evans why we should look beyond the usual 1939 to '45 narrative, and towards a much more global picture.

issues.title: New psychology research sheds light on why certain pop song hooks stick in your head
issues.summary: New research in Psychology of Music indicates that repeated listening makes unfamiliar pop hooks feel more memorable, while verbal distraction dulls them. The findings offer clues into how earworms take hold.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
Listeners judge musical hooks in unfamiliar pop songs as more attention-grabbing and memorable when they hear the songs multiple times, while an auditory verbal distraction makes those hooks feel less catchy, according to new research published in Psychology of Music. Across two laboratory experiments, chorus sections consistently stood out over other parts of a song even when listeners were distracted, suggesting that catchy pop phrases rely on both songwriting structure and human memory and attention.

In popular music, a hook is a distinct melodic, rhythmic, or lyrical phrase that grabs a listener’s attention and sticks easily in memory, such as the repeating nonsense syllables in Kylie Minogue’s “Can’t Get You Out of My Head.” Because modern pop recordings layer vocals, drums, bass, and harmonies all at once, the brain cannot process every detail equally and instead filters for standout moments. Researchers think these phrases lodge in verbal working memory, the short-term mental workspace often described as an “inner voice” that lets people silently rehearse words and melodies.

Earlier music psychology research began tracing how repetition and attention shape this process, particularly in relation to earworms, the everyday experience of a musical snippet looping involuntarily in the mind. For instance, a 2015 experiment co-authored by one of the new study’s researchers found that playing unfamiliar songs repeatedly made those tunes more likely to resurface spontaneously later on. Meanwhile, a 2021 pair of laboratory experiments indicated that catchy songs occupy verbal working memory much like automatic mental singing, interfering with how well people perform unrelated verbal tasks.

Building on that work, a 2025 study led by the same researcher, Timothy P. Byron, and his colleagues asked listeners to rate short, isolated clips from famous pop songs directly. Participants consistently judged vocal lines, choruses, and phrases combining multiple hook elements as standing out and being most memorable, a direct-rating approach supported by a psychology review paper arguing that self-report measures often outperform indirect tests in capturing people’s thoughts and feelings.

Still, testing hit songs that listeners already knew made it difficult to separate whether a phrase felt catchy because of its musical design or simply because people had heard it countless times before. The new research, led by doctoral student Bethany T. Nixon and Timothy P. Byron of the University of Wollongong, tackled that problem by playing unfamiliar pop songs under controlled levels of repetition and distraction to see how both factors alter listeners’ conscious judgments of musical hooks.

“Pop music is a dominant music genre in many parts of the world, and musicians and musicologists talk about pop music being focused on ‘hooks,’ which are ‘catchy’ musical and lyrical phrases that are salient and memorable,” study co-author Timothy P. Byron, a senior lecturer in the School of Psychology at the University of Wollongong and co-author of the 2022 book “Hooks in Popular Music,” told PsyPost.

“We suspect that hooks are better at using our attentional and memory resources, but there is little research on why hooks stand out and linger in our memory. So we started with the question: if hooks are better at using our attentional and memory resources than other phrases, what happens to ratings of hooks if we make it harder to use those resources?”

In Experiment 1, 66 Australian undergraduate psychology students (52 women, 10 men, and four nonbinary or other participants, with an average age of about 20) listened to two of four unfamiliar pop songs spanning styles such as dance-pop and hip-hop-pop. The tracks were “LA in Two” by ELIO featuring Valley, “KEYS” by Neko Pink, “Hold Your Head” by Ruben Dawnson, and “Tangerine” by grouptherapy featuring Jadagrace and TJOnline. All four followed standard verse-chorus structure, had not appeared on the Australian Top 50 charts, and ranged from roughly 11,000 to 3 million worldwide Spotify streams at the time, with every participant confirming afterward that the songs were new to them.

Each participant listened to one assigned song once and the other five times, with song pairings and task order balanced across the group. During one song, participants solved easy printed sudoku puzzles while the music played, whereas during the other they simply listened. After those initial listens, participants heard each song one additional time without distraction, a rating pass that was not counted as an experimental repetition, making it either their second or sixth total listen. During that final listen, they moved an on-screen continuous slider from 0 to 100 in real time to indicate when parts of the song stood out and felt easily remembered, and they rated their overall enjoyment of each song on a 10-point scale.

Before analyzing the Experiment 1 data, the researchers switched from their originally planned statistical test to a mixed-effects model better suited to repeated measurements, retaining their initial sample-size benchmark of 54 participants, which the final group exceeded. Neither experiment was preregistered, and the underlying datasets were not posted publicly because participants did not consent to public data sharing, though the data are available from the authors upon request.

Repeated exposure boosted how strongly the songs registered with listeners: when participants rated a track on their sixth listen rather than their second, their hook ratings rose by an average of 6.76 points on the 100-point scale. Chorus sections received higher ratings than verses and other song sections, and participants who enjoyed a song more also gave higher hook ratings, with each 1-point increase in enjoyment linked to an average 2.33-point rise on the slider.

Contrary to the researchers’ expectations, solving sudoku puzzles while listening did not produce a statistically significant difference in hook ratings, and there was no statistically significant interaction between repetition and distraction. The authors propose that sudoku relies mostly on visual processing and may not have interfered directly with auditory memory, or that participants quickly caught up on details they had missed during the final undistracted listen while operating the slider.

“We had assumed that the Sudoku task in Experiment 1 would be a good distraction task, but it didn’t seem to distract participants from building up a coherent image of the music in their heads,” Byron said. “But in retrospect that makes sense – pop songs are often listened to as background music, so they’re probably often worming their way in while we’re not paying much attention to them.”

To test a distraction that competes more directly with music for verbal and auditory attention, the researchers conducted Experiment 2 with a larger recruited sample of 98 Australian undergraduate psychology students (79 women, 16 men, and three nonbinary or unspecified participants, with an average age of about 21). Seven participants were excluded from the analysis for already knowing the songs, leaving 91 in the analyzed sample. The team also changed how ratings were collected so participants would not receive an extra undistracted full listen beforehand, and added a 40-question survey, the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index, to check whether musical background shaped hook judgments.

Using the same four songs, participants listened either once or four times, once with no distraction and once while completing an auditory verbal memory test called the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. During the distracted condition, a researcher read aloud lists of 15 words and asked participants to recall as many words as possible across repeated rounds while the song played in the background.

Immediately after listening, participants heard 20 short, isolated clips (2 to 7 seconds long) extracted from each song using track-separation software, half featuring vocal lines and half featuring backing instruments. To capture a wider range of musical moments, Experiment 2 compared chorus clips against non-chorus sections broadly rather than verses alone. Participants rated each clip on a 7-point scale separately for whether it “stood out” and whether it was “easily remembered.”

In Experiment 2, both repetition and verbal distraction shaped how listeners judged the musical phrases. Hearing a song four times instead of once raised excerpt ratings by an average of 0.27 points on the 7-point scale, a small-to-medium effect, whereas completing the verbal recall task lowered ratings by an average of 0.85 points, a medium effect. Average ratings across the four experimental conditions were highest after four undistracted listens (4.71) and lowest after a single distracted listen (3.84).

As in Experiment 1, no statistically significant interaction emerged between repetition and distraction. Chorus clips also scored higher than non-chorus clips by an average of 1.10 points on the 7-point scale, a medium effect.

Musical background played only a modest role: after the researchers tested all subscales of the musical sophistication survey, only self-reported perceptual abilities and emotional engagement with music remained in the best-fitting model, showing small positive links that together accounted for roughly 10 percent of the variance in ratings. Participants also rated clips slightly higher on memorability than on standing out by an average of 0.24 points, with no statistically significant interactions across conditions, leading the authors to suggest that listeners may not sharply separate what catches their attention from what feels memorable.

In explaining why the word-recall test lowered ratings when sudoku did not, the researchers point to two possibilities. The verbal test may have competed directly for the same verbal working memory system used to encode music, or it may simply have placed a heavier overall mental load on participants than easy sudoku puzzles.

Even when listeners were verbally distracted, however, chorus sections maintained their overall advantage over other parts of the songs. “Our Experiment 2 found that repetition had a small effect on how participants rated excerpts, and that being distracted had a medium effect size. So if a phrase is an effective hook, it will get a fairly high rating from participants even if they heard it once while distracted,” Byron explained.

“So chorus excerpts on average got higher ratings than verse excerpts, no matter what condition – people were still rating catchy hooks pretty highly even if they were distracted during the one listen to the song they had. That said, ratings were shown to be significantly affected by distraction and repetition,” he continued.

The repetition findings align with an earlier behavioral and brain-imaging study, which similarly found that repeated exposure to unfamiliar melodies boosted how favorably listeners evaluated them, though that work examined musical liking and brain reward responses rather than ratings of how memorable or attention-grabbing musical phrases were.

Because hearing a song less often or while verbally distracted weakened how catchy its phrases seemed, the results also suggest a practical takeaway for anyone hoping to keep an unwanted song from looping in their mind. “We suspect that very catchy hooks play some role in earworms – songs getting stuck in your head – so this suggests that one way to avoid earworms is to avoid building up a coherent, clear memory of the song in the first place,” Byron noted.

There are a few caveats to keep in mind when interpreting the results. Both experiments relied exclusively on young Australian undergraduate psychology students who were predominantly female, so patterns of attention, musical multitasking, and memory may differ in older or more diverse groups. Because the researchers deliberately chose obscure tracks so participants would be hearing them for the first time, the hooks in these songs may not be as potent as those in major chart-topping hits, and self-reported ratings can blend unconsciously with simple liking rather than strictly reflecting salience and memorability.

“Sometimes people think there is just one hook in a song – but more than one phrase in a song can be shown to be salient and memorable,” Byron pointed out. “It is also important to remember that this study was conducted on a typical Australian undergraduate student population who were likely culturally familiar with the music styles in the [songs] we chose – pop music is popular around the world, but is quite diverse culturally and historically, and it seems likely that people with different backgrounds will have quite different reactions to these songs.”

In future work, the authors suggest testing listeners across broader age groups, cultural backgrounds, and musical genres outside pop, as well as systematically comparing visual and verbal distractions at different difficulty levels. Pairing self-report ratings with behavioral memory tests or physiological measures could also help show how musical hooks transition into involuntary musical memories.

“This research was originally motivated by trying to understand something more about the musical material that ends up as earworms, so the long-term goal is to understand what role these hooks play in songs getting stuck in people’s heads,” Byron added.

Running the experiments also came with an ironic side effect for the researchers themselves. “If you run an in-person study playing unfamiliar catchy music to participants, and hear them over and over again, you definitely will get those songs stuck in your head whether you like it or not!” Byron remarked.

The study, “Ratings of Musical Hooks in Unfamiliar Pop Music Are Influenced by Repetition and Distraction,” was authored by Bethany T. Nixon, Sara C. Hamden, and Timothy P. Byron.

issues.title: Acceptance and commitment therapy linked to neural shifts in the depressed brain
issues.summary: An eight-week therapeutic program aimed at improving psychological flexibility helped patients with depression reduce obsessive rumination. Brain scans show the therapy strengthened neural connectivity in regions responsible for emotional regulation.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy reduces depression symptoms and is associated with changes in brain activity in areas responsible for emotional regulation. Brain scans of adults with major depressive disorder showed that this specific therapeutic approach alters neural connectivity related to obsessive, negative thinking. The small study was published in Brain Imaging and Behavior.

Major depressive disorder is a widespread psychiatric condition that causes persistent sadness and a lack of interest in life. While antidepressant medications and traditional talk therapies help many people, a large portion of patients do not experience full recovery. Because of this, mental health professionals continue to explore alternative therapeutic methods.

One such method is Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. Unlike traditional cognitive behavioral therapy, which attempts to change the content of a person’s negative thoughts, this alternative encourages people to change their relationship with those thoughts. The goal is to build psychological flexibility so that patients can live a meaningful life even when experiencing internal distress.

A primary concept in this therapy is cognitive fusion. This happens when individuals treat their internal verbal thoughts as absolute truths or literal reality, rather than just passing mental events. For instance, a person might have the thought “I am a burden” and treat it as a factual reality, leading to psychological distress and avoidance behaviors.

Therapists use this framework to promote cognitive defusion, helping patients distance themselves from rigid thought patterns. While clinical trials show that the therapy works well for depression, the biological changes it produces in the brain remain largely unmapped. Brain imaging research on this specific therapy is scarce compared to traditional cognitive behavioral therapy.

To understand how this intervention physically affects the brain, researchers in South Korea organized a clinical trial. The investigative team included Sang Won Lee, Seungho Kim, Hyunsoo Kim, Yongmin Chang, and Seung Jae Lee from Kyungpook National University. They wanted to track neural activity before and after patients completed a specialized treatment program.

The research team recruited 42 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder. The researchers note that this relatively small sample size limits the generalizability and statistical power of the findings. Differences in baseline age and education between the participants were not statistically significant.

Half of the participants were randomly assigned to an eight-week, group-based Acceptance and Commitment Therapy program. The other 21 participants were placed on a waitlist. This waitlist group served as a baseline comparison to help the researchers measure the specific effects of the therapeutic intervention.

All participants underwent clinical evaluations and functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, before the eight-week period began. An fMRI scanner tracks blood flow in the brain to measure neural activity in real-time. During the scanning sessions, the researchers asked participants to complete a specific psychological task.

The task was designed to trigger cognitive fusion by forcing participants to merge their thoughts with real-world consequences. Before entering the scanner, patients provided the names of two people they felt close to, as well as two neutral acquaintances. Inside the machine, participants read negative statements involving these individuals.

For example, they were prompted to imagine one of their close friends or family members experiencing a severe car accident. The patients then rated the intensity of their emotional response using a simple scale and recorded how quickly they reacted. This exercise forces the brain to process distressing, imaginary scenarios as if they were actual events.

After eight weeks, both the therapy group and the waitlist group returned for a second round of psychological assessments and fMRI scans. The researchers then compared the pre-treatment and post-treatment data to look for biological and behavioral shifts.

The behavioral results showed that the therapy group experienced distinct improvements. Patients who completed the eight-week program reported a reduction in the severity of their depressive symptoms. They also displayed lower levels of cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance compared to their baseline scores.

During the imaginary accident task, the therapy group showed reduced emotional intensity. They also reacted faster to the negative prompts. The waitlist control group did not display these behavioral improvements, remaining relatively unchanged from their initial tests.

The brain imaging data provided a biological mirror for these psychological changes. The researchers observed increased activation in two specific brain regions among the therapy group. These regions are the medial prefrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate cortex.

The medial prefrontal cortex is located near the front of the brain and helps manage attention and emotional responses. The anterior cingulate cortex, situated deeper in the brain, plays a major role in emotional control and processing conflicting information. In people with depression, these two regions often show reduced activity during emotional tasks.

The therapy program appeared to boost activity in these regulatory centers. The researchers noted that higher activity in these areas correlated with a drop in depressive symptoms and obsessive thoughts. The faster reaction times during the scanner task also lined up with increased activation in these emotion-regulating zones.

Beyond overall activity levels, the researchers looked at how different parts of the brain communicated with each other. They found enhanced neural connectivity between the medial prefrontal cortex and a region called the posterior cingulate cortex. These linked areas are part of the brain’s default mode network.

The default mode network usually becomes active when a person is resting, daydreaming, or engaging in self-reflection. In depression, the default mode network is often associated with rumination. Rumination is the habit of continuously dwelling on negative feelings and past events.

The brain scans showed that stronger communication between the medial prefrontal cortex and the posterior cingulate cortex correlated with lower scores on a rumination questionnaire. By strengthening this neural pathway, the therapy may help patients break out of repetitive, negative thought loops.

While the results provide biological context for how the therapy works, the experimental design has several limitations. The trial compared the therapy to a waitlist group rather than an active alternative treatment. As a result, the researchers cannot state whether these neural changes are unique to Acceptance and Commitment Therapy or if they would occur with any form of structured psychological support.

Additionally, most participants continued taking their prescribed antidepressant medications throughout the eight-week study. The study could not completely isolate the effects of the talk therapy from the ongoing effects of the medication. The chemical influence of the antidepressants might interact with the behavioral therapy in ways the scans cannot fully separate.

The psychological surveys used to measure concepts like psychological flexibility and experiential avoidance also present measurement challenges. One of the questionnaires, the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II, overlaps with general feelings of distress, depression, and anxiety. This overlap makes it difficult to tell if patients truly improved their psychological flexibility or simply felt less distressed overall.

Finally, the researchers only measured outcomes immediately after the eight-week program ended. It remains unknown how long these brain alterations persist after the treatment concludes. Future studies with extended follow-up periods will be necessary to determine the long-term durability of these neural changes.

The study, “Neural correlates of acceptance and commitment therapy in major depressive disorder: a task-based fMRI study,” was authored by Sang Won Lee, Seungho Kim, Hyunsoo Kim, Yongmin Chang, and Seung Jae Lee.
