issues.summary: The post Freewell and Dunna Did It launch ultra-slim modular filter system for photographers and filmmakers appeared first on Digital Photography School . It was authored by Sime . We missed the launch of this one, but the pricing is GREAT right now, so thought we’d share for the guys at Freewell x Dunna Did It (and he certainly did, these look great!) A new locking filter system from Freewell and
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Freewell and Dunna Did It launch ultra-slim modular filter system for photographers and filmmakers appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

We missed the launch of this one, but the pricing is GREAT right now, so thought we’d share for the guys at Freewell x Dunna Did It (and he certainly did, these look great!)

A new locking filter system from Freewell and photographer and filmmaker Dunna Did It combines magnetic attachment with a mechanical locking mechanism, allowing photographers to share filters across lenses with different thread sizes.

Freewell has teamed up with photographer, filmmaker and YouTube creator Dunna Did It to launch a new modular camera filter system designed to make switching filters between lenses quicker and easier.

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System uses a combination of magnetic attachment and a mechanical locking mechanism. Rather than needing a separate set of filters for every lens, photographers can use a single collection of filters across lenses with thread sizes ranging from 49mm to 95mm, simply by changing the base ring.

The system is available in two configurations: a Videography Kit aimed at filmmakers and hybrid creators, and a Photography Kit designed primarily for still photographers.

One filter system for multiple lenses

Anyone with a growing collection of lenses will know that filter sizes can quickly become a bit of a headache. Even when lenses have similar focal lengths, their filter thread sizes can vary, potentially leaving you with multiple versions of the same ND or polarising filter.

Freewell’s new system aims to address that problem by separating the filter itself from the lens mounting ring.

A dedicated base ring attaches to each lens, with the filters then transferred between compatible rings. Magnets help guide the filter into position, before a short clockwise turn engages the mechanical lock.

The system supports ten filter thread sizes: 49mm, 55mm, 58mm, 62mm, 67mm, 72mm, 77mm, 82mm, 86mm and 95mm.

There are a few other interesting details worth noting:

  • Ultra-slim design: The fixed ND filters measure just 2.95mm thick and weigh 18.4g, helping minimise additional bulk and weight, particularly useful for handheld and gimbal-based video work.
  • Magnetic attachment with mechanical locking: Magnets help position the filter, while a short clockwise twist locks it in place.
  • Colour accuracy: Freewell says the filters are designed to minimise colour shifts, helping maintain natural-looking skin tones, greens and skies.
  • Stackable filters: Compatible filters can be used individually or stacked to combine different effects, including exposure control, reflection reduction and diffusion.

Two kits for different creative needs

The system launches with two kits, each offering a different selection of filters.

Videography Kit

Designed with filmmakers and hybrid shooters in mind, the Videography Kit includes:

  • ND4 (2-stop)
  • ND8 (3-stop)
  • ND16 (4-stop)
  • ND32 (5-stop)
  • Glow Mist 1/4

The kit also includes a selected base ring, protective caps (including one with built-in reference targets) and a fitted carry case.

The range of ND filters provides exposure control across different lighting conditions, while the Glow Mist filter adds a diffusion option for video and still photography.

Photography Kit

The Photography Kit takes a slightly different approach, with a selection of filters aimed at everyday photography and longer exposures.

It includes:

  • UV filter
  • ND64 (6-stop)
  • ND1000 (10-stop)
  • CPL (circular polariser)
  • Glow Mist 1/8

As with the Videography Kit, it comes with a selected base ring, protective caps and a fitted carry case.

The combination covers lens protection, reflection control, long exposures and a touch of diffusion without requiring multiple filter systems.

Developed in collaboration with Dunna Did It

The system was developed over nearly a year in collaboration with Dunna Did It, a photographer, filmmaker and music producer based on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

With an audience of more than 440,000 YouTube subscribers, Dunna regularly creates photography and video content, including gear reviews and tutorials.

The collaboration focused on refining the physical design and practical workflow of the system, including its locking mechanism, overall profile and ease of use when moving between lenses.

Pricing and availability

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System launched online on 26 August 2026.

Both the Photography Kit and Videography Kit have a launch price of US$299.99, reduced from the regular retail price of US$349.99.

Customers choose a base ring to suit their existing lens, with additional ring sizes available for use across the rest of their lens collection.

For more information, visit the Freewell product page or watch Dunna’s product introduction video on YouTube.

issues.summary: The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School . It was authored by Sime . Yes. That’s as simple as the answer need be, but that’s not the point of this article. Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just ann
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

Yes.

That’s as simple as the answer need be, but that’s not the point of this article.

Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just announced the Smartphone Xenon Flash A2, and their tagline is “Your phone, now a pro camera” which isn’t exactly factual, but also, the definition of “pro camera” is very loose.

The thing to keep in mind with ANY small light source is that its going to be harsh – there’s stuff you can do about it, though. You can diffuse it, bounce it (though a small light like the A2 might not give quite enough output to do much there) but even things like bouncing it off a close wall or even a sheet of paper in a pinch – use what you have, experiment.

I love the idea of small portable lights, this one is certainly an interesting addition to your phone photography – maybe worth giving a try, it’s certainly a good starter to your photography lighting journey.

Here’s the Godox Press Release (With a little bit of my own ramble)

Smartphone Photography, Now With More Zap

Phone cameras keep getting better, but low light, backlighting and mixed lighting can still make them sweat. Enter the Godox A2: proper pro-style lighting for your phone, with more control over your light and a lot more room to play.

Its short, punchy burst of xenon light freezes motion in its tracks, which is great for action shots and stylized looks.

Xenon Flash: Bring Your Subject to Life

Go bold with direct flash, or add a subtle lift to a backlit portrait. With a guide number of roughly 15 (ISO 100, metres), the A2 has plenty of oomph for close-range shots. When flash is your main light, that quick burst also helps freeze movement. *For best results, keep the A2 within 2 m of your subject. Want more power or wider coverage? Pair Godox’s upcoming smartphone wireless flash trigger (sold separately) with Godox speedlights or outdoor flashes.

TTL and Manual Modes: Stay Spontaneous, Get Precise

Fast and flawless when the moment’s fleeting, or hands-on when you want to flex your creative muscles. TTL and Manual modes have you covered both ways.

High-Speed Sync: Find Your Balance

Why banish that bright background when it can star in the story? With high-speed sync up to 1/8000s, the A2 lets you control ambient exposure while lighting your subject. Balance a face against a sunlit scene, or go for a faster shutter speed to keep the action crisp.

Bi-Color LED: True Color for Everyday Stories

Truer colors and flattering skin tones make portrait videos look natural and beautifully textured. Low light or indoors, the results feel authentic and ready to share. Your content doesn’t just look good, it feels right, and it’s always social-media ready.

Godox Camera App: Your Look, at Your Fingertips

Find your look right on your screen. Built on Godox’s TTL know-how, the Godox Camera app keeps exposure simple in Auto (A) mode, with Natural, Even and Contrast flash effects to try out. Feeling fussy? Switch to Manual (M) mode and tweak shutter speed and flash output yourself. Bluetooth with NFC-assisted setup lets you adjust flash and LED settings wirelessly, on or off camera.

Dual-Side Magnetic Mounting: Snap On, Explore New Angles

The A2’s dual magnetic design isn’t just for the back of your phone. Snap it to any metal surface or pop it on a stand and you’re ready to roll. On the front, the magnetic ring lets you attach accessories to shape the light exactly how you like. Simple, flexible and always creative.

Magnetic Accessories: Change the Light, Set the Mood

Go moodier and more dramatic with optional extras like a honeycomb grid, barndoors or a snoot to aim your light and tame the spill. Add a touch of warmth with a full CTO magnetic filter. *For best results, use the A2 off-camera with light-shaping accessories.

Compact. Magnetic. More Ways to Light.

Pro flash power in a palm-sized body. Pocketable, portable and happy to go anywhere you do.

Four Colors, A Style of Your Own

The A2 brings pro lighting to your phone in four distinctive colors. Pick a finish that suits your everyday style, and make your kit as personal as the photos you take.

issues.summary: The post Do people still print their photographs? appeared first on Digital Photography School . It was authored by Sime . The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Do people still print their photographs? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is still printing out their photographs?

We celebrated my dad’s life recently, and at the wake my brother had printed out a couple hundred photographs that showed the life and times of dad and those he cared about. There’s something very real about having a print you can hold in your hand, nothing to log in to, no computers to boot up, just a square of paper and your memories.

Before we share this press release, here’s a challenge: In the next couple of months, aim to have one of your photographs printed, and to take that one step further, I was just listening to a clip from a podcast (You can see it here) Print Swap, what a great idea, print one of your images and send it to someone – to have and to hold.

Right, the Godox P100, it’s not an A3 Epson printing onto some beautiful Canson Rag, but it’s WITH YOU, you can print images and have them. (I’ve been grabbing frames with the beautiful FujiFilm Instax Mini 99 which prints a little 45x62mm photo)

On with our press release, please keep in mind we have not tested the P100 ourselves.

Godox Introduces P100 Portable Color Photo Printer

Godox has announced the P100 Portable Color Photo Printer, a compact dye-sublimation printer designed to turn digital images into physical prints wherever you are.

The P100 uses 300 dpi high-precision dye-sublimation printing, with 1,256 printhead heating elements and support for 16.7 million colours. According to Godox, the combination is designed to produce smooth colour gradations, fine detail and vivid colour reproduction.

Each print also receives an automatic protective overcoat, helping protect the finished photo from dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion.

Print and personalise from your phone

The P100 connects to the Godox Cam APP via Bluetooth, while NFC tap-to-connect provides another quick way to pair the printer.

From within the app, users can capture and print photos directly, or work with images already on their device. Creative options include filters, frames, stickers and templates, along with tools for creating ID photos and collages.

The app also allows users to check remaining paper and battery levels, making it easier to keep track of the printer’s status.

Designed to travel

With its compact design and lightweight construction, the P100 is intended to be easy to take along to parties, family gatherings, housewarmings and other everyday occasions.

Rather than leaving photos sitting on a phone or buried in a cloud library, the P100 gives users a simple way to turn them into physical prints that can be displayed, collected, added to a scrapbook or shared with friends and family.

Automatic protection

The P100’s automatic lamination process adds a protective overcoat to every finished print. Godox says this helps protect prints against dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion, as well as humid conditions.

The process happens automatically after printing, so there is no additional lamination step for the user.

All-in-one cartridge

The P100 uses an all-in-one photo paper cartridge, designed to make replacing the printing supplies quick and straightforward.

Combined with wireless connectivity and the Godox Cam APP, the system is designed to keep the process from capturing a photo to holding the finished print as simple as possible.

A physical home for digital memories

The P100 is ultimately aimed at something increasingly familiar in photography: we take plenty of photos, but relatively few ever make it off our phones.

By combining portable dye-sublimation printing with a range of simple editing and personalisation tools, Godox says the P100 is designed to make printing those images easier, whether you’re sharing them with friends at a gathering or simply putting a favourite photograph somewhere you’ll actually see it.

The Godox P100 Portable Color Photo Printer is now part of Godox’s expanding range of photography accessories.

You can get them online for around $200 Aussie, do a Google and see what you can find!

Don’t forget, PRINT YOUR WORK.

issues.summary: Plus: Joyce Awards winners announced, Agnes Gund's gift to art in schools, and Derrick Adams and LEGO make a splash in Miami.
issues.author: Valentina Di Liscia
issues.content_html:
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence

The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

issues.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M
issues.summary: The 1920 painting smashed its original sale estimate and the previous benchmark for a work by the Swedish forebearer of abstraction.
issues.author: Anna Lee
issues.content_html:
Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million)at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

issues.title: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
issues.summary: Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy.
issues.author: Eileen G’Sell
issues.content_html:
ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Born and raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4, and at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition was curated by Meredith Malone and James McAnally.

issues.title: Was Grandma Moses a Foil to Modernity, or a Product of It?
issues.summary: Her landmark survey is on view at Crystal Bridges.
issues.author: Emily Watlington
issues.content_html:
Grandma Moses’s landmark survey at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Arkansas opens with a flash of fire. A scene of a bridge burning in Troy is ablaze in red and orange; another painting, Fire in the Woods (1940), crackles with flames and smoke. This emphasis on fire, thunderstorms, and extreme weather in the first room seems to be an anticipatory rebuke to any potential complaints about Moses’s relentless good cheer. Despite a long and often sorrow-filled life—Anna Mary Robertson (“Grandma”) Moses lost five of her 10 children in infancy—Moses held fast to life’s joys in her art, and most of the paintings in the show are happy scenes of work, celebration, and family.

Starting with fire does prime the viewer to recognize the heat of Moses’s oeuvre, an intensity she channeled into careful, repetitive marks—tidy stacks of hay, carefully shaded leaves, the checkered grid of farm fields. Cambridge Valley (1942) is a scene of steady eye, mind, and hand, an expansive view of the New York countryside rendered with lovingly topographic attention. There’s almost no loss of detail as you look across the valley, a result of Moses’s unhurried care. People appear in nearly all her works, simply rendered and adding elements of humor, like a man’s hat blown off by the wind in 1948’s The Thunderstorm, a perfect “O” flush against the picture plane. The fire returns, however, in Moses’s many maple sugaring scenes, flames licking the base of large pots in which sap is boiled down. Even snow scenes are made to sparkle, radiating light through Moses’s use of glitter, a new technology she applied amply to her canvases against the advice of her dealer.

Moses was no stranger to patient work, having spent her life on farms in New York state and Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. Her memory of these years provided ample subject matter for the painting she took up in her late 70s, though one of the claims of the exhibition was that Moses was making art her whole life. A fireboard from 1918 was what she called her first “large picture,” while yarn pictures from the 1930s show her capacity to work with a limited palette of solid colors. These craft activities, usually cordoned off from the realm of serious art, gave Moses a point of entry into visual representation as a way of telling her own story.

Spanning 101 years, from 1860 to 1961, her life story ran parallel with a century of massive transformation and the rapid emergence of a modern, industrial world. That her style and subject matter remain largely unchanged over the course of her decades-long painting career—the 80 some works in the show have more similarities than differences—suggests Moses’s indifference to the revolutions happening around her. Instead, the exhibition catalog argues, Moses was in dialog with changing notions of the elderly, the increasing representation of labor in 20th-century art, and Cold War politics that sought to export a vision of American goodness.

Was Grandma Moses a foil to modernity, or a product of it? While her work eschews direct portrayals of industry, she reportedly solved the compositional dilemma of capturing sprawling valleys by glimpsing a reflection in a hubcap, introducing the gleam of the automobile into what feel like entirely timeless views. Her art was held up by contemporaries as an example of the “primitive,” exhibited as the quaint musings of an aging farmwife. She seemed to give America a soul, something it appeared to be lacking in the postwar era of big capital. And yet she amassed quite a lot of capital herself, through lucrative partnerships with Hallmark among other companies. She was media-savvy, appearing on talk shows and in documentaries, leveraging the perceived powerlessness of a little old woman to charm and disarm her critics. In the end, there’s nothing more modern than nostalgia for the lost authenticity of the countryside, an authenticity Moses returns us to in her sincerely merry paintings.

issues.title: Christie’s Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy
issues.summary: “The estimates were too high for this market,” dealer Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn said, on her way out of the sale.
issues.author: Brian Boucher
issues.content_html:
Christie’s finished out New York’s fall auction week on Thursday evening at its Rockefeller Center salesroom, bringing in $145.9 million in a 56-lot sale of 21st-century art (after works by Jeff Koons and Ed Ruscha, estimated to sell for as much as $11 million between them, were withdrawn). Leading the sale was a $32.9 million Jean-Michel Basquiat painting that fell just shy of its low estimate.

The sale included 20 works from the collection of Antonio Homem, longtime director of the storied Sonnabend Gallery, which was founded by his adoptive mother, Ileana Sonnabend. Sold to benefit their foundation, the works totaled $41.9 million. Also on offer were 10 works from the estate of beloved New York philanthropist Agnes Gund, who died last year, totaling $25.7 million.

After the withdrawals, the sale was estimated to bring between $126 million and $192 million; the hammer total on the night fell considerably shy at $117.7 million. Over the two-hour sale, the house found buyers for 51 lots, for a sell-through rate of 91 percent. Works by John Currin, William Eggleston, Wade Guyton, Gerhard Richter, and Yayoi Kusama failed to sell.

Many prominent advisors were in the room, including Erica Barrish, Amy Cappellazzo, Ralph DeLuca, and Gabriela Palmieri, as well as well-known dealers like Marianne Boesky, Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn, and Christophe Van de Weghe. But there were a notable number of empty seats, and the atmosphere was unmistakably enervated after a long week of sales.

The sale started inauspiciously, with the first 19 lots, all from the Sonnabend collection, failing to hammer above their estimates. Bidding picked up only on the final lot of that trove, Jean Prouvé’s Table “Centrale” (“Trapèze”), petit modèle. The piece sold after five minutes of bidding between several specialists and a bidder in the room, before Sara Friedlander, Christie’s chairman of postwar and contemporary art in the Americas, nabbed it with a winning bid of $1.3 million. With fees, the total came to $1.7 million on a $700,000–$1 million estimate. But, all told, 10 of the 20 Sonnabend lots hammered below estimate. The collection hammered for $33.4 million, or $41.9 million with fees, against a pre-sale estimate of $35.25 million to $53.15 million (minus the withdrawn Koons, Wild Boy and Puppy). Not great any way you slice it.

The most notable of the Sonnabend works was Andy Warhol’s 1962 painting Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), tagged at $6–$8 million. The soup cans show one of Warhol’s most iconic images and are practically synonymous with Pop art. Adrien Meyer, global head of private sales and the auctioneer at Tuesday evening’s 20th-century sale, traded bids with a bidder in the room, who nailed it down with a $7.3 million bid, translating to $9 million all in.

Also from the trove was Roy Lichtenstein’s Large Spool (1963). Standing nearly six feet high, the work had been off the market since the Sonnabends bought it from Leo Castelli Gallery four years after it was painted. It has hung in museums all over the world, and its sale comes amid a major Lichtenstein retrospective at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art. Auctioneer Yu-Ge Wang tossed out a handful of absentee bids from the rostrum before Friedlander got it for her client with a $7 million bid, for a total of $8.6 million with fees. The work’s pre-sale estimate was $10 million to $15 million.

Jeff Koons’s six-foot-high sculpture Hulk (Friends), 2004–12, also from the Sonnabend collection, shows the comic-book hero with small creatures perched on his shoulders and was estimated at $3.5–$5.5 million. It hammered after only a few bids at $3.3 million, or $4.15 million with fees, to the house’s Michael Baptist. (Koons was also a seller this week, bringing seven artworks to auction at Christie’s on Tuesday night, totaling $104 million.)

Bidding improved marginally from there, but for the most part, this was a sleepy sale. Even the biggest attraction of the night, Basquiat’s much-touted painting Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), which dates to 1983 and measures seven feet square, failed to generate much excitement. Wang opened the bidding at $23 million, and for a few long moments it seemed there would be no bids. Then Ana Maria Celis, head of postwar and contemporary art, rescued the painting, beating out Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president and global chairman of 20th- and 21st-century art. It hammered at $28 million and sold for $32.9 million with the house’s fees.

The hammer price was just shy of the $30–$50 million estimate. But the work, inspired by a sketch by Leonardo da Vinci, had been off the market for two decades, so the seller no doubt made a tidy profit. The painter’s auction market has famously exploded in the intervening years: every one of his paintings to sell for more than $10 million, all 83 of them, has done so since then.

The large canvas, featuring the artist’s trademark scratchy messages and the titular sketchy heads against an orange background, had appreciated enormously since its previous trips to the block. It appeared at Sotheby’s London in 2000, when it fetched just above $400,000, within estimate, and again at the same house five years later, when it tripled in value to bring an above-estimate $1.3 million.

Vija Celmins’s 1990 painting Untitled (Ocean) was one of the few lots of the evening to generate a genuine bidding war. The painting came from the Gund estate; Gund bought it the year after it was painted. It drew bids from Joanna Szymkowiak, head of private sales; Arco Yu, a Christie’s Hong Kong specialist; and a woman bidding in the room. For four minutes, the three traded incremental bids until the room bidder won out. Still, that brought the hammer to only $5.75 million, just under the $6 million low estimate. With fees, the total came to $7.1 million.

The 10 Gund works fared better than those from the Sonnabend collection, hammering for $20.4 million on a $16.95 million to $24.65 million pre-sale estimate. With fees, the total squeaked past the high estimate to reach $25.7 million.

There wasn’t much rhythm to the proceedings. A 1990 Gerhard Richter Abstraktes Bild painting from the estate of legendary art dealer Marian Goodman, who long represented the artist and bought the work from him that year, carried a $6 million to $8 million estimate. It failed to sell after garnering no bids. Three lots later, another Abstraktes Bild, from 1991, measuring three feet square and dominated by red, blue, and green, sparked a short contest between Friedlander and Rotter. Rotter eventually won it with a $7.6 million bid. With fees, the total came to $9.4 million. The painting’s pre-sale estimate was $7 million to $10 million.

“The estimates were too high for this market,” Greenberg Rohatyn told ARTnews on her way out of the salesroom partway through the night. “We need to readjust, and the houses need to be at the forefront of managing expectations.”

Boesky agreed that the estimates were too high. “And the energy was low,” she said on her way out. “The lots that were estimated too high were punished, and those estimated low were rewarded.”

On a brighter note, a few records were notched: Jim Nutt ($1.1 million), Antonio Santín ($486,400), and Julia Jo ($409,600).

The Jo, a swirling, gestural abstraction of fiery oranges and yellows breaking against cool blues and teals, was the night’s final lot, estimated at $30,000–$50,000. Sold to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, the abstraction generated arguably the most spirited bidding of the evening. Wang opened bidding at $20,000, and it quickly climbed into the hundreds of thousands as a cacophony of specialists and a bidder in the room called out bids. It eventually went to the room bidder at a hammer price of $320,000, or $403,200 with fees. That set off a hearty round of applause, at least for one lot.

The sale finished out an auction week that started Monday with a two-part $378.7 million Sotheby’s auction including works from cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum as well as a various-owner The Now and Contemporary sale. Christie’s staged a nearly three-hour 20th-century sale on Tuesday that totaled $626.6 million, led by a record-breaking $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The same night, Phillips sold $104.4 million in modern and contemporary art on Tuesday, led by a $44.6 million Amedeo Modigliani sculpture. On Wednesday, Sotheby’s staged a $777.8 million Impressionist and modern art sale, led by a record-breaking $190.4 million Vincent van Gogh.

issues.title: The Landing, Beloved Los Angeles Gallery with a Keen Eye for Pairing Historical and Contemporary Artists, Closes After 14 Years
issues.summary: Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.
issues.author: Maximilíano Durón
issues.content_html:
The Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was defined by its unique pairings of historical and contemporary artists, announced that it had closed. Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.

On the gallery’s website, founder and owner Gerard O’Brien wrote, “the Landing Gallery at 5118 W Jefferson Blvd is now closed. We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.”

In an Instagram post, Gerard O’Brien put it more simply, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Galley 2004-2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012 -2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”

O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an off-shoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a big difference,” he said of the distinction between art and design. He chose the name for its original location, a spot within Reform: “he cleared out the landing atop a short staircase in his furniture gallery and dedicated it to shows of art, bringing in work by artists both contemporary and historical to display just above his design wares,” as a 2016 blog post by book publisher Phaidon reported.

In 2015, O’Brien decided that it was time for the Landing to grow, opening in a 2,800-square-foot gallery space on Jefferson Boulevard with a solo show for the late California artist JB Blunk.

Over the years, the Landing would become known for its pairings of historical and contemporary artists. At the time of its closing, its roster included four deceased artists (Jeremy Anderson, Richard Bowman, Leslie Kerr, and Fred Reichman) and five living contemporary artists (Yevgeniya Baras, Ryan Fenchel, Matt Phillips, Jonathan Ryan, and Amanda Valdez).

The gallery was also known for regularly staging off-kilter group exhibitions, with titles like “Rat Bastard Protective Association” (2016), “The Useful and the Decorative” (2017), “New Iconography: Artists Raising Children” (2021), and “Consensual Ennui (2023). The first of these, “3 Women” (2016) took its name from a 1977 Robert Altman film as a way “to create a cross-generational dialogue that explores the intersections of craft and fine art, influence and homage,” per a release. It featured the work of Lenore Tawney from the 1960s and ’70s paired with textile pieces by Tanya Aguiñiga and paintings by Loie Hollowell. The exhibition marked the first time Tawney’s work had been exhibited in LA in nearly 50 years.

In an Artforum review, Erin Kimmel wrote, “The Landing’s handsome, restrained exhibition showcased the exquisite detail of [Tawney’s] works, which reward prolonged scrutiny with seemingly boundless formal revelations.”

To mark its 10th anniversary at its Jefferson Boulevard space, the Landing mounted a two-part anniversary exhibition. The first part, which opened in November 2025, focused on contemporary art and design and featured the work of Ruth Asawa, Wallace Berman, Bruce Conner, Lyne Foulkes, and Doyle Lane. The second part, which opened this past April, featured gallery artists as well as others who had exhibited there, including Brenda Goodman, Sam Jablon, and Lukas Geronimas.

In a release for part one, O’Brien wrote, “10 Year brings together the feeling of the earliest days of the Landing Gallery when two years of exhibitions took place inside Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue. Exhibiting art in a salon style in dialogue with decorative arts is how tL began.”

The Landing’s closure is the latest in an extended wave of closures that began in mid-2025. Los Angeles galleries have particularly been affected, with Murmurs, the Box, LA Louver, and Blum all shuttering, along with the LA outposts of Marian Goodman Gallery and Tanya Bonakdar.

In his statement on the gallery’s website, O’Brien added, “While our gallery doors have closed, our commitment to art and artists continues. Watch this space for news of future offsite exhibitions, activations, and special projects. Thank you for being part of the Landing’s ongoing narrative.”

issues.title: Frieze Abu Dhabi Debuts to Brisk Sales and Confident Dealers
issues.summary: The art fair had a strong participation pull with private collectors and institutions spending liberally, from sold out booths to a seven-figure sale.
issues.author: Hikmat Mohammed
issues.content_html:
On the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The crowd in Abu Dhabi, at least, had other things on their minds: the fair was about to open, with millions of dollars’ worth of art ready to be sold. Members of the royal family were back after getting a sneak peek yesterday, alongside politicians and celebrities including tennis star Venus Williams and architect Kulapat Yantrasast.

“It’s about time. Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews, cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects.

The dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening. At Thaddaeus Ropac, three of Imran Qureshi’s Water Bodies sold for $60,000, each to a UAE-based collection, though the gallery declined to specify whether this was a private or institutional collection.

“There is a great energy around the fair in Abu Dhabi this week. We’re having good conversations with collectors who are well-informed about the artists we are presenting, and you can feel the impact of the institutional scene here,” Xenia Geroulanos, director at Thaddaeus Ropac, told ARTnews.

The fair is under the umbrella of Frieze and has rebranded from Abu Dhabi Art fair, and attendees are noticing a difference. The exhibitor list has been streamlined to 89, down from 142 last year. Dealer Asmaa Al-Shabibi told ARTnews that when she walked through the fair’s new entrance, it felt “a little bit like going into Frieze London, and it feels like a different fair.”

Samy Ghiyati, co-founder of art advisory NG Partners, agreed. “The quality is definitely higher, and galleries made an effort to bring very good inventory. Usually fairs in the region are slower and sales happen over the course of several days,” he told ARTnews.

One of Ghiyati’s clients placed three orders on pieces ranging from $10,000 to $400,000. Within an hour of opening, dealer Sundaram Tagore had already placed two works on hold, one by Hiroshi Senju and another by Chun Kwang Young, ranging from $40,000 to $400,000. By late afternoon, Timothy Taylor had sold its entire solo presentation of paintings by Hilary Pecis to institutional and private collections in the region and internationally, to the price of $65,000-$205,000. The London-based antiquities gallery David Aaron sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele for a seven-figure sum to a private collector, while Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects also sold out its booth of mosaic works depicting 70s-era architecture in Abu Dhabi.

Regional collectors reportedly spent big at Frieze Abu Dhabi. Iris Projects sold two works by Shamsa Al Omaira, a sculpture acquired by a new foundation in the UAE for $32,000 and an acrylic on canvas by Juma Al Haj for $20,400. UAE-based collectors also bought two ceramics by Eman Al Hashemi, priced at $17,000 and $15,000, an oil pastel on linen by Dhabia Al Qubaisi for $10,500, and a photograph by Ammar Al Attar for $12,500.

By then, Lawrie Shabibi had sold seven pieces by artists Hamra Abbas and Shaikha Al Mazrou, priced from $10,000 to $120,000. “People are recognizing the work when they’re coming here,” said the gallery’s cofounder Asmaa Al-Shabibi, referring to a new client who bought a work by Al Mazrou, who has a solo exhibition at the Cultural Foundation.

Rayan Ben El Mlih, sales and marketing manager at Waddington Custot, told ARTnews that a large contingent of collectors with reserves hailed from Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Qatar and Bahrain. The gallery brought works by Etel Adnan, Sophia Vari and Fabienne Verdier.

Dealers noted that local collectors, some of whom began their collections by acquiring Western artists, are now deepening their collections with more historical pieces by regional artists.

“We’ve been seeing European collectors diversifying their collections, too,” said Ghiyati. Dubai’s Carbon 12 sold a painting and a sculpture by 28-year-old artist Sarah Al Mehairi, as well as two works by Mexican artist Edgar Orlaineta, priced between $17,570 and $35,000 (€16,000-€32,000).

“We’ve engaged mostly with collectors that we’ve cultivated relationships with for a while, and this is our home fair,” Judy Karkour, associate director of Carbon 12, told ARTnews.

Collectors are branching out beyond SWANA this year, with notable interest in art from the African continent and its diaspora and Latin America. Meanwhile this year’s Frieze Masters section is dedicated to trade across the Indian Ocean, taking its cues from the Louvre Abu Dhabi’s current exhibition “Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean.” An hour into the fair, Efie Gallery had placed two works by Malian artist Abdoulaye Konaté on reserve, both priced between $45,000 to $65,000, in addition to two works by Cuban artist Maria Magdalena Campos Pons ($27,500-$55,000).

“Frieze Abu Dhabi has got off to a strong start for us with a high volume of enquiries in the first few hours from both institutions and private collections,” Kwame Mintah, cofounder of Efie Gallery, told ARTnews, which specializing in artists of African descent. “One of the more encouraging developments across the Gulf has been the gradual maturation of its collecting community, accompanied by a growing appreciation for artistic practices beyond established geographical and institutional frameworks,” he added.

At Daniel Crouch Rare Books, a private collector bought the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832. While dealer Daniel Crouch declined to say how much the map sold for, he priced the booth’s total value between $10,073 and $1.19 million (AED 37,000 to AED 4.4 million).

“Abu Dhabi is becoming a cultural hub in the region with a lot of development,” Crouch said. “It’s the logical place to come to for dealing in the larger Indian Ocean region and the Louvre Abu Dhabi exhibition has attracted quite a lot of attention—we’ve obviously jumped into it with alacrity.” London-based antiquities gallery ArtAncient, carrying pieces ranging from $5,000 to $5 million, sold a collection of shipwreck jewels for an undisclosed sum—the gallery also had a visit from Venus Williams, who was admiring the Graeco-Roman mummy portrait Portrait L, which had recently been dubbed the “Mona Lisa of the Middle East.”

Throughout the opening, the blue-chip-leaning powerhouses, including Gagosian, Pace Gallery, Thaddaeus Ropac, and Victoria Miro, boasted crowded booths. Gagosian’s dedicated Roy Lichtenstein booth became the step and repeat for many visitors—the gallery said it “placed many” orders without revealing specifics.

Judging by its debut, Abu Dhabi has become a no-brainer stop on the art fair calendar. The emirate is slowly integrating into the art circuit. Earlier this month, Christie’s hosted its first fine art auction there, with Sotheby’s own version due next month, joining a colorful lineup of events that includes the Formula 1 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Finance Week and Culture Summit Abu Dhabi.

Several dealers cited the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi’s upcoming December opening with the strong pull to participate in Frieze Abu Dhabi, characterizing the museum as a bridge between West and East.

“The Guggenheim is going to open now in the next few weeks, it’s literally where contemporary art gets space to breathe and to grow,” said Milo Gatti, fair coordinator at Galleria Continua.

issues.title: Dramatic Waves Crash on Iceland’s Coast in Photos by Vilhelm Gunnarsson
issues.summary: Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas on the Reykjanes Peninsula. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? The article Dramatic Waves Crash on Iceland’s Coast in Photos by Vilhelm Gunnarsson appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson, Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.

Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it. Explore a larger archive on Instagram.

issues.title: A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work
issues.summary: "He was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat." Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.

As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

issues.title: Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York
issues.summary: A blockbuster solo show in New York has people lining up down the street. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center, where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.

Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.

Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery, 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.

Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.

Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake. The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.

As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”

The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.

issues.title: ‘We’re Still Here’ Celebrates Remarkable Quilts by 15 Contemporary Black Artists
issues.summary: "Black history is American history," says curator, historian, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article ‘We’re Still Here’ Celebrates Remarkable Quilts by 15 Contemporary Black Artists appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising.

Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson—the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.

For quilter Rosy Petri, Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery.

The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network (WCQN), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.

L’Merchie Frazier’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix—in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.

In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”

We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release, Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers.

The exhibition “Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective” will be the first major U.S. museum exhibition of her work in more than 20 years. The show will comprise roughly 200 artworks and archival material drawn in part from the Estate of Ana Mendieta. On vi
issues.author: Katie White
issues.content_html:
The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) has announced a major exhibition of the Cuban-American interdisciplinary artist Ana Mendieta, opening in December 2027. The exhibition “Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective” will be the first major U.S. museum exhibition of her work in more than 20 years.

The show will comprise roughly 200 artworks and archival material drawn in part from the Estate of Ana Mendieta. On view from December 12, 2027, through April 15, 2028, the show is organized by Beverly Adams, curator of Latin American Art at MoMA, and Sophie Cavoulacos, film curator, with Caitlin Chaisson as curatorial associate. The last major American retrospective of the artist was “Ana Mendieta: Earth Body, Sculpture and Performance,” organized by the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in 2004. Currently, a major retrospective of Mendieta’s work is on view at the Tate Modern in London, through January 2027.

"Ana Mendieta rigorously investigated the physical, conceptual, and emotional potential of materials like soil, sand, water, blood, leaves, wood, and fire to create images that speak across time and geography,” Adams said in a statement. “In doing so, she redefined the boundaries between sculpture and action, object and image, and private and public.”

Cavoulacos framed the show within Mendieta's biography, with her work in nature unfolding alongside an investment in artist networks across the places she lived and traveled, from the University of Iowa, to Latin American diasporic circles in 1970s New York, to the return to Cuba in the early 1980s. “From a contemporary perspective, her legacy remains at the center of conversations about migration, exile, race, gender, and identity,” noted Adams.

Born in Havana and sent to the U.S. at age 12 through Operation Peter Pan following the Cuban Revolution, Mendieta studied at the University of Iowa, where she began as a figurative painter before moving into the performative body art and land art for which she became known. The exhibition will open with early paintings, including an untitled work from the early 1970s that will be shown in New York for the first time. The exhibition will then follow Mendieta’s practice in the experimental Intermedia program at the University of Iowa, where she frequently collaborated with German-born Hans Breder, her former professor and longtime romantic partner.

The exhibition will also focus on her best-known body of work, the “Silueta” series (1973–80), in which she staged her body or its imprint across natural environments in Mexico and Iowa. Later sections will highlight her “Esculturas Rupestres” (Rupestrian Sculptures), which she carved into the landscape of Cuba's Parque Jaruco in 1981 during one of her first return trips to her home country, as well as her public commissions in New York, and the sculptures and ink-wash drawings she made during her 1983–85 Prix de Rome residency. The show will trace Medieta’s practice up until she died in 1985 at age 36.

issues.title: 8 Irving Penn Photographs for Vogue That Explain His Lasting Influence on Fashion
issues.summary: Jessye Norman, New York, 1992, 1992 Irving Penn Thaddaeus Ropac The history of fashion photography has few clear turning points. Irving Penn is one of them. Throughout his nearly seven-decade career, the American photographer developed a visual language that transformed the way fashion was photographed. This year, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) in Paris celebrates its 30th annivers
issues.author: Zeynep Gülçur
issues.content_html:
Jessye Norman, New York, 1992, 1992
Irving Penn
Thaddaeus Ropac

The history of fashion photography has few clear turning points. Irving Penn is one of them. Throughout his nearly seven-decade career, the American photographer developed a visual language that transformed the way fashion was photographed.

This year, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) in Paris celebrates its 30th anniversary with “Penn & Fashion,” a major exhibition tracing Irving Penn’s distinctive approach to fashion photography throughout his six-decade collaboration with Vogue.

Bringing together works from the museum’s collection and international loans from the Irving Penn Foundation, the Nicola Erni Collection, and the Miyake Issey Foundation, the exhibition shows how fashion evolved during this period through Penn’s lens: the changing face of the industry, from its designers and models to the silhouettes and styles that defined each era.


Born in 1917 in Plainfield, New Jersey, to Russian immigrant parents, Penn studied graphic design at the Philadelphia Museum School of Industrial Arts. There, he trained under Alexey Brodovitch, the art director of Harper’s Bazaar, who introduced him to the possibilities of modern design and photography. Penn later worked as Brodovitch’s assistant before moving to New York, where he took on various art direction jobs.

A turning point came in 1943, when Alexander Liberman, Vogue’s art director, hired him as a graphic designer to work on layouts and cover ideas for the magazine. Liberman soon recognized Penn’s photographic talent. Speaking at the press preview, the exhibition’s curator, Pascal Hoël, put it simply: “Liberman encouraged him and let him do whatever he wanted.”

Penn quickly established himself as one of Vogue’s most distinctive photographers. His assignments took him around the world, but he increasingly favored the controlled environment of the studio. Rather than relying on elaborate sets or decorative backgrounds, he used simple backdrops and carefully arranged lighting to bring attention to his subjects. The result was a style that was instantly recognizable, defined by its mastery of composition, contrast, and meticulous attention to detail.

He was deeply involved in the printing process, experimenting with techniques and carefully overseeing the production of his work. Hoël explained, “All the photographs presented in the exhibition were printed by Irving Penn himself.” For him, the final print was an essential part of the work.


Over the decades, his photographs stripped away much of the artifice traditionally associated with fashion imagery, allowing silhouette, gesture, texture, and form to speak for themselves.

Penn’s collaboration with Vogue lasted 66 years, from his first credited photograph in August 1943 to his final publication in August 2009. The photographer died in October of that year at the age of 92.

Here, Artsy highlights eight photographs that reveal why Irving Penn’s fashion photographs remain some of the most influential of the 20th century.

Man Lighting Girl’s Cigarette (Jean Patchett), New York, 1949

Standing Woman with Braids, Cuzco, 1948

Harlequin Dress (Lisa Fonssagrives-Penn), New York, 1950

Girl with Tobacco on Tongue (Mary Jane Russell), New York, 1951

Balenciaga Rose Dress, Paris, 1967

Issey Miyake Fashion: Face Covered with Hair, New York, 1991

Woman in Feather Hat, New York, 1991

Bee on Lips, New York, 1995

issues.summary: Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky ’s Betonte Ecken (Accentuated Corners) (1922–23), sold for $85.8 million with fees at Christie’s 20th-century evening sale in New York on November 17th, setting a new auction record for the artist. Bidding opened at $54 million, a price already about $10 million above Kandinsky's previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sothe
issues.author: Artsy Editorial
issues.content_html:
Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken(Accentuated Corners) (1922–23), sold for $85.8 million with fees at Christie’s 20th-century evening sale in New York on November 17th, setting a new auction record for the artist.

Bidding opened at $54 million, a price already about $10 million above Kandinsky's previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sotheby’s in 2023. Three bidders competed for the work, including art advisor Ralph DeLuca. Ultimately, Christie’s global president Alex Rotter won the painting for an anonymous client at a hammer price of $74 million.

The painting, estimated at $60 million to $80 million and backed by a third-party guarantee, was consigned by the Nahmad family, which purchased it at Sotheby's New York in 1986 for a hammer price of $1 million.

The nearly four-foot-square abstract composition, painted during Kandinsky’s early Bauhaus years, has a storied provenance. It was acquired in 1929 by Hilla Rebay, who became the Guggenheim Museum’s first director. She gave it to the museum in 1941. The Guggenheim deaccessioned it, along with dozens of other Kandinskys, at Sotheby’s in London in 1964. There it was sold to New York dealer Stephen Hahn before passing to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar and then to the Nahmads.

The other star lot of auction night was Gustav Klimt’s Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), which sold for $82.3 million. It came into the sale as the highest-estimated lot of the evening. Together, the Kandinsky and the Klimt accounted for nearly 27 percent of the sale’s total of $626.6 million ($521 million at the hammer). The evening auction closed at the low end of its $511 million to $743 million estimate range. The sale itself was uneven and selective. Other lots included a group of seven small Jackson Pollock paintings, a 1915 Amedeo Modigliani portrait, and a Léger canvas, all of which went unsold. An 11-foot bronze horse by Fernando Botero, meanwhile, set an artist record at $5.2 million.

Kandinsky has had a strong year at auction. Born in Moscow in 1866, Kandinsky helped found the Blaue Reiter group, taught at the Bauhaus in Germany, and later had dozens of his works seized by the Nazis as “degenerate art” before he died in France in 1944. Earlier this October, Christie’s London sold the artist’s 1907 painting Das bunte Leben for £31,560,000 ($41.5 million).

issues.title: 5 Artworks We’d Gift Ourselves this Holiday Season
issues.summary: Shopping for an art lover is hard. Shopping for yourself is harder: Even if you’ve been saving and wishlisting all year, it’s easy to be overwhelmed. So we sorted our holiday gift list by collector type. Meet the Tiny Treasure Hunter , the Analog Enthusiast , the Dopamine Decorator , the Surrealist at Heart , and the Plant Parent : five collections for five art lover identities. Then we asked our
issues.author: Artsy Editorial
issues.content_html:
Shopping for an art lover is hard. Shopping for yourself is harder: Even if you’ve been saving and wishlisting all year, it’s easy to be overwhelmed.

So we sorted our holiday gift list by collector type. Meet the Tiny Treasure Hunter, the Analog Enthusiast, the Dopamine Decorator, the Surrealist at Heart, and the Plant Parent: five collections for five art lover identities. Then we asked our team to pick one work from each that they’d gladly give, or keep for themselves. Here’s what they chose.

Marlon de Azambuja, Mundo, 2025

Instituto de Visión

Price: $1,500

From: The Tiny Treasure Hunter

Mundo, 2025
Marlon de Azambuja
Instituto de Visión

I’ve always loved tiny things, from dollhouse furniture to small dogs, so The Tiny Treasure Hunter is very much a collecting identity that resonates (and full disclosure, I helped curate it). It’s full of gems, like a beach scene painted on a slice of toast and a little gold ceramic alien who looks like E.T. But at the top of my wish list is Mundo (2025), a thumbprint-sized snail shell by Spanish Brazilian artist Marlon de Azambuja.

It’s made of concrete, the pale gray stuff of smooth sidewalks, yet it looks delicate and organic. The sculpture was recently featured in “Light Field,” de Azambuja’s fall exhibition at Instituto de Visión in New York, which explored how small interventions can transform our perception of space. Mundo does just that: At just over an inch and a half tall, it hangs on the wall like a tiny talisman, as if resting before slithering off.

I love shells of all sorts but snails bring me back to childhood—they’d emerge after it rained and we’d go looking for them to collect them. “Mundo” of course means “world,” and so I’m also reminded that snails appear in creation myths across cultures, symbols of renewal and the cycle of life. I love how this tiny sculpture can hold an entire world of meaning and still it’s just such a delight.

—Casey Lesser, director of editorial and content


Herman Leonard, Louis Armstrong, Paris, 1960

Ellen Miller Gallery

Price: $5,000

From: The Analog Enthusiast

Louis Armstrong, Paris, 1960
Herman Leonard
Ellen Miller Gallery

There’s something quite wonderful about seeing Louis Armstrong like this. Not on stage, trumpet raised, nor posing with that signature warm smile, but sitting quietly, a hand resting on his instrument, seemingly lost in thought. I was actually listening to Armstrong’s 1957 album Under the Stars recently, and was reminded how his music can make even an ordinary evening feel magical.

Herman Leonard—who was to jazz photography what Mick Rock was to ’70s rock—took this photograph backstage at the Olympia Theatre in Paris in 1960. Armstrong was in the city performing and filming Paris Blues, which also starred Sidney Poitier, Paul Newman, and Duke Ellington (worth a watch!). I love that it captures a rare moment of pause in the life of someone whose music and energy brought so much joy to the world.

We see the man behind that magic. There’s a warmth to it, despite the black and white, and something deeply human about seeing him in this unguarded moment.

I’d hang it near a record player, or somewhere to unwind with a drink and some good music. For the music lover in your life, it makes a personal and timeless gift.

—Arun Kakar, senior art market editor


Patrick Hughes, Dancing, 2017

Flowers

Price: £600 ($789)

From: The Dopamine Decorator

Dancing, 2017
Patrick Hughes
Flowers

One of my most-played songs of 2025 was Robyn’s dancefloor banger named after the thrill hormone dopamine, so this collection really speaks to my need for a little visual joy. That also applies to the art that surrounds me. Whether it’s Sarah Morris’s massive neon print with a message or a cartoon-quoting aluminum wall sculpture by Andreas Stylianou, it’s hard not to be drawn to works that immediately lift you up and send you on a high.

Patrick Hughes’s “Rainbows” series is all about that high: in screenprints and paintings he rearranges the typical colorful arc from its spot on the horizon into unlikely scenarios. When a rainbow appears, after all, it brings an immediate hit of dopamine, both in the spontaneity of a one-off moment, and the optical pleasure of every color transitioning into a new one. In Dancing (2017), Hughes repurposes two rainbows as legs against a shocking blue sky, with a shiny red high-heel pump on the end of each. I love how they seem to saunter across the cloudless background, sassy and glamorous.

—Josie Thaddeus-Johns, editor in chief


Johanna Seidel, Sweetwater (II), 2026

Galerie Laetitia Gorsy

€3,900 ($4277)

From: The Surrealist at Heart

Sweetwater ( II ), 2026
Johanna Seidel
Galerie Laetitia Gorsy

The end of the year always takes on a strange dimension, with the days blending together into a blur and waves of the year’s memories flooding back to mind. During these long nights of winter, the magical possibilities of talking animals or women floating through the skies don’t seem so farfetched. This collection of Surrealist-inspired artworks taps into my end-of-year reverie in just the right way. From the chimerical, whimsical beasts of French artist Jacques Merle to a delightfully comical snake-like lady by Lebanese artist Annie Kurkdjian, there are more than a handful of works in the collection that I’ve been pining over.

But it’s German artist Johanna Seidel’s Sweetwater (II) (2026) that I kept returning to, with its uncanny depiction of a brown-haired girl submerged up to her neck in water, ringlets of hair haloing around her, and a swan swimming behind her. The sky is a wash of wild pinks and purples of dawn or dusk. The painting is in keeping with Seidel’s hazy, poetic imagery which draws from history, mythology, and dreams. Here, she references the myth of Leda and the Swan, as well as John Everett Millais’s famed painting Ophelia (1851–52), the tragic heroine of Shakespeare’s Hamlet. Sweetwater (II) is both beautiful and dreamy, but also a deeply uncertain image. Is the swan a friend or foe? In that sense, I think the painting captures some of my own amorphous hopes and anxieties as we head into a new year.

—Katie White, senior staff writer

Nourhan Tchelebi, Bouquet de tulipes jaunes, 2026

L’Original

Price: $445

From: The Plant Parent

Bouquet de tulipes jaunes, 2026
Nourhan Tchelebi
L'Original

During the pandemic, while many people were baking focaccia and sourdough, I picked up a different domestic hobby: raising plants. I’d buy them online and have them shipped across the country so I could nurse them back to health on my windowsill. That changed when I adopted my cat, Martini, who quickly decided he was also interested in gardening and began digging up all of my succulents. No more plant adoptions for me.

Now, to bring plants into my home, I have to get creative. This collection reminded me of all the ways I can add shades of green, bright botanicals, and dappled light back into my life. My favorite work from the bunch is Bouquet de tulipes jaunes (2026) by Nourhan Tchelebi. I love the shape of the work (no need to find a frame!), which is bold and clean, contrasting the hazy strokes and soft outlines of the tulips themselves. The colors also stand out—plants are never just green, and the blend of blues, greens, and yellows in the leaves and the backgrounds makes this bunch feel particularly alive. I’m also drawn to the happy, oversized heads of the tulips themselves, forever at full bloom. I’d put this piece by my windowsill (bright indirect light is best, I hear) to mark the start of a new collection of plants that never need to be watered (and can’t poison my cat).

—Sydney Gelman, copywriter
