issues.title: Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states
issues.summary: In at least four states, hyperscale facilities account for 10 percent or more of the electricity sold.
issues.author: Clayton Aldern
issues.content_html:
It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet translating “a lot” to real numbers pinned to individual facilities requires usage data, something that data-center operators are loath to disclose.

A Harvard-led study published this week in Nature Sustainability gets us closer to these numbers. Researchers extracted locations and building footprints for as many U.S. hyperscale data centers as possible, ultimately cataloguing 403 of the warehouse-sized facilities across the country. Translating power capacity to theoretical electricity usage, the authors estimated these facilities gobble up roughly 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes. They suggest this electricity is associated with about 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

The 82-TWh estimate corresponds to about 2 percent of U.S. electricity. Though noteworthy in its own right, that figure shrouds high state-to-state variability, with many states boasting data-center electricity shares in the double digits. When viewed as a fraction of the retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) in 2024, Oregon’s studied data centers used the equivalent of 18.6 percent of the electricity sold in the state. In Virginia and Iowa, data centers consumed 15.5 and 13.1 percent, respectively.

Hyperscale data centers used nearly one-fifth of Oregon’s electricity in 2024 Estimated electricity use of 403 hyperscale data centers as a share of each state’s 2024 retail electricity sales, top 10 states Guidi et al. (2026) model data-center electricity use from May 2024 to April 2025. We compare these data with metered sales from calendar year 2024. Source: Guidi et al. (2026) / EIA Clayton Aldern / Grist / İsmail Enes Ayhan / Unsplash

While data-center electricity consumption remains a national issue, electricity prices and utility planning look very different from state to state. And the speed of hyperscale buildouts mean these figures can change quickly.

In Oregon, for example, the state’s data-center share of electricity use grew from about 3 percent in 2015 to about 23 percent in 2025, according to analyses presented to the state by energy economics firm ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia. The group estimated that data centers were associated with approximately 96 percent of the state’s electricity sales growth between 2020 and 2025.

Hyperscalers can “no longer be understood as a marginal component” of Oregon’s electricity demand, the authors wrote — and in the Wild West of hyperscaling, it’s a component poorly matched to current regulatory structures. In its most recent biennial energy report, the Oregon Department of Energy noted that the state “currently lacks a policy mechanism to address emissions from data center load growth.”

Data centers’ share of Oregon’s electricity rose from 3 percent in 2015 to 23 percent today Estimated electricity use of Oregon’s data centers as a share of retail electricity sales Source: ECOnorthwest / UVA Weldon Cooper Center / EIA Clayton Aldern / Grist / Kirill Sh / Unsplash

Many states are grappling with the ramifications of recent data-center buildouts. Because the Harvard study was limited to hyperscale facilities the authors could verify, its electricity-use estimates are likely undercounts. In Virginia, for example, the study’s 142 included facilities account for about 15 percent of the state’s electricity sales — itself a staggering sum. But Dominion Energy, the largest seller of electricity in the state, has estimated that data centers purchased 28 percent of the electricity its Virginia subsidiary sold last year.

Currently, there is no federal apparatus to track or check these figures, as surveys of utilities’ sales tend to label customer segments as merely residential, commercial, industrial, or transportation-related. In March, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley wrote to the EIA, arguing: “Without this data, policymakers, utility companies, and local communities are operating in the dark.” The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the infrastructure permitting bill currently under consideration in the Senate, would direct the agency to explicitly measure data-center electricity usage.

Hyperscale electricity can also be understood in terms of the plant-warming gases emitted during its generation. Together, the facilities catalogued by the Harvard researchers emit more annually than the carbon-dioxide equivalent of countries like Jordan, Kenya, and Guatemala.

State context matters here, too, since emissions estimates depend on a given state’s grid, which vary by energy mix. The Nature Sustainability study’s authors used federal power-plant data to estimate the average per kilowatt-hour emissions for each confirmed data center. The resulting rates range from Washington’s hydropower-heavy 10 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour to Virginia’s fossil-fuel-backed 325.

Read Next What’s behind your eye-popping power bill? We broke it down, region by region. Naveena Sadasivam & Clayton Aldern

Yet even grid averages fail to capture the growing phenomenon of on-site power plants. Frequently gas-fired, these generators are built at or near hyperscale campuses to generate electricity directly for the data centers themselves. Electricity usage from on-site power can be harder to measure, given it is often “behind the meter” — that is, the electrons might never touch a public grid. As of June, about 2 GW of gas generators powered four data centers around the country, including Elon Musk’s xAI sites in Memphis, Tennessee. There are 143 GW of gas plants currently proposed to power data centers around the United States, according to the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP), a watchdog group.

Most of this proposed on-site power could push the hyperscale buildout outside the Harvard study’s map. West Virginia, for example, hosts exactly zero of the data-center campuses confirmed by the Nature Sustainability study. Yet the state is second only to Texas in proposed on-site gas capacity, with more than 15 GW tagged by EIP.

If built, these projects could reshape the geography of U.S. data centers — and make their electricity use less visible in utility-sales and grid-demand data. Behind-the-meter power doesn’t show up as utility purchases.

Most gas proposed for data centers is in states with little hyperscale capacity today Existing data-center capacity and gas proposed to power data centers directly, gigawatts by state Logarithmic scale. Proposed gas is each plant’s full capacity, including plants that would also sell power to the grid, as of April 30, 2026. Source: Environmental Integrity Project / Guidi et al. (2026) Clayton Aldern / Grist

It’s possible many of these proposed plants will never actually break ground; only about two dozen of the 74 proposed plants tagged by EIP are currently permitted for construction under the Clean Air Act. Yet if the recent supercharged data center build-out offers any indication, applications for new on-site facilities will continue to roll in.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the Nature Sustainability study, in a statement. Forget 2 percent: The electricity and emissions estimates offered by his team “could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states on Nov 20, 2026.

issues.title: Is it OK to want a ‘normal life’ during the climate crisis?
issues.summary: A home, a family, a vacation — therapist Leslie Davenport weighs in on how to reconcile life goals with guilt and fear about climate change.
issues.author: Leslie Davenport
issues.content_html:
“I would love to be a parent, but I worry it is unethical to bring children into a world that is wrecked by climate change.”

“It feels kind of silly to be bothering with working a normal job and planning for retirement in some distant future, given the overall circumstances.”

“Sometimes I feel hypocritical, working toward a better, more sustainable future while not fully reflecting those values in my own daily choices.”

“My partner and I are thinking about buying our first home together and becoming parents. How can I make plans for the future in a world that is unravelling?”

In the many questions we’ve received through the Ask a Climate Therapist form, I’ve noticed a theme running through several of them. People longing to have children, but grappling with the ethics of that decision. People wanting to enjoy occasional travel or an omnivorous diet, but feeling the sting of guilt. People hoping to plan for retirement or home ownership, but unsure how to reconcile those long-term visions with their fears and doubts about our climate future.

I’d sum it up like this: Knowing what we know about the climate crisis, and knowing that we each must do our part to contribute to a liveable future, is it OK to want to enjoy life, too?

Ask a Climate Therapisttackles your questions about how to navigate the emotional side of climate change, with leading climate-aware therapist Leslie Davenport. Have a question? Ask it here!

Climate change is a systemic problem, but the choices we make in our own lives still matter as we push for large-scale change. Some choices are more impactful than others — but it’s important to remember that guilt isn’t a very discriminating guide.

A practice for distinguishing guilt from true impact

Pick one or more of the decisions that’s been bothering you or causing guilt. Sit with it for five quiet minutes and then ask:

  1. Whose voice is this?
    Sometimes guilt helps you see your true values. Sometimes it’s a voice you’ve internalized from a friend, a parent, a headline, or a stranger online.
  2. In reality, how large are my impacts?
    Do a little research — and remember to zoom out. Rather than agonizing over one flight, for instance, consider how often you’re flying and what guidelines you might want to set for yourself there, or elsewhere.
  3. Is it a one-time or built-in impact?
    Decisions that lock in years of extra emissions — like where you live and how you get around — are where personal choices matter the most.
  4. What does this choice offer me?
    Name it honestly: connection, security, rest, love. These personal values count.
  5. Is there a more sustainable option that also keeps alive the most meaningful connections?

When a choice comes out heavy in impact and light in meaning, it’s worth changing. When it comes out light in impact and full of love, put the guilt down. Most choices land somewhere in between, and that’s where question five supports you the most. Keep what matters and adjust what you can: Buy the house and plan its first upgrades around efficiency. If you have kids, let raising them bring your family into your community’s climate efforts. When you’ve stopped agonizing over the decision, you can put the energy you’ve freed up where it counts the most: advocating within your sphere of influence, showing up for local policy meetings, voting, and talking honestly about climate with the people in your life.

A warming world asks you to pursue your dreams more intentionally. It doesn’t require you to abandon them. A home, a family, time away — these things already look different for everyone, and what counts as “normal” or aspirational may shift, but the wish for a place to belong and people to love is an ancient human drive.

I’d even go so far as to say that life is what we’re fighting to protect when we work for a healthier, safer, and more just future.

Rest, joy, and your love of life are what will make a lifelong commitment to the planet possible. In my experience, the people who stay engaged for decades always make time for what matters most to them. So take the trip and let yourself relax and rejuvenate. Love deeply. Then come home and continue to defend our planet, where your dedication will help shape the future for all of us.

In this with you,
Leslie

I’m Leslie Davenport, a licensed therapist, educator, speaker, consultant, and internationally recognized voice on the emotional and psychological dimensions of climate change. If you’ve got a question about climate and mental health, please consider submitting it for a future column. Submit a question for a future Ask a Climate Therapist column

issues.title: Even the ‘good guys’ of AI are locking in fossil fuels
issues.summary: Anthropic claims to be developing AI safely. Why doesn’t its own climate impact make the cut?
issues.author: Kate Yoder
issues.content_html:
Anthropic became one of the most valuable companies on the planet on Wednesday, valued at $1.5 trillion after its IPO. Known as one of the “good guys” of AI, Anthropic was founded by employees who left OpenAI over disagreements about ethics and safety. But despite the company’s emphasis on responsibility and preventing AI from killing everybody, one thing you don’t hear Anthropic talking about much is its contribution to climate change.

Ahead of the initial public offering this week, Greenpeace accused the company of “asking average investors to join them in throwing the planet into the climate furnace.” AI data centers are causing electricity demand to soar and fueling a surge in natural gas plants. A recent report found that the biggest data centers in the United States emit about as much carbon dioxide as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark. Anthropic is contributing to that: It reportedly signed a $3.4 billion deal with the Texas-based company OnePWR Solutions in September to power data centers with gas-fired engines — the largest known single purchase of its kind by an AI lab.

“It signals what direction they’re taking very clearly,” said Charlie Cray, a senior strategist at Greenpeace USA. The company is locking in fossil fuels at a time when scientists say the world is certain to overshoot the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees C. Anthropic’s reputation for being the most responsible of the AI giants means it should be minimizing its climate impact, Cray argued: “Show the world that you can do it better.”

The company has been lauded for focusing on safety and “alignment,” trying to ensure that AI acts in accordance with human values — or as its website puts it, “training Claude to be helpful, harmless, and honest.” Earlier this year, Anthropic got into a dispute with the Pentagon when it refused to give the Department of War unrestricted use of AI for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. This summer, Dario Amodei, its CEO, called for the government to regulate the industry and for AI development to slow down. But Anthropic’s actions are decidedly less “aligned” with efforts to preserve the stable climate that allowed complex human civilizations to grow and flourish.

In the hundreds of pages of its IPO filings, the maker of Claude mentioned climate change sparingly, laying out a number of ways that the warming planet could threaten its business. One risk is higher operating costs: Anthropic said that higher temperatures “can increase the power consumption and water usage required to cool equipment at the facilities on which we depend.” In addition, fires, hurricanes, and floods amped up by climate change could disrupt its operations, it noted.

Read Next On Wall Street, the ‘energy transition’ includes natural gas and data centers Austin Corona

Environmental policies pose another set of risks to the company’s resource-intensive business. Anthropic acknowledged that some investors may choose not to invest in the company if its sustainability measures are seen as inadequate. On the other hand, implementing such goals “could be difficult to achieve or costly to implement,” it wrote in the filings, adding that navigating various climate and sustainability disclosure laws in California, the European Union, and the United Kingdom could require “significant time and resources.”

That good-guy reputation might also take a hit. The filings suggest that AI’s environmental harms could hurt Anthropic’s image, as its brand is “subject to heightened scrutiny with respect to perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety-related impacts.”

“At least they admit that climate change is a threat when they say it’s a risk to their own operations,” Cray said, “but they’re not taking responsibility for their own contribution.”

In the broader public discussion about AI, concerns about global warming have been drowned out by a more immediate existential threat. One of Anthropic’s researchers, Jacob Coxon, accused the company of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives” when he resigned in September; then the lead of its alignment division, Evan Hubinger, said he thought there was a greater than 10 percent chance that “AI could kill all humans” within the next decade.

Assuming humans avert an AI apocalypse, we’ll have to contend with the reality of living on a rapidly warming planet. Some experts are trying to bring sustainability into the conversation about how to use AI responsibly. “The entire sector needs to be scrutinized closely as to what choices they make and how much transparency is in their reporting — which in this case, is not a lot,” Cray said. A recent analysis from the firm Integrum ESG compared Anthropic to 14 peer companies across the AI supply chain and found that all of them except Anthropic and SpaceX reported their direct greenhouse gas emissions and the indirect emissions from the energy they purchase (called Scope 1 and 2 emissions in energy wonk-speak).

Anthropic has pledged to cover the electricity price increases from its data centers so the public wouldn’t have to pay those costs and committed to “being a responsible neighbor” and addressing its environmental impacts, such as by deploying “water-efficient cooling technologies.” In June, it joined other major corporations in backing the carbon removal industry. (Anthropic did not respond to a request to comment.)

Cray has ideas for how Anthropic could apply its ethical standards to the problem of climate change. In addition to greater transparency, the company could commit to a timeline for powering its data centers with only renewable power and set firm climate targets. “They shouldn’t be building data centers that are powered by natural gas without a timeline for phasing that out and replacing it,” he said.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Even the ‘good guys’ of AI are locking in fossil fuels on Nov 19, 2026.

issues.title: As black lung disease surges, the Trump administration proposes ‘deregulatory’ protections for miners
issues.summary: A Biden-era guideline on deadly silica dust has been revised by the Trump administration. Miners' advocates argue it’s a handout to coal companies.
issues.author: Katie Myers
issues.content_html:
Coal mining is dangerous and takes a toll on the body, but a miner working underground can earn enough to buy a house, drive a nice car, and send the kids to college. There was a time when John Robinson thought the trade-off was worth it. No longer. He was diagnosed with black lung disease at age 47, a consequence of inhaling toxic silica dust in the mines of Virginia.

“These companies will bait you in with this big money,” said Robinson, who is now 60 and vice president of the National Black Lung Association. “When you get down and out, well, guess what? You’re like an old wore-out tire on the car or something. They’ll throw you to the side ’cause you ain’t worth nothing.”

For more than 50 years, coal miners, their families, and advocates have pressed the federal government for stricter limits on silica exposure, stronger enforcement of rules meant to protect miners, and improved health benefits for those disabled by the disease. In 2024, the Biden administration set the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica at 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air, matching the Occupational Safety and Health Administration threshold for workers in other industries. The rule was finalized in 2024, with coal companies required to comply beginning in April 2025.

That regulation was meant to update protections in coal mines and in what regulators call metal and nonmetal mines, which extract everything from copper and critical minerals to stone, sand, and gravel. All of them carry a risk of inhaling silica dust, whose fine particles can lodge deep in the lungs. But research over the past two decades has shown that Central Appalachian coal miners have experienced an acute increase in exposure and the most severe forms of lung disease associated with it, including progressive massive fibrosis.

Though the Biden-era revision wasn’t perfect, advocates like Robinson and his wife Vonda Robinson, who is president of the National Black Lung Association, were hopeful. It seemed as though decades of organizing for a stronger standard were finally coming to an end. But a federal appeals court put the rule on hold last year while it considered legal challenges filed by the mining industry. Now the Mine Safety and Health Administration wants to revise the rule.

Its proposal would retain the 50-microgram silica limit while changing several requirements governing how mines monitor exposure and protect workers. Brendan Muckian-Bates, a policy analyst with Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center, said those revisions could substantially weaken the protections behind the stricter limit.

Black lung is the common name for coal worker’s pneumoconiosis, an incurable, progressive, and fatal respiratory disease caused by inhaling coal dust and fine silica particles, which can cause severe inflammation in the lungs. Over time, that irritant scars and stiffens lung tissue, making respiration increasingly difficult until many of those afflicted with it cannot breathe at all.

In the 1960s and 1970s, according to the National Institutes of Health, as many as 1 in 3 miners with more than 25 years of work experience were testing positive for black lung. The United Mine Workers of America agitated for stricter protections again the disease, and in 1969, Congress passed the Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act, which required regular inspections. Disease rates plummeted to a historic low in the 2000s, only to begin climbing again.

Rates of black lung are now at a 50-year high and still climbing. A study led by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, or NIOSH, found these increases across all age groups, including miners in their 20s and 30s, although rates remained highest among those who had spent decades underground. In routine health screenings by the agency during the past three years, more than 1 in 3 miners in Central Appalachia once again tested positive for the disease, making the epidemic into a U-shaped curve.

The new rule was published in the Federal Register on November 12 and will be open for public comment until January 11. Although the stricter limit of 50 micrograms remains, Muckian-Bates said the fine print matters: Other changes in the rule undermine that threshold and give mine operators greater control over how it is enforced.

“On the one hand, it looks on the surface like the administration is saying, ‘Yes, we agree that silica is the leading cause of the black lung right now,’” Muckian-Bates said. “However, they’ve provided these measures to effectively nullify that.”

Among them is a 21 percent margin of error in testing, meaning companies would only be fined if a sample exceeded the 50 microgram limit by at least that amount. That effectively gives companies a 10 microgram increase in the amount workers can be exposed to, according to Muckian-Bates.

The 2024 rule enforced regular silica monitoring by requiring air sampling in each underground mine every six months. The proposal eliminates that schedule, instead requiring mine operators to assess when changing conditions could increase exposure and test “as frequently as necessary.” Mines could therefore go longer than six months without being sampled if operators determine additional testing isn’t needed, as long as they remain below the exposure limit.

The proposed rule also would also make medical exams voluntary for new metal and nonmetal miners; the 2024 rule made them mandatory. Advocates and health professionals say those initial exams establish a baseline that can later help determine whether lung disease developed from workplace exposure rather than an earlier condition or exposure. That is particularly important because the consequences of silica exposure may not become apparent for decades.

“What we have in the pipeline right now is not going to show up until like 20 years later,” Muckian-Bates said. “That just means we’re going to have a new crop of sick miners who we don’t know are getting sick, and they don’t know they’re getting sick, until it’s too late.”

The Mine Safety and Health Administration did not respond to questions. A spokesperson for the Department of Labor said in an email that anyone interested in offering feedback can do so within the 60-day window that opened on November 12, or during a virtual meeting on December 15.

“MSHA looks forward to reviewing all stakeholder comments before publishing a final rule to better protect the health of the Nation’s miners,” the email stated. The agency noted in the Federal Register that “this rule, if finalized, is expected to be a deregulatory action,” quoting President Donald Trump’s executive order titled “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.”

MSHA estimates the proposed rule will save the industry $28.7 million per year, mostly from changes in monitoring. Of that, coal companies would save $2.43 million.

With the 2024 rule on hold, miners remain subject to silica standards whose basic framework dates to the early 1970s and effectively allows exposures of roughly 100 micrograms per cubic meter of air. Virginia Tech mining expert Emily Sarver said a tighter limit is so overdue that she would rather see the proposal move forward than face years of further delay.

“I don’t think our current legacy rule is sufficiently protective,” Sarver said. Among other things, she considers the 2024 rule’s sampling scheme, involving many different labs rather than MSHA labs, chaotic, making enforcement difficult. “I think the new rule that was passed in 2024 on paper looks more protective, but I think there’s certain problems with it.”

As for John and Vonda Robinson, they plan to keep fighting for stronger protection of those who work the mines.

“If us older coal miners don’t get nothing out of this,” John Robinson said, “we can help the next batch of coal miners [that] is going to come up, that’s going to be extremely sick. This don’t go away. This is going to last for years and to [their] death.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline As black lung disease surges, the Trump administration proposes ‘deregulatory’ protections for miners on Nov 19, 2026.

issues.title: One in four land reptiles depends on rock habitats. Lack of protection leaves them in a hard place
issues.summary: More than a quarter of the world’s land reptiles depend on rocky habitats, yet these areas are often overlooked in conservation efforts, according to a recent study. For cold-blooded lizards, snakes, and worm lizards (legless lizards), rocks often provide warmth for basking, shelter from predators, and places to hunt, socialize, and breed. However, the number […]
issues.author: Shreya Dasgupta
issues.content_html: More than a quarter of the world’s land reptiles depend on rocky habitats, yet these areas are often overlooked in conservation efforts, according to a recent study. For cold-blooded lizards, snakes, and worm lizards (legless lizards), rocks often provide warmth for basking, shelter from predators, and places to hunt, socialize, and breed. However, the number of reptile species globally that use rocky habitats like cliffs, outcrops, or karst systems, and how threatened they are, still remains uncertain, researchers write in the study. To fill the gap, the researchers analyzed 9,729 terrestrial species belonging to the order Squamata, which includes all lizards, snakes, and worm lizards. For each species, they consulted the IUCN Red List, which documents its conservation status, habitat requirements, and threats. Their analysis found that 2,479 species, or more than 25% of those studied, use rocky habitats. Of these, 1,022 species, or 10.5%, were entirely dependent on rocks — that is, they lived almost exclusively on rocks and used rocks for breeding, shelter, and to regulate their temperature. Of the studied species that use rocks, nearly 30%, or 676 species, are classified as threatened on the IUCN Red List, the study found. Species that depend entirely on rocky habitats were 51% more likely to be critically endangered than those that use them only occasionally. Some of these rock-dependent critically endangered reptiles include the rough-bellied round-eyed gecko (Cnemaspis tropidogaster), native to India’s Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Emirati leaf-toed gecko (Asaccus caudivolvulus), the United Arab Emirates’s only endemic vertebrate,…This article was originally published on Mongabay

Top priorities include more money for protection of forests and other landscapes, funding to help vulnerable communities and economies adapt […]
issues.author: Charles Mpaka
issues.content_html: As the 2026 edition of the annual U.N. Climate Change Conference reaches its conclusion in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 20, African governments are arguing for increased financial and technical support to respond to climate change. Top priorities include more money for protection of forests and other landscapes, funding to help vulnerable communities and economies adapt to a changed climate, and financial backing for a just energy transition for fossil-fuel producing and consuming economies on the continent. Access to energy and what role remains for fossil fuels are contested topics, with many African governments planning continued reliance on coal, diesel and natural gas for transport, industry and electricity generation. Jane Mbabazi Byaruhanga, responsible for environmental and social affairs at Uganda’s Petroleum Authority, is among the thousands attending the summit. Africa’s households, schools, health centers and businesses lack access to affordable, reliable energy, she told Mongabay in a phone interview from Antalya. Two in five Ugandans lacked access to electricity from the national grid in 2025, according to government records; in rural areas, access was 43% of the population. This situation is mirrored across the continent: The International Energy Agency estimates that nearly 600 million of the continent’s 1.5 billion inhabitants do not have access to electricity. “Africa, to begin with, needs reliable and affordable energy to enhance their development, and we should always aim at the continent to have energy that is produced and also used responsibly,” she said. issues.title: Nickel linked to deforestation in Indonesia traded on London Metal Exchange, says report
issues.summary: Two companies approved for trading nickel on the London Metal Exchange (LME) could be linked to supply chains that have cleared primary rainforest in Indonesia, according to a report published by the NGO Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). The NGO investigated two LME-approved Indonesian refiners – PT CNGR Ding Xing and PT Eternal Nickel Industry (ENI) […]
issues.author: Naina Rao
issues.content_html: Two companies approved for trading nickel on the London Metal Exchange (LME) could be linked to supply chains that have cleared primary rainforest in Indonesia, according to a report published by the NGO Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). The NGO investigated two LME-approved Indonesian refiners – PT CNGR Ding Xing and PT Eternal Nickel Industry (ENI) – and traced each of their corporate ownerships to mines driving extensive deforestation across Sulawesi and the North Maluku islands. The investigation claims that the companies’ supply chains were possibly linked to clearing up to 7,270 hectares (17,965 acres) of primary rainforest in Indonesia. Current LME rules require metal brands to comply with the OECD’s Due Diligence Guidelines, which provide government-backed management recommendations for “responsible supply chains of all minerals”, including their refined metal derivatives. However, the guidelines lack binding environmental criteria for deforestation, biodiversity loss or Indigenous land rights, according to the EIA. “The LME has put in place solid requirements on metal sellers to address supply chain issues like conflict financing and child labour,” said Colin Robertson, EIA Forests Campaign lead for mining, told Mongabay over email. “Deforestation caused by mining is a growing problem and it seems to be a blind spot for the LME and for the mining and metals sector in general.” Neither company publicly discloses its mine suppliers under current LMEpassport rules, the digital platform for recording and sharing information about the physical metal that enters the LME system. issues.author: Mongabay.com
issues.content_html: Every year around the Hindu festival of Diwali, or Deepavali, residents in Nepal observe Kaag Tihar, an annual festival day dedicated to worshipping house crows as divine messengers. However, in the country’s capital, rapid urban sprawl, habitat degradation and changing perceptions toward the bird are testing human-crow relations, reports Mongabay’s Gobinda Pokharel. Satellite analysis shows Kathmandu’s urban build-up area expanded by 124% between 1989 and 2018, while another study found municipal green space plummeted by 54% between 1975 and 2025. Meanwhile, the removal of more than 2,000 mature trees along major thoroughfares like the Kathmandu Ring Road has forced house crows (Corvus splendens) to nest on utility poles and electrical wires, according to a 2024 study led by Tribhuvan University researcher Dinesh Bhusal, in Nepal. “When old and large trees are cut down, specialist birds lose their habitats,” said Hem Bahadur Katuwal, a bird ecologist at the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, southwest China. “Eventually, only functional generalist species, such as crows, which can survive under almost any conditions, remain.” Compounding the population shift is Kathmandu’s unmanaged refuse. Open dumping of waste along riverbanks and uncovered trash at meat shops provide abundant forage, attracting dense concentrations of crows and black kites (Milvus migrans). “Large quantities of discarded food and exposed waste from meat shops have contributed to the unusual increase in crows and kites in Kathmandu,” said Kamal Raj Gosai, an ornithologist and associate professor at Tribhuvan University’s Tri-Chandra Multiple Campus. issues.title: Fernando Alonso returns to Dakar: Why his first rally-raid experience was a shock to the system
issues.summary: Fernando Alonso still believes his Dakar project is "almost impossible", but sees his participation in 2027 as another step towards one of his remaining goals: winning the world's toughest rally
issues.content_html:
While Fernando Alonso reiterated in Las Vegas that, in his view, Formula 1 has thrown away 16 years of pure racing before the return of V8 engines in 2030, the Spaniard continues to seek those pure challenges outside the pinnacle of motorsport as well.

It had been known in the paddock for some time that Alonso would return to the Dakar Rally this winter for the first time since 2020, although the two-time F1 world champion still played games with the media ahead of the official announcement.

Read Also: Fernando Alonso to return to Dakar Rally with Aston Martin in 2027

Asked whether he would actually head to the Dakar, Alonso replied that he considered it “almost impossible”, particularly because the challenge is so different from F1.

Now that it has been officially confirmed that Alonso will indeed compete in a Prodrive car based on the Dacia Sandrider and featuring Aston Martin colours, the Spaniard laughs: "I didn't change my opinion [about it being almost impossible]! I think the Dakar in 2027 will be a much bigger challenge than it was for me in 2020.

"Back then I had six months of preparation. I went to different countries to test, including Qatar, Namibia, Morocco and Poland. It was quite an extensive program. Plus, I did two rallies in Saudi. Now I have two days in Morocco and off we go," Alonso said, when asked about the extent of the challenge by Motorsport.com.

"That's a bit short, but at the end of the day we decided, together with the Prodrive and with Aston, that it's still a good experience for all parties, especially for me, because there's no secret that one day I want to win Dakar. It will not be possible this time, but I think it's an investment for the future in terms of accumulating more kilometres and knowing more about the series."

The fact that the focus is primarily on gaining experience, and that winning will be particularly difficult, is also reflected in Alonso's approach to the upcoming Dakar.

Aston Martin 2027 Dreadnought

"I think this is one of the biggest challenges of the ones that I have attempted because of the lack of preparation, but I will try to test in the first week and hopefully race in the second week."

According to Alonso, what makes it such a major challenge is that it is the complete opposite of much of what F1 is about. His very first experience of rally-raid racing even came as a shock to the system.

"I remember the first days when I tested in Dakar, I had a headache in the night. I think it's coming from the level of focus that I'm not used to. The eyes, you cannot blink for four or five hours," he said.

"While here, we change things on the steering wheel, we talk on the radio, we look at the screens and we follow the race, because you are in the same little environment lap after lap. In Dakar, it's into the unknown, every meter is new."

As a result, Alonso feels that he has full control of the car, but not of the conditions, unlike in F1.

"What I don't have is full control of the speed I approach dangers with, even though I have a great co-driver with Marc Coma. After you go full throttle for 10 kilometres in the middle of nothing, then in the distance he sees a little bit of vegetation or something green, and he always tells me that when there is something green or vegetation, it means a bumpy ride," Alonso explained.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin

"So these kind of things I'm learning while driving, thanks to his experience, but I imagine that for the other drivers, all these things come automatically because they went through all these things. I'm in a fast-learning process while I'm in the middle of the race, but that's fascinating for me as a driver."

One day, it should lead to a Dakar victory, a triumph Alonso would love to add to his impressive motorsport CV, but he believes his rivals still have a significant advantage heading into this winter's edition.

"I think, coming from my background, the challenge is going to be bigger than if you grew up in that environment. I think I was competitive [in 2020], but as I said, I had a good six months of preparation. I had a good few thousands of kilometres before that, which I don't have now.

"My team-mate Sebastien Loeb is probably the greatest rally driver in history. He tried Dakar nine or 10 times and he didn't achieve the win yet. I'm fully aware of the difficulty.

"It's a very big challenge, but that's why it's appealing. That's why it's interesting and that's why I want to, in the future, try to win it one day."

Read Also: Fernando Alonso rules out staying in F1 for V8 return: "16 years of pure racing lost"

issues.title: Leon Smith to end 16-year stint as GB’s Davis Cup captain after 2026 Finals
issues.summary: Smith will remain in post for next week’s Finals in Bologna, where GB play Germany in the quarter-finals
issues.content_html:
Great Britain’s Davis Cup-winning captain Leon Smith will mark his final tournament in charge at next week’s Finals before stepping down after 16 years at the helm.

Smith took over from John Lloyd in 2010 and has since become GB’s longest-serving Davis Cup captain, overseeing an historic win over Belgium to claim the trophy in 2015.

When the Scot took over GB had just suffered an embarrassing loss to Lithuania and faced relegation to the bottom tier of the tournament, billed as the ‘World Cup’ of men’s tennis.

But he managed to revive GB’s fortunes, significantly aided by Andy Murray, who he had coached as a junior, and ensured GB’s return to the top tier as well as their first trophy since 1936.

Announcing the news of his departure, Smith said: “It has been an enormous privilege to lead the team for so many years, and I feel now is the right time, both for me personally and for the team moving forwards.

“Winning the Davis Cup in 2015 will always be one of the proudest moments of my career, but there are countless other experiences and memories that I’ll cherish forever.

“For now, I’m focused and really looking forward to captaining Great Britain for one more week in Bologna next week and hopefully creating a few more special memories together.”

He will remain in post for the Finals in Bologna at the end of November, where Britain face Germany in the quarter-finals on Thursday.

Murray, who won all 11 singles and doubles rubbers he contested in 2015, as well as 33 out of 36 in singles in the competition overall, paid tribute to Smith.

The three-time major winner said: “Winning the Davis Cup in 2015 with Leon as captain was one of the proudest moments of my career. He did a great job of bringing everyone together and making sure we all felt we had a part to play.

“I’ve obviously known Leon a long time, since he coached me as a kid. I think the most fun we had together was when I was playing Davis Cup and Leon was on the bench.

“I wish Leon all the best as he steps down, and good luck to the new captain.”

Smith will continue as the LTA’s head of men’s tennis.

A new captain has not yet been confirmed, with PA reporting Murray - who currently has a role coaching former world No 4 Jack Draper - is not in the running for the position.

issues.title: Rawalpindi Test: Pakistan end two-year drought as Sri Lanka suffer historic low with four straight away series defeats
issues.summary: Pakistan secured a Test series victory against Sri Lanka by winning the second Test in Rawalpindi. The team chased down a target of 90 runs after limiting Sri Lanka's second innings to 316 runs. Aamer Jamal and Azan Awais played crucial roles in achieving this win. Meanwhile, Sri Lanka continued to struggle on overseas tours, marking their fourth consecutive series loss.
issues.content_html:
A new-look Pakistan side ended a two-year wait for a Test series triumph, overpowering Sri Lanka by eight wickets in the second Test in Rawalpindi on Friday to clinch the two-match series 1-0. The defeat extended Sri Lanka's miserable overseas run, leaving them with four successive away Test series losses and a calendar year without a single Test victory for the first time since 1997.

Chasing a modest target after restricting Sri Lanka to 316 in their second innings, Pakistan raced to 90/2 in just 13 overs during the first session on Day 4. Aamer Jamal provided the finishing flourish with an unbeaten 34 off 22 balls, smashing five fours and a six, while Azan Awais remained not out on 32.


The victory was Pakistan's first Test series win since beating England at home in October 2024. It was also only their third win in 11 matches in the current World Test Championship cycle.

Pakistan captain Babar Azam was particularly pleased with the way his relatively inexperienced side responded to the challenge.

"Very satisfying, the way the team performed. We had a young team, many players grabbed their opportunities. The environment in the dressing room is very positive, we just need to stay stable and focus on the game. All the players gave 100% to their roles and that was nice to see," Babar said.

Sri Lanka's overseas struggles deepen


The series defeat added another unwanted chapter to Sri Lanka's recent Test record. Their last overseas series victory came against Bangladesh in March 2024, and they have now lost four consecutive away series.

The Islanders will also finish 2026 without a Test victory for the first time since 1997. Pakistan, meanwhile, have won three of their last four Test series against Sri Lanka, whose previous series triumph over Pakistan came in September 2017.

Sri Lanka's troubles in Rawalpindi began in the first innings when Pakistan's seamers bowled them out for just 98 inside the first two sessions on the opening day. The visitors conceded a massive 227-run first-innings lead, leaving themselves with a mountain to climb.

They showed greater resistance in the second innings, with Milan Rathnayake remaining unbeaten on 66 to help extend the contest. However, Mohammad Abbas, who claimed 3/55 in the innings, ended the resistance by trapping Asitha Fernando lbw in his first over on Friday.

Abbas, who was named both Player of the Match and Player of the Series, said his performance had been overdue.

"The performance was due, I spoke before the series and the challenges before it, still have to take a 5-wicket haul, hopefully I will do it. I assess the conditions, make sure that my economy is low and it helps the other bowlers as well. I only advised them to hit the areas well, Saqib became unfit unfortunately, that made my responsibility more," he said.

Babar praises youngsters as Mendis looks ahead


Pakistan's victory was particularly encouraging given the number of fresh faces in the squad, with four players making their debuts during the series. Babar singled out wicketkeeper-batter Ghazi for making the most of his opportunities and also credited fast bowler Razaullah's pace and first-innings contribution.

"If you have a bowler who can bowl at 145 kmph, it gives you confidence. His spell in the first innings was vital and that was one of the main reasons for our series win today," Babar said.

Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis acknowledged that his side's poor first-innings batting had proved costly.

"Honestly, we didn't bat well in the first innings, including me. I got out at a crucial time. We bowled well and batted well in the 2nd innings. Bowling wise, I thought we hit the areas well," Mendis said.

He also thanked Pakistan for hosting the team during a tour that included a 2-1 T20I series defeat and a loss in the ODI tri-series final.

"We've stayed here for more than one month, we enjoyed Pakistan and have had positives in both Tests. The fast bowlers bowled well and I'm happy with the improvement. Looking forward to the tour of New Zealand. Hopefully, I will be back here in the PSL or some other tournament. I thank Pakistan for hosting us, we enjoyed our stay here," he added.

issues.title: 'There is certainly no bitterness' – Case against truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin won't continue due to his ill health
issues.summary: Wolfgang Rieke unfit to participate in appeals trial after suffering stroke in 2024
issues.author: Dani Ostanek
issues.content_html:
The hearings into the case of Wolfgang Rieke, the truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin, have concluded with no charges brought.

Two years ago, a first-instance trial concluded with Rieke being sentenced to a four-year jail term after hitting and killing Rebellin in 2022. However, the Venice Court of Appeals ruled last week that Rieke is unfit to participate in an appeal trial, so the case has been dropped, according to the Ansa news agency.

Rieke, 66, currently resides in a nursing home after suffering a stroke in 2024, and this summer his lawyers obtained a doctor's report on his psychological and physical ability to participate in the trial. The report concluded that Rieke is mentally unable to stand trial.

"The family acknowledges what happened. There is certainly respect for the judicial decisions and today's. There is certainly no bitterness; there is acknowledgement and respect for his health," said Rebellin's family's lawyer, Davide Picco.

"Justice has certainly worked, given that the Prosecutor's Office transferred the defendant from Germany to Italy. He served several months in prison and then under house arrest. His health condition then led to today's sentence."

Rieke, who had previously pled guilty to a non-fatal hit-and-run and drunk driving, struck and killed Rebellin as he was on a training ride in Montebello Vincentino on November 30, 2022, shortly after he retired from racing. He then fled the scene, leading authorities to launch a multi-country search.

He turned himself in to German police in June 2023 and was later handed a four-year sentence after the judge rejected several initial plea deals. After suffering a stroke two years ago, the case against him will not continue.

"We are satisfied that the judges have accepted our requests, acknowledging Mr. Rieke's current health conditions, which prevent him from consciously participating in the trial," said Rieke's lawyer, Andrea Nardin, according to the Corriere del Veneto.

issues.title: Why a 37-year-old Primož Roglič is still a great signing and how more freedom at NSN can unlock his five-time Grand Tour-winning best
issues.summary: Slovenian remains among the best riders in the world as he heads towards 'final chapter' not 'just to race, but also achieve things'
issues.author: James Moultrie
issues.content_html:
The further into the off-season it went, the more likely it seemed that five-time Grand Tour winner Primož Roglič's career was going to end before he wanted it to.

Without a team for 2027 and running out of options – with a potential return to Visma and a move to Lotto Intermarché among the rumours that came to nothing during the Autumn – Roglič found the lifeline he was looking for at the last gasp, extending his stay in the peloton for one more year with NSN Cycling.

It wasn't like most of the big-name moves in modern cycling, which are signposted months in advance, but it did finally bring an answer to the question that Roglič had been answering with "We'll see, ah" and "I don't know yet" ever since July, when Red Bull team boss Ralph Denk confirmed he would be leaving.

The idiosyncrasies that have made him one of the peloton's most popular and compelling riders won't be going anywhere, instead just repackaged in the Swiss team's colours for, as they described it, the "final chapter".

Though it should be noted that Roglič hasn't ruled out a similarly complicated re-up of his time in the sport 12 months from now, more openly putting it down to needing "some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never."

Tudor, Pinarello Q36.5, Unibet Rose Rockets, and XDS Astana were among the other speculated landing spots for the Slovenian, but clearly none could muster up the perfect mix of financial resources, a fitting contract, or the desire to bring him in, but NSN have found room for the GC star.

Importantly, it means that instead of a nondescript 68th-place finish at Il Lombardia, 37-year-old Roglič is now in control of where his final chapter as a professional comes to an end, and he certainly won't be looking to go out with a whimper.

"I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself," he said, when his surprise move to NSN was announced on Wednesday evening. "I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."

After his home heroics in Slovenia late in the season, Roglič will start his 12th year in the WorldTour as the reigning European time trial champion, which he wasn't even sure he'd get to wear in a race after he won it: "Maybe I'll only wear it at home. Because we haven't decided yet what I'll do next, but no matter what, I'll wear it."

But aside from that, he also proved there was life in the old dog yet, as he came second overall at the Vuelta a España – a race he's won four times – behind Enric Mas in September. And both of those key 2026 feats came after he was knocked off his bike by a driver just a month ahead of the Vuelta's start in Monaco.

Off the bike for 10 days and unsure if he would have even taken the start if it wasn't where he lived, Roglič's late-season results should be looked at with the context that what he did was nothing short of miraculous when it came to recovery. This is far from the sort of moves that saw the then Israel-Premier Tech – which was rebranded as NSN a year ago – criticised as something of a "retirement home".

Roglič may be a veteran, but he is still one of the top riders in the world.

Still able to compete with the best

Roglič raced 53 times in 2026, with mixed success, but importantly, still with success.

He opened up his campaign with a solid performance at Tirreno-Adriatico, finishing fifth overall and helping teammate Giulio Pellizzari to third on GC behind winner Isaac del Toro, and followed that up with more success in Italy by taking third at Milano-Torino.

From here, things slowed down for the Slovenian, finishing 16th at Iztulia Basque Country, and failing to impress at the Tours de Romandie and Suisse as compatriot Tadej Pogačar dominated the racing to take both titles. Roglič only managed 18th and eighth overall, respectively.

He turned things around at the Slovenian national championships, ramping up his performance with a win in the ITT and fourth in the road race, ahead of his already confirmed major goal of the Vuelta, where he was looking to stand alone at the top of the history books for the most overall titles – which he currently shares alongside Roberto Heras on four.

However, it was soon after, on July 31, that Roglič revealed he had been halted in his plans: "Got hit by a car few days ago…" read a post on his Instagram. "I won't be participating in San Sebastian and in Burgos unfortunately... not the best scenario, but it's life, eh. Now it's all systems go towards La Vuelta; we work and hope things will turn around!"

He did make it to the Vuelta, and while there were no Roglifications of old – as it was Enric Mas who stepped into the spotlight and claimed red after Pogačar crashed out – when all was said and done in Granada, Roglič could only describe second as feeling "like a victory to me".

Mas rightly took the majority of headlines as he made history for Spain, but there was a more visceral reaction from the press room as second-place Roglič answered his final question in the longer post-race press conferences. It felt like a goodbye to the race where he had enjoyed his most successful moments, with no one in the room, nor he, knowing where he'd end up next as the room filled with applause and matching gratitude from the Slovenian.

The same feelings returned at European Championships and Il Lombardia, where the enigmatic Roglič was none the wiser, still saying, "You never know when is the last one. Like everything in life, it can be a bit emotional," as he conceded that the Italian Monument could be the endpoint.

Into the off-season, Roglič next resurfaced at the Taiwan Cycling Masters, where a KOM challenge south of Taipei saw the Slovenian drop no hints at whether he'd signed a contract – instead, he continued to be cryptic in his comments.

"The people that you collect on the way, or they collect you, that you have around, they help the influence at the end on you," he said in a promotional video for the event.

"I think yes, they left a mark on me, like I said I'm always open to learn, to know more, and the more you know, the more you know that you don't know, so it's a never-ending process."

Well now we do know, as does he, that life in the pro peloton will be continuing, and while those previously ruthless punchy legs perhaps lack the same bite they had five-eight years ago, he has a diesel engine that can still power him up the highest mountains.

In his best results at the Europeans and Vuelta, it's key not to forget that it wasn't against weak fields by any means; at the former, Bruno Armirail, Stefan Küng, and Jakob Söderqvist were among those unable to live with Roglič's time, and at the latter he emerged ahead of Giro runner-up Felix Gall, new teammate Richard Carapaz, and Oscar Onley for his second place on GC.

How he could fit into NSN's plans

Even with Roglič clearly proving his worth as an asset into his late 30s, there still remains the question of how NSN will deploy their new leader and fit him into their schedules after such a late pick-up.

The team's media day is next week, and the thoughts will already be on December and January training camp ahead of the start of the 2027 season on January 1, with rider schedules among the news set to be confirmed in the coming weeks.

With Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt, NSN had already been looking to improve their stock as a GC-hunting outfit, having failed to finish in the top 10 of all three Grand Tours in 2026. Their best results were 12th at the Giro, 68th at the Tour, and 15th at the Vuelta, but with those three mentioned above and Roglič, they suddenly have a chance at finishing in the top 10 and potentially higher of all three.

Carapaz has already suggested that it is a return to the Giro where he wants to target an overall placing, and while this would seem to interfere with a potential Slovenian homecoming for Roglič, it's actually the Tour and Vuelta that look like more likely targets.

Sharing the leadership among their new star signings lessens any chance for internal bickering, and also opens the door to Carapaz potentially chasing GC at one Grand Tour and then stages and the mountains classification at another – as he'd been doing successfully for EF in recent years.

NSN's new foray into the GC hierarchy also represents more freedom for a rider like Roglič, who has been bitten by bad luck and crashes several times in the most pressure-filled moments riding for Visma and Red Bull – teams where you have to maintain GC success to keep your spot.

Roglič should get the freedom to pick the plan which suits him best and allows him to build up in the ways he knows will work for GT success. NSN will also offer up what Red Bull didn't in his final Vuelta for them this past summer, where a young team lacking in climbing support saw them struggle to front up numbers to muster a major challenge consistently against Mas – even if it likely would have had no effect on the final red jersey standings.

NSN can commit their younger riders Buitrago and Van Eetvelt, and the experience of George Bennett and Nick Schultz to a full-blown Roglič bid, be that at the Tour or Vuelta. And while in an age of Pogačar, Vingegaard, Evenepoel, Seixas, and Del Toro, any entrance into the top-five seems unlikely, this summer proved that anything can happen, even to the big stars, with Pogačar crashing out of the Vuelta and Vingegaard from the Tour, so it's not out of the realms of possibility that he is able to score one final Grand Tour podium, which would be his 10th, or indeed a sixth victory.

In reality, Roglič's goals could become a final stage win at the Tour – to add to the three he already has, 10 years after his first into Serre-Chevalier on stage 17 of the 2017 race – the GC title at the Tour de Suisse, which remains the only major one-week stage race missing from his palmarès from the seven, or indeed that elusive fifth Vuelta title.

Even with Pogačar probably taking the start, living by the words "Never say never" has got Roglič this far, and he'll be hoping his new team's name can carry him to the last hurrah which he deserves. There's a degree of risk in not allowing that European title win on home roads to become the denouement to his great career, but as one Slovenian famously said en route to one of his Vuelta titles: "No risk, no glory."

issues.title: Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, Paul Seixas among cycling stars set for audience with Pope Leo XIV
issues.summary: Mark Cavendish, Annemiek van Vleuten, Greg LeMond, and Elisa Longo Borghini also in cycling delegation attending November 23 event
issues.author: Dani Ostanek
issues.content_html:
A host of representatives from the cycling world, including Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, and Paul Seixas, will attend an audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican next week.

UCI President David Lappartient described the November 23 event as "an opportunity to strengthen cycling's commitment, as a sport, to promoting peace and intercultural dialogue among peoples."

The Dicastery for Culture and Education and the Vatican's multi-sport association are organising the audience in collaboration with the UCI.

Past and present Grand Tour champions are among a group of over 100 "distinguished guests" attending, in addition to organisers of all men's and women's Grand Tours and other races, and representatives from various cycling federations.

Vollering, Merckx, and Seixas will be joined by a host of current and former road riders, including Bernard Hinault, Annemiek van Vleuten, Greg LeMond, Elisa Longo Borghini, Francesco Moser, Miguel Indurain, Jeannie Longo, Vincenzo Nibali, Chris Froome, and Mark Cavendish.

Multiple para-cycling world champion Ricardo Ten Argilés, multiple BMX world champion Mariana Pajón, and Ukrainian cyclist Anna Kolyzhuk, who suffered a serious spinal injury in a crash during a race this year, will also attend.

Ahead of the event, Lappartient "highlighted the longstanding historical roots between cycling and the Catholic Church, from races organised by parish communities and cycling teams inspired by Gospel values, to the various meetings with Popes throughout the 20th century and the recent passage of the Giro d’Italia through the Vatican during the 2025 Jubilee."

The event will see Pope Leo XIV take an audience with the riders before the UCI symbolically donates several bicycles to Caritas Rome, a charitable organisation founded by the Episcopal Conference of Italy.

The audience isn't the first time the Pope and the cycling world have come together. In 2025, the Pope blessed the peloton ahead of the final stage of the Giro d'Italia, which started in the Vatican. The stage was dedicated to Pope Francis, who died in April.

Several other Popes have addressed the Giro in the past, including Pope Paul VI in 1964 and Pope John Paul II in 2000. Pope John Paul II also offered his support to the Amore e Vita cycling team in the 1990s and 2000s.

Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the
issues.author: Andrew Lawrence
issues.content_html:
The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric

Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out three years ago. He wore dark glasses and dressed head to toe in black.

“The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling,” he wrote on Instagram of his visit, before turning the lens on himself. “I know so many people that feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.”
