issues.content_html:
#​495 — October 30, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Putting MUI, Mantine, Ant Design
and React Spectrum Under Load

Den Odell wanted to see how popular design systems cope when you give them real work, so he timed ten of them, including MUI, Mantine, Ant Design and React Spectrum, and profiled the slowest cases. "Performance belongs on the design system team's priority list, next to accessibility," he says. Some highlights:

  • 📊 With the CPU slowed 4x, opening a 249-country dropdown took 84ms in Mantine and 134ms in Ant Design, but over 200ms in MUI and React Spectrum, both of which froze the UI past his 100ms budget.

  • 🔍 React Spectrum's problem was React Aria measuring options one at a time and forcing layout for each. Den filed an issue and a fix is in review.

  • ⚖️ Framework alone didn't decide the results as non-React Ionic was by far the slowest to open (1,266ms) yet was quick at checking 100 checkboxes, while MUI handled them in 70ms compared to Ant Design's 421ms.

  • 🧪 Want to try this on your own components? Den's Playwright tests are available on GitHub.

Agentic Mobile Development Needs Mobile AI Infrastructure — Your agent writes mobile screens fast. Getting them built and into the App Store is where it stalls. Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: native builds, store submits, over-the-air updates and workflows your agent can run. Start free.

Expo sponsor

TanStack Redact: A Smaller React for the Browser — A drop-in replacement for React/React DOM in the browser. Add it to your build config (Start, Vite, Vinext and Next.js are supported) and ship less JavaScript. But it renders synchronously, with no time slicing, so the compatibility guide is handy.

Tanner Linsley

💬 Does Redact pay off? On r/reactjs, commenters pondered who needs it and how it differs from Preact, while one tester found re-renders cost about twice the CPU across two production sites.

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Next.js has a security release scheduled for November 3, fixing seven medium-severity vulnerabilities. Advisories will be published with the patches.

  • Dan Abramov is fuzzing React's Flight protocol, the format behind Server Components, by streaming random value graphs through the real server and client. It's turned up six stream bugs and three writer bugs so far.

  • TanStack AI 1.0 is stable: a vendor-neutral AI toolkit with React hooks like useChat(), 23 provider adapters and MCP support.

  • 📱 React Native Windows 0.85 completes its move to the New Architecture, and there's more React Native on the desktop with Expo Desktop (an independent project – not by Expo) and Legend Spark for macOS.

React.lazy, Suspense and the Hidden 300ms Startup Delay — A lazy component can suspend on its first render even when its code is already loaded, and React can throttle reveals of suspended content to once every 300ms. Here's how one team traced the delay, and what fixed it.

Matthew Wong (Tab Widgets)

TanStack DB 1.0 RC1, and How 'Oracles' Found Its Bugs — The reactive client data layer is now API stable, but check the migration guide, as mutation handlers, hooks and errors have changed. Kyle explains how agents, checked against simple reference models, found many of the bugs fixed.

Kyle Mathews (TanStack)

🤖 Ship Less JavaScript in Next.js with Your AI Agent – A new skill hunts bundle bloat using Turbopack's module graph. Will Binns-Smith (Vercel)

📄 Porting 287,000 Lines of React to Foldkit in 3 Days – Focuses on how they built a harness to ensure visual and behavioral parity. David Granzin (Maple)

📄 Async React and Progressive Server Actions – How to keep server action forms working before hydration, even with optimistic UI. Jacob Ebey

📊 React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked Waseem Anjum

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Puck 0.24: The Visual Page Editor for React — A drag-and-drop page editor you embed in your own app, using your own components. 0.24 lets you lay out a component's settings panel as you wish, improves drag and drop, and more. GitHub repo.

Fede Bonel Tozzi

react-window 2.5: Virtualized Lists That Scroll with the Page — Brian's long-standing virtualization library adds a scrollElement prop, so lists/grids can scroll along with the page or an ancestor, plus a headless useVirtualizer() for building your own virtualized layouts. Docs and demos.

Brian Vaughn

Vinext 1.4: The Vite-Powered Next.js Reimplementation Gets Faster — A Vite plugin that reimplements the Next.js API so you can deploy anywhere. 1.4 focuses on performance, with a Hacker News clone example now using 43% less server CPU per request vs 1.3, putting it slightly ahead of Next.js in that test.

James Anderson

  • OpenTUI 0.8 – Terminal UI library with React bindings that powers OpenCode. Now repaints only what changed each frame.

  • React Hook Form 7.91 – Lots of useFieldArray and async validation fixes, plus fewer re-renders. v8 is also now at beta 5.

  • React-Toastify 11.2 – Popular toast notification library. Now with theme="auto" to follow the OS color scheme.

  • emoji-picker-react 5.1 – Full-featured customizable emoji picker. Live demo.

🎃 And finally…

Halloween is almost upon us, so how about a round of Graveyard Pinball? It's built with React Three Fiber, with skulls, cauldrons and a skeleton mage. Its creator explains more about how it works here, including how the 3D table actually uses 2D physics.

issues.content_html:
#​494 — October 23, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

TanStack Start Reaches 1.0

After a year as a release candidate, TanStack Start 1.0 is officially stable. Tanner Linsley explains how it grew out of TanStack Router, and is candid about RSC, which felt like "this box we had to check to be taken seriously as a React framework", and which tanstack.com itself no longer uses. Plus:

  • 📊 The same app in Start and Next.js 16.4, benchmarked – Start handled 2.9x-8.6x more dynamic requests and built ~1.7x faster with type-checking included.

  • 🚚 Moving over? There are official guides for migrating from Next.js and from the RC. Sarthak Mishra moved his site over from Astro (and explains why) and Lovable offers older projects a migration option (here's how one went).

  • 💬 Ryan Carniato called it "a React metaframework with an architecture I can get behind", while in the r/reactjs thread Tanner explained why '1.0' is listed as 1.169 on npm.

TypeScript in the Age of AI — Knowing TypeScript deeply is how you get better code out of AI. Adam Rackis of Spotify shows you how to steer AI toward simpler, correct types and catch the mistakes it slips in.

Master.dev sponsor

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Last week, Next.js patched two critical RCEs, one rooted in React Server Components, and a public PoC is now out. Update Next.js to 16.4.1 or 15.5.28; for other RSC setups, update the react-server-dom-* packages to 19.3.1 (or 19.2.9/19.1.10/19.0.9).

  • React DevTools for agents now has official docs, covering how it exposes profiling and component data to coding agents through Chrome DevTools MCP.

  • 📱 Expo SDK 58 is out, using the new React Native 0.88, targeting iOS 27 and ready for the iPhone Duo on day one.

  • React Native for Web has active maintainers again and is moving to the React Foundation's GitHub org.

  • TypeScript 7.1 is now in beta, adding a programmatic API and more speed. Type-checking MUI's docs is 1.9x faster and uses half the memory.

Improving Navigation Experience in v0 with Next.js 16.4 — How the Next.js team used Partial Prefetching, intent-based prefetching and the new navigation() API to cut loading skeletons across its v0 AI app builder.

Aurora Scharff (Vercel)

React Only Where Needed: Owner's Next.js to Astro Move — Owner's 10,000+ restaurant sites now run on Astro and Cloudflare Workers, keeping React for interactive islands. Menu-page p75 LCP went from 5.4s to 0.7s.

Selden and Hanford (Owner)

Dead Code Shouldn't Exist — The slides and transcript from a popular talk Dominik has given at several conferences this year on how Sentry removed 28K lines of unused code with Knip.

Dominik Dorfmeister

🤖 Testing AI-Generated Code: Lint the Pattern, Test the Decision – Structural lint rules and shared harnesses beat a test beside every component. Robin Wieruch

📱 Apple Didn't Invent the Foldable. It Might Make You Support One. – Getting a React Native app ready for the iPhone Duo's three compatibility tiers. Sean Barker (Infinite Red)

📄 Loading a 9MB WebAssembly Module Earlier Made Recraft's Editor 17% Faster – Suspending components left the module's download waiting its turn in the React tree. Sergey Patrakeev (Recraft)

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Pixel: Build Graphical Applications in the Terminal — Like Ink, but with "pixel perfect" graphics. It's a React renderer that draws rounded corners, gradients and proper fonts in terminals that support the Kitty graphics protocol, and that can even embed Chromium WebViews to run web apps in a pane(!)

Rob Pruzan (Zenbu Labs)

TanStack Hotkeys Beta: A Type-Safe Library for Keyboard Shortcuts — Hotkeys takes care of the fiddly, cross-platform edge cases of keyboard shortcuts, sequences, and user-recorded hotkeys. The beta adds scopes, so that, say, a dialog's Escape doesn't close the panel behind it. Try the demo on the homepage.

TanStack

React Router 8.5 Hands View Transitions Over to React — Its own view transition APIs are deprecated in favor of React 19.3's <ViewTransition>. Migrating starts with wrapping an <Outlet> and removing the old props and state styling. There's also an unstable 'API-only' mode that serves static HTML but keeps a server for loaders and actions.

Remix Team

env.style: Style Every Environment with Colors or Custom Icons — A utility that wraps your Next.js config or Vite setup to tint the favicon per environment at build time, so you can see at a glance where you are.

Ryan George

Tamagui 3: One React UI Codebase for Web and Native — A styling system and UI kit for sharing one codebase between React web apps and React Native. v3 adds an opt-in (beta) C++ native runtime that applies theme changes without re-rendering, plus React Strict DOM and Tailwind-style syntax.

Nate Wienert

  • Hydrogen 2026.10 – Shopify's commerce toolkit is now a library you can drop into existing Next.js or React Router apps.

  • Morphicons 2.0 – Spring-physics morphing between SVG icons. Now filled icons morph too, not just stroked ones. See it in action on its homepage.

  • Unistyles 3.6 – High-performance React Native styling library. Now with an experimental zero-config Metro integration instead of the Babel plugin.

  • Motion 14.6 – Adds keyboard grab-and-move to Reorder lists, plus stepFrames for deterministic animation testing.

📰 Classifieds

Build and deploy durable AI agents in TypeScript, without managing your own infrastructure. Ship your first agent with Trigger.dev.

Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: Your agents build, test and ship iOS and Android apps, and you approve what goes out. Try it.

🎶 And finally… make a little noise

Fancy making a little music with React? Strudel Flow 2 is an open source React app built with React Flow and shadcn/ui. Connect instruments and effects to generate Strudel code, or load a community patch and start turning knobs.

The source code offers a neat extension point: define an instrument or effect in a small .node.ts file, then supply a React component for a custom interface. As the team says, "coding is a fun thing to do for its own sake." 🤘

issues.title: 🎙️ How I AI: Fable 5.2 Review + How I fight token fraud as a solo founder + Building a Claude Code family OS
issues.summary: Your weekly listens from How I AI, part of the Lenny's Podcast Network
issues.author: Lenny Rachitsky
issues.content_html:
Claude Code + Obsidian: My family’s AI brain | Scott Farrar

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Jira Product Discovery—Prioritize with insights, build with confidence

Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who built a shared household brain using Claude Code and Obsidian. In this episode, he shows how the system tracks appliances and warranties, compares insurance quotes, organizes family projects, and keeps household tasks moving through a shared to-do list and wall display. He also explains why persistent files work better for him than long AI chats, and how the same philosophy shapes his approach to using AI without taking the thinking away from students.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The problem with chat is not intelligence, but memory drift. Scott moved to Claude Code because it stores context in Markdown files he can inspect, correct, and reuse across sessions. His memory is no longer trapped inside an opaque conversation.

  2. Let the AI tell you what context it needs. When Scott asked Claude how to document his home, it suggested photographing every appliance. Those photos became a searchable inventory of model numbers, serial numbers, and warranty details.

  3. Unstructured input is fine when the system handles the organization. Scott gives Claude raw information and lets it maintain the underlying files. A custom linter prevents verbose agents from bloating documents such as his household to-do list.

  4. Better context helps people ask better questions. Claude compares insurance quotes with detailed information about Scott’s home, identifies potential coverage gaps, and prepares specific follow-ups. He no longer has to rely entirely on the agent selling him the policy.

  5. One master list can eliminate a house full of mental clutter. Scott and his wife captured every household task they could think of, then Claude organized them by priority, cost, and supporting information. The system now surfaces overdue work before it becomes another fire.

  6. Multiplayer household systems require practical compromises. Claude recommended GitHub to avoid file conflicts, but that added more complexity than Scott’s wife wanted. They settled on GitHub for shared scripts and Dropbox for everyday files, matching the tools to how they actually work.

  7. A household system becomes more useful when it leaves the laptop. Scott’s wall display shows upcoming trips, open tasks, recent wins, and small daily suggestions. It turns a private collection of files into something the whole family can see and use.

  8. Scott rebuilt his father’s file cabinet as an AI system. His dad saved every receipt and warranty and could explain repairs from decades ago. Claude now gives Scott that same dependable household memory, only searchable through conversation.

  9. AI should help children think, not think for them. Scott prefers tutors that ask students to explain their reasoning and work through productive struggle. He also believes some children may share unfinished ideas more comfortably with AI than with another person.

  10. Infinite patience is not always good teaching. Scott wants AI to act as a “warm demander” that encourages students without doing the work for them. When his own agent goes off track, he starts fresh or investigates its reasoning before incorrect information reaches his memory files.

Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode:

Claude Code and Obsidian: Scott Farrar’s Household Brain: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/claude-code-and-obsidian-scott-farrar-s-household-brain
↳ Create a Live Household Dashboard with Claude and DAKboard: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/create-a-live-household-dashboard-with-claude-and-dakboard
↳ Manage a Household Project Using an AI Knowledge Base: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/manage-a-household-project-using-an-ai-knowledge-base
↳ Build a Household Knowledge Base with Claude and Obsidian: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/build-a-household-knowledge-base-with-claude-and-obsidian

How I fight token fraud as a solo founder

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Auros—The human network behind AI

In this solo episode, Claire explains how token fraud cost ChatPRD tens of thousands of dollars and consumed much of her engineering time. She walks through six forms of abuse, including farmed free trials, resold promo codes, card testing, product relays, and a custom MCP running as a 24/7 compute worker. She also shares the business and technical defenses she built, how Jev classifies suspicious activity in real time, and why she ultimately eliminated free trials.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Token fraud is a business risk most AI founders underestimate until the bill arrives. Unlike traditional SaaS abuse, every fraudulent model call costs real money. It cost Claire tens of thousands of dollars despite ChatPRD being SOC 2 compliant, regularly penetration-tested, and run by an experienced technical founder.

  2. Free trials may no longer work for AI products. Fraudsters automated account creation and used ChatPRD’s most expensive models for unrelated work. Claire ultimately removed free trials, sacrificing a valuable source of product-led growth and enterprise leads after credit-card gates and paid trials also failed.

  3. Promo codes have become a serious attack vector. Codes intended for partners were stolen, resold, and used to power other AI businesses. After discovering that roughly half of her promo codes had reached resellers, Claire stopped issuing them entirely.

  4. MCP access creates a new category of abuse. One fraudster turned ChatPRD’s custom MCP support into a compute worker that ran around the clock. Claire responded by restricting approved hosts and blocking free tunnels and infrastructure that did not appear connected to legitimate companies.

  5. Cheap decision models can classify fraud in real time. When a session crosses ChatPRD’s abuse threshold, a zero-data-retention Jev loop categorizes the activity. Confirmed fraud results in either a ban or a silent downgrade to a less expensive model.

  6. AI support agents need firm boundaries around fraud. After mass bans, ChatPRD received both clumsy appeals and polished messages written by AI. Claire equipped her support agent with fraud tools and explicit rules preventing it from restoring accounts or distributing promo codes.

  7. Blunt defenses are sometimes the most effective. Blocking traffic from certain countries using Vercel Firewall significantly reduced abuse and forced Claire to reconsider ChatPRD’s international strategy. Her new default is simple: trust must be earned rather than assumed.

  8. Token fraud is affecting companies of every size. Claire found the same people abusing ChatPRD through rotating proxies across several major AI products. She has started discussing the problem publicly and filed FBI cybercrime reports with help from Codex.

  9. If a company sells AI, it is ultimately selling compute. Founders should track dollars instead of requests, monitor model spending continuously, close every free entry point, and verify the client rather than only the account. Claire also learned that fraud disappears quickly when expensive models are no longer available to steal.

I was a Claude hater. Fable 5.2 changed my mind.

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

In this solo episode, Claire tests Claude Fable 5.2 to see whether Anthropic has finally built a model she enjoys using. She turns a tweet into an animated marketing video, creates assembly instructions from photos of unboxed furniture, reworks a complex ChatPRD pipeline, and builds a fully functional 3D typewriter. She also explains where Fable fits alongside Opus 5.5, why its creative work impressed her, and why she still would not trust it to design a website on its own.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Fable 5.2 turned Claire from a Claude skeptic back into a fan. She found the original Fable difficult to understand and unpleasant to use, with Opus 5 offering little improvement. Fable 5.2 feels fast, capable, creative, and dramatically easier to work with.

  2. Fable 5.2 complements Opus 5.5 rather than replacing it. Opus remains the better default for most coding and knowledge work. Fable is the model Claire would choose for greater complexity, broader scope, or tasks that demand more creativity.

  3. Its speed changes how the model feels to use. Many benchmark tasks finished in under a minute, and even a complex animation took only 16 minutes. Fable also communicates sparingly during autonomous work, surfacing only the moments that require input.

  4. Fable 5.2 made AI video feel animated instead of assembled. From one tweet and the CXO.dev brand guidelines, it created a narrated story featuring custom invader-bot sprites that walk, jump, and cheer. No other model Claire tested produced anything comparable, so the task is becoming a permanent benchmark.

  5. Its spatial reasoning solved a real-world problem every other model failed to. Claire gave Fable low-resolution photos of an unassembled piece of furniture with no instructions. It identified the parts, created a diagram, and produced the correct assembly sequence, which her household successfully followed.

  6. Fable 5.2 is unexpectedly funny. It designed a bug-fighting game around real engineering tradeoffs, then made a trailer in which finance sees the token bill and downgrades the team to a cheaper model. The humor felt intentional enough to make Claire genuinely laugh.

  7. It also holds up on serious engineering work. Fable created a sensible migration plan for ChatPRD’s messy product-intelligence pipeline and aligned closely with Claire’s own roadmap. It worked autonomously and paused at appropriate moments, though the migration is still underway.

  8. Fable needs strong direction for visual design. It follows an existing brand system well, but its unguided web and storybook designs were unattractive. Claire expects to pair it with Opus 5.5 for frontend work and use a separate image model when original visuals are needed.

  9. The 3D typewriter was Claire’s “AGI moment.” Fable built a working keyboard in one shot, then added white-out, music, weather, timers, writing prompts, and multiple immersive settings. It turned an idea Claire never imagined building into a tool she wants to use every day.

  10. Fable 5.2 is available now, with an even faster mode coming. It is launching across the Claude API, cloud platforms, Claude apps, and Claude Code. Claire plans to compare it with the other new models in a full How I AI benchmark.

issues.title: 🔮 What Anthropic is really listing
issues.summary: Tithes, not tokens
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

It’s Anthropic’s big week. It will become the first real AI company in the West to list on a public market.

Anthropic has an extraordinary market opportunity. The battle hangs on the sustainability of its business model – whether falling token costs or competition from open-weight models won’t simply erode its margins. These forces, no doubt, exist. The bear case claims the company is merely a peddler of progressively devalued tokens. This misses the point.

Anthropic is building an ever-improving system that produces machine intelligence. That machine intelligence is valuable because of the nature of modern economies. Most value in our economies now comes from intangibles, scientific knowledge, patents, software, brand, and data. If Anthropic’s machine intelligence can create intangibles like these – breakthrough science, information, or software – then it should be able to create extraordinary value.

Over the past fifty years, value in the S&P 500 has shifted from tangibles, things you can count in warehouses or can stub your toe on. Most value now resides in that ethereal flim-flam of the intangible: brand, customer lists, patents, and software.

Put another way, Anthropic’s machine intelligence lets it compete for 92% of the value of the S&P 500 before it needs to deploy a single robot.

That is the big macro-level survey that paints the opportunity. But I’ve been digging deeper. My conclusion is that AI companies in general, and Anthropic, are in a unique position. Look at the chart below. Each time Anthropic announced a new product feature that encroached on a given sector, the stock prices of firms in that sector responded as you’d expect.

AI companies might be able to extract a permanent tithe on the economy. Anthropic, as the leading player, is best positioned to do that.

The following are my sketches. They’ll give you a sense of the direction that I think merits further exploration.

Capturing the intangible

Anthropic has three approaches to capturing value in an intangible economy:

  1. It can ask companies to pay to defend their assets. As I wrote in The Internet’s Wuhan moment, AI has laid bare the software’s non-existent security model. Anthropic’s Mythos is the world’s most powerful security-oriented AI.

issues.title: 🔮 The $22 billion question about AI self-improvement #610
issues.summary: Plus: Cheap solar, who pays for Claude & DNA immunotherapy++
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
It’s simply the best, data-rich source for the money on how AI is reshaping the economy. — Matt G., a paying member

Subscribe now

My AI agent bought an iPhone for me this week. For an Uber, I’d still reach for the app.

That’s where we start today – I look at which jobs are worth handing over to AI, and why more Brits are paying for Claude. We’ll also look at what cheaper renewable power still needs and whether AI self-improvement owes more to intelligence or a massive research budget.

If you’re a member of Exponential View, join me in the subscriber chat:

Claude Britannia

Brits are spending more and more on AI. One in twenty adults in the UK pays for AI, spending more than $1.3 billion a year. Five percent is early days, but it is a fast ramp – it was 1% two years ago, and 2.5% a year ago. London is the hotspot; the professional skew is predictable, with those involved in tech, finance, education, and PR. And we are increasingly falling for Claude. Its share has quadrupled in a year.1 Was the trigger the improved harness on Claude Cowork?

Separately, made his first purchase using his Instinct agent, sweaters for winter. My Instinct agent secured my iPhone Duo for me on Tuesday. ’s agent booked a squash court for a showdown with . We’re playing around with them and finding them quite useful.

But in general, agent-based shopping is still early. Uber says four rides out of 320 million during Halloween week were booked by agents. I’m not sure I’d use an agent to book an Uber yet; hitting the app is easier. But getting an iPhone Duo, which involved checking Apple’s website every few minutes from 7 am, is a perfect job for them. So is finding finicky, complicated products like surge-protected power extensions, medicine pouches, or, in Will’s case, woolly jumpers.

Subscribe now

Fair-weather friends

The technology is doing its bit. Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the median cost from $105 to $86 per MWh. North of Milan and Montreal (yes, they are on the same latitude), it falls from $164 to $99. Based on hourly modeling over ten years, and reckon that sun and wind mostly cover for each other – except for a difficult combined lull for about a week every four.

Ember also finds that 83% of the 750GW of fossil plants being planned sit where reliable renewables (with a bit of gas backup) cost under $100/MWh (which is roughly implied with oil at $60 a barrel).

My take is that technology costs will keep falling, and those that haven’t yet benefited from reductions (like panel installations) will start to yield as robotics improve. But redesigning the grid into a largely renewable-based one also requires more than better technology. It’ll need both a better cost of capital (gas plants still find capital cheaper than solar) and financial instruments that match energy prices to the volatility renewable-based energy brings.

issues.title: 🔮 What does it cost to make a worker?
issues.summary: Some early sketches of the economics of manufactured intelligence
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas that haven’t been fully polished. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

Here is another peek into my sketchbook. I’m trying to understand the economic trade-off between getting work done by an AI or a human. One way of doing this is to look at tasks in the economy and see how much it costs a human to do them compared to a machine.

Another way is to view the worker as an entity the economy needs, and to consider the minimum cost of creating one. (Of course, humans are much more than that, but I’m limiting the frame purely to economics here.) Those costs include the parenting, educating, and feeding from bairn to adult. We can then compare that to the cost of bringing in a machine capable of doing the same types of work using AI.

AI is manufactured intelligence. That is not the same intelligence that we humans have, but it’s clearly something that looks like intelligence.

While it is being manufactured, it’s highly replicable and follows the classic learning curve I described in my first book. And in my forthcoming second book, I extend these ideas.

Economically useful human intelligence is created very differently. It takes much longer than making a chip, and you don’t know the outcome for a long time.

issues.title: 🔥 Jensen Huang and the future of the AI boom
issues.summary: Good news for some, not so good news for others
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Jensen Huang has resigned.

The company is in an awkward position, having refused to put a succession policy in place. Colette Kress, the CFO, will step in until it finds a replacement.

Company scandal aside, and there has been a lot, it’ll have a big impact on the AI boom.

Nvidia has been, without doubt, the linchpin of that boom. In the five years to 2026, the firm sold nearly 14 million flagship AI chips. They account for 85% of the market. The company has provided financial guarantees to the constellation of upstart AI infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds, so they can get their business moving. It has been a substantial venture capital backer of AI companies, with nearly $10 billion across Europe in the last year – the biggest investor there.

The numbers don’t do justice to how important Jensen himself has been. This isn’t like Apple without Steve Jobs. When Steve Jobs relinquished the CEO role in 2011, shortly before he passed away, he left a well-briefed successor and a management team known to customers and the market alike. And if Nvidia has been the linchpin of the AI boom, Jensen has been the linchpin of Nvidia.

I thought of him as the person with the best visibility into what was going on in AI, simply because everything ran on his chips. He advocated open-source models, including, uncomfortably now, Chinese ones. And pushed for a more accommodating approach to China.

I’ve seen him in London a couple of times. Once, he arrived on stage from down the street with then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in tow. He brings energy and hands out billions of dollars. Calling out a startup’s name, followed by “I’m backing you with $500m” or whatever the number was. He returned a printout of our State of the AI Economy report, his signature across the front in gold marker, telling me it would be worth more now. Maybe even more after today.

The linchpin seems to be made less of solid steel and more of a well-worn leather. Will the ecosystem that depends on it stay on the road?

The current wave of AI investments, in model makers and infrastructure, is predicated on massive customer demand, not rampant oversupply. The industry’s common refrain over the past two years has been consistent: we are short on capacity. Not tomorrow, but today. That is why the spot prices for AI chips stay high even as they age. It’s why Anthropic has lined up $900bn of computing supply over the next 15 to 20 years – to make sure they don’t run short.

We’ve estimated that in the last 12 months, total revenues in the AI sector (outside of China) came to $188bn, growing faster than 4.2x a year. About 75% of that ends up at the infrastructure layer: the companies that own and operate the chips that do the calculations that make ChatGPT run for you.

The vast majority of revenue comes from chips made by Nvidia.

And the lack of capacity is what has created opportunities for new infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds. These young pups don’t have the track record of Microsoft or Google, so they have had to lean on Nvidia, their main supplier, for various kinds of guarantees. These guarantees range from the reasonably above-board to things that smell circular. While the numbers are large, for some companies (like Anthropic or XAI), Nvidia’s contribution is not a do-or-die proportion. But the man behind it all is leaving the building.

Demand stays

issues.title: The best pay leaders don’t want to run HR
issues.summary: They’d rather sit next to the CFO. Here’s why.
issues.author: Maria Colacurcio
issues.content_html:
A few months ago I was on a Zoom call with two business-unit CFOs at a company with 100,000 employees. They had just paid a big consulting firm to look at their pricing. The firm found the company was charging less than its own strategy called for. Fixing that added a point or two of margin, and the consulting project paid for itself.

So then I asked: Would you do the same thing for pay?

A long pause. Shrugs. Then one of them said, “Everybody believes we’re making the right ‘people’ decisions. Nothing is obviously broken.”

It almost always is broken. Just not in ways executives can see until someone adds it all up.

Pay is one of the biggest costs a company has. Most companies have a pay strategy on paper: where they want to land against the market, how they use salary ranges, what they say they reward. The finance department watches the total. It knows whether department leaders came in on budget with headcount projections. But the individual decisions behind it (offers, raises, bonuses, promotions) leak millions per year. And under new right-to-information and pay-transparency laws, pay that drifts from the agreed-upon strategy one decision at a time gets awfully hard to explain.

In the data we’ve analyzed so far, about 6% of accepted offers land outside the company’s own ranges, and one company was at 16%. At one company the written policy says offer around the middle of the band; only 19% of hires landed there. Often there’s a good reason. It just isn’t written down anywhere so nobody can explain it.

Added up, though, that’s money walking out the door, and it rarely shows up as a problem. The budget looks fine overall, so nobody goes looking. Across our customers, companies come to us having paid 6% to 7% more than they needed to, mostly because pay in certain functions just veers off course. Some of it is what we lovingly call Special Snowflakes: the vaunted hires, the one-off exceptions. Or it’s the manager who wanted to keep someone happy. Each exception seems reasonable at the time. Add enough of them up and you’ve got a pay strategy built on one-offs.

Compensation is a tough job right now. The market has split in two. On one hand, wage growth is flat and so is voluntary attrition. Nick Lichtenberg at Fortune summed up the week’s data in one line: “Workers are scarce, and they’re still losing ground.”

On the other hand, there are hypercompetitive pockets in AI, AI infrastructure and security. AI and machine learning engineers earn 15 to 20% more in base than comparable technology roles, and at senior levels the premium runs up to 30%. Employers are paying bonuses worth 20 to 24% of base for AI engineering, cybersecurity and data architecture skills.

Compensation teams sit between talent, finance and legal. Talent wants competitive offers to nab top people. Finance doesn’t want to spend more than necessary. Legal wants no pay-equity risk.

And pay compression, as it’s known, is very real: new hires are coming in at close to, or above, what long-time employees make. Three out of four companies in our data select “time at the company” as a factor to reward in their pay model. But in the regression models that look at actual impact, that factor explains nothing: at the typical company, tenure accounts for 0% of the difference in pay. And when tenure does have a measurable impact, 93.5% of the time it actually works against people. The people who stayed are the people whose pay fell behind.

The people who run pay, the heads of Total Rewards, feel this every day. They know with pay transparency looming, an explainable, consistent pay strategy will be crucial. And who makes the call on pay is shifting.

This fall, I was talking with the executive who runs pay at a large company where the head of HR had just announced their retirement. I asked whether they were going to go for the job. The answer? A firm no. They’d rather keep the seat next to the CFO and in front of the board’s compensation committee. That’s where the big decisions about money get made, and pay is money.

Right now, companies control pay with blunt instruments: cap the budget, freeze hiring and raises or lay people off.

Finance is also the only department in the company that has to show its work to someone outside it. Every year an auditor asks where a number came from, who owns it, and whether the trail holds up. That question is now reaching the numbers AI helps produce. In BDO’s survey of 200 finance leaders this fall, 99% said AI touches at least one estimate their auditor reviews, and fewer than half have a way to substantiate every result. The auditors will not let that stand for long. Nobody asks those three questions about a job offer or a bonus payment. The pay leaders who moved next to the CFO expect someone will, and they would rather be in the room that already knows how to answer.

As pay leaders move closer to the CFO and the board’s compensation committee, they can offer something better for the company and its people. Pay decisions that follow the strategy, hold up to scrutiny and can be explained to anyone who asks.

The payoff is millions in savings. Top talent hired for reasons you can actually defend. A system that keeps working as the company grows.

Remember those two CFOs on the Zoom? They didn’t blink to have someone check their pricing. But it didn’t occur to them to check on pay. That’s why the best pay leaders are clamoring for the seat next to the CFO — because pay is money.

It’s time it actually got looked at that way.

issues.title: Anthropic just set an IPO record nobody’s bragging about: $20 billion left on the table
issues.summary: The stock’s opening-day surge meant institutions, favored retail investors and the deal’s underwriters captured billions Anthropic could have kept for itself.
issues.author: Shawn Tully
issues.content_html:
The Anthropic IPO just delivered Wall Street’s AI bulls a strong vote of confidence. The Claude-purveyor’s big jump on its opening day of trading for now dispelled fears that investors’ faith in the profitability of this era’s signature technology was fading.

Here’s an issue that the bulls are ignoring, and that’s getting virtually no coverage in the media: Anthropic left an enormous share of the IPO’s proceeds on the table. We’re talking about roughly $20 billion that could have flowed into spending on AI infrastructure that instead went to big institutions, and privileged retail investors, that reaped a gigantic, one-day windfall, as well as the underwriters that will feast on big commissions they’ll receive from the clients they awarded shares at what looks like bargain prices.

The “left on the table” phenomenon looks amazingly like the scenario surrounding the SpaceX debut in June, though all told, the Anthropic forgone funding number’s even bigger. So let’s start by comparing the two offerings. In total amount raised, Anthropic edged SpaceX as the biggest IPO of all time, collecting a headline, gross amount from the shares sold to the public of $81.34 billion versus $75 billion for SpaceX.

For additional insights into the similarities and contrasts between the two IPOs, I spoke to Jay Ritter, professor at the University of Florida and the world’s leading expert in the field. First, Ritter noted that the percentage fees paid the underwriters are the two lowest numbers he’s ever witnessed, chiefly because the deals are so immense that even at what sounds like a tiny number, the dollars going to the underwriters are the biggest ever collected. The percentages are just a hair apart, 0.666% on SpaceX and 0.676% for Anthropic, a difference of just one-hundredth of 1%. All told, Anthropic is paying the syndicate led by Goldman Sachs$550 million versus $500 million for the SpaceX IPO, where Goldman also served as chief or “lead left” underwriter.

Second, Ritter notes that Anthropic is following SpaceX in departing from the usual practice by paying no fees on the 15% “over allotment” shares reserved for the underwriters to sell at the offering price in case the issue is over-subscribed, as in both of these super-coveted IPOs. On a third issue, the two offerings diverge substantially. “Anthropic is unique having a large amount of shares held by employees and investors that have no lockup period at all so they can be sold immediately at the market price,” says Ritter. He notes that the ability of these investors to place shares on the market on day one creates extra liquidity that may smooth potential price volatility in early trading.

On opening day, SpaceX shares jumped 19.2%. Hence, it collected $14.417 billion less than if it had sold at the price folks and funds were willing to pay—for example, had it deployed a “Dutch auction” instead of a traditional underwriting. That difference, Ritter notes, is known as the “amount left on the table,” or the forgone proceeds. By contrast, the Anthropic pop was slightly lower; shares rose from the offering price of $83 to $97.17 at the close, for a jump of 17.1%. But since Anthropic raised several billions more than SpaceX, the dollars left on the table figure was practically identical at $14.337 billion, or a mere $80 million less.

That near tie doesn’t tell the whole story. In addition to the $81.34 billion offering to the public, Anthropic also conducted a private placement that sold $26 billion in its non-voting N shares to a group including Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia. When sold, the N shares convert to the regular A voting category. Those legends of tech and other investors also paid 17.1% less than the market judged the shares were worth at day end. That’s an extra $4.4 billion that didn’t go to Anthropic’s treasury. Next comes the over-allotment, also known as the “greenshoe.” Selling another 15% of the shares at 17.1% less than the price at the market close amounts to an additional $2 billion “discount” from the price at 4 PM on November 19.

All told, the total comes to just over $20 billion. “Then you include everything, it’s the largest number left on the table in the history of IPOs,” says Ritter. It’s a superlative few on Wall Street are mentioning.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year
issues.summary: “If you go to any kind of [fashion] supply chain, whether it’s fabric production or garment production, most people are just kind of amazed by how chaotic it is."
issues.author: Jim Edwards
issues.content_html:
The fashion business thrives on the conceit that it is modern, on-trend, and all about what’s happening right now. But behind the scenes—in the textile mills and garment factories that supply major brands—is an industry that runs much as it did in the 1970s. Its supply chains are splintered, chaotic, and based in warehouses that are so old-fashioned they may not even be on the internet, according to Max Easton, CEO of Smartex.AI.

Most of the work is done by hand. Checking the quality of the fabric, for instance, will be performed by a worker holding a handful of color swatches, watching a roll of cloth go by all day.

“They’re looking for simple physical defects like holes, needles, the wrong yarn, something that would be noticeable in a garment, right?” Easton said to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon this year. For most brands, there is no such thing as a “white” T-shirt. It needs to be exactly the right shade of white—which might be a brilliant white or a creamier off-white.

But because the work is inspected by humans, fashion brands can never be quite sure that the quality of the fabric they’re buying is going to be consistent, or even match what they ordered.

“If you go to any kind of [fashion] supply chain, whether it’s fabric production or garment production, most people are just kind of amazed by how chaotic it is,” Easton said.

The chaos ends now, Smartex hopes.

The company has been working with Tony Fadell, the legendary codesigner of the iPod, iPhone, and Nest doorbell, to launch a physical AI product that can perform fabric quality checks continuously, at three times the speed of a human. Fadell—who has invested roughly $10 million in the company—is coming aboard as Smartex’s chairman. Strategic suppliers to H&M, which is also an investor in Smartex, are among its launch customers. Smartex has about 65 employees, revenues in the low millions annually, and has installed 800 of its older monitoring systems at clients in 10 different countries. The company’s valuation four years ago was $55 million; Easton declined to give an updated number.

The company is rolling out two new products: Smartex Inspect is a physical AI camera system that attaches to existing textile machinery to monitor the quality of the material as it goes by. And Smartex IQ generates intelligence from the supply-chain data that comes from Smartex’s suite of products.

Fabric inspection is “very, very technical, and it’s highly prone to human error,” Fadell told Fortune. “Depending on whether it’s in the morning or in the afternoon or on Friday afternoon … it’s all subjective. There’s no Pantone color for quality inspection.

“If you walked into a mill or a garment facility 50 years ago, and you walk into it today, it’s almost exactly the same—same processes, same equipment, same everything. It’s not been upgraded in any way. They might have email. In some cases they don’t even have Wi-Fi,” he said.

Companies are at the mercy of independent operators in multiple foreign countries. “They have zero visibility, even when [the product] arrives. They don’t know when it’s going to arrive,” Easton said.

For any player in the apparel chain, 50% of their cost base is fabric. But because the product is so variable in quality, a company like H&M will typically over-order about 5% more fabric than they need—in the sure knowledge that some of it won’t be good enough to use.

“So globally [at H&M], that’s like 2.5 billion meters of fabric every single year, just in case,” Easton says. At $4 a meter, that adds up to $10 billion in fabric costs. Easton reckons Smartex might save H&M $100 million annually simply by reducing its waste.

There are four things that H&M cares about, Fadell said: price, speed, quality, and sustainability. “A lot of times they commit to making this garment. They presell it online, but they can’t deliver it because the fabric shows up at the garment house, and they can’t make the garment because the fabric’s wrong in some way,” he said. “Reducing waste means better margins.”

The challenge isn’t as simple as pointing a camera at a textile processor and sending it to a computer. The system has to take into account changes in lighting, the speed at which the fabric is moving, small variations in color, and calibrate all that against a client’s own standards. Smartex has a library of 50 billion images of fabric to do that.

It is, admittedly, somewhat odd to hear Fadell—famed for creating some of the most iconic consumer products ever made—enthusing over loom quality and stitching. Still, he said: “This is something I’ve been investing in for a decade now, because I believe in very, very applied AI in the physical world, but you’ve got to make it really easy for the customers to use.”

issues.title: Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Ukraine
issues.summary: Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our … Continue reading "Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Uk
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our world.

Our mission at RSE is to help Americans better know and understand our neighbors through travel. But when we bring travelers to another country, we also bring their dollars — dollars that would support Putin’s aggression. Therefore, as of today, we have canceled all 2022 tours that include a stop in Russia.

Of course, we will keep a close eye on unfolding events and monitor any travel impacts through the rest of Europe. But it is important to keep geographic realities in mind and remember that a war in Ukraine is as far from our European vacation dreams as a war in Guatemala would be from Texas or Florida. For 40 years now, we have lived, worked, and traveled through many periods of tragic warfare in lands far from where we lead our tours (and some closer). And at this time, we see no reason to change the rest of our travel and touring plans.

The tragic reality unfolding in Ukraine only reminds me how important it is for Americans to keep on traveling and to do so in a way that makes us better and more engaged citizens of our world. I’m flying to Europe next month for a 40-day trip through a dozen great cities from London to Athens — and I’m proud that thousands of my fellow travelers will experience the European trip of their dreams while having rich learning experiences far from home on a 2022 Rick Steves tour.

In the meantime, let’s be thankful for our blessings, support our nation’s leaders as they do their best to navigate this crisis, and keep the troubled corners of our world (Ukraine, Russia, Afghanistan, and more) in our thoughts and prayers.

—Rick

issues.title: The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way
issues.summary: At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me. For total novices like Shelley … Continue reading "The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me.

For total novices like Shelley and me, it’s wise to be proactive about health and safety. Here are some tips I learned along the way:

Good boots, liner socks, slippery powder, and moleskin for tender skin are essential. We kind of became gear geeks — investing in good day bags (Osprey), woolen clothes (socks, underwear, shirts), and great hiking shoes. I was never so thankful for a wool cap in Europe.

I was skeptical about a lot of “good ideas,” but two things I eventually appreciated were a daily baggie of trail mix and my metal water bottle. (I complained about its steep $40 price tag…but soon came to recognize it was a great value).

I must say, if the weather turned bad and it rained hard, I think much of the trail would become no fun at all. In fact, it would be dangerous. Hiking poles are essential, and even in perfect weather, I would have been worried about a stumble without my own trusty set.

Eat a solid breakfast. The one day we had breakfast with no protein, climbing was tougher.

Put on sunscreen, even if the weather’s bad.

After learning my lesson on other long hikes, I decided to be religious about stretching on the Tour du Mont Blanc from the start. I had a routine of six stretches and spent time throughout the day making sure I didn’t tighten up. Very important!

Don’t be a hero. If skin is getting hot, wrap it up. I did the entire TMB hike without a blister — and then just got one on purpose in the last two hours.

Good gear, smart and proactive ways to stay healthy, stretching, and taking it easy… it all worked just great.

On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was … Continue reading "Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was the uphill part, and for others (with weak knees), it was going downhill. We just took it easy, with lots of little breaks.

For long climbs, steady, smaller steps are best. The trail could be really rocky, and I can’t imagine doing it without hiking poles. The trail signs were great, and apps made staying on the trail easy: Just follow the blue dot. And I got good use out of a top-quality printed map. (I’d spend time the night before reading up on the hike and familiarizing myself with the trail on the map.)

While the weather forecast looked threatening, we hiked six days (in September, during the last week of the season) and, thankfully, had only one hour of rain. Still, each day we’d pack rain gear, and we’d add on and take off layers as we gained and lost altitude. After four days, we had it sorted out, and it occurred to us rank beginners, “We’re getting good at this.”

As we were hiking in a big circle around a big clump of mountains and sleeping in charming towns each night, every day seemed to be up and over a daunting mountain pass. A nightly treat was a stroll under a milky blanket of stars.

issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Hiking Europe’s Tour du Mont Blanc was a totally different slice of European culture for me: Coming upon a remote farmhouse-turned-thriving-cafe serving wonderful lunches…flowers and cows (with classic bells) scenically sprinkled throughout…and an esprit de corps where everyone is like family.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends with fellow hikers. It seemed like half the people on the trail were from the US, and I met lots of Seattleites.

And in the interest of hiking light, lunches were very simple — just a sandwich from the hotel, maybe a carrot, a piece of fruit, and water. But upon reaching the mid-day summit, lunch was a marmot’s banquet. (Speaking of marmots, we saw no wildlife except a couple of mice that had been squished under hiking boots on the trail.)

issues.title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
issues.summary: TP-Link's struggle illustrates how Trump admin wields control over device makers.
issues.author: Jon Brodkin
issues.content_html:
TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

But a Stat report on MAHA's own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group's priority was ever winning elections in the first place.

The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.

The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA's clout in the midterms. issues.title: Think It, Say It: A Two-Step Guide To Writing
issues.summary: Everyone has the ability to write, especially when called into service, whether to pen a novel or an important press release.
issues.author: Andrew Welsh-Huggins
issues.content_html:
Today’s guest post is by author Andrew Welsh-Huggins.

Good writing advice can come in the most unexpected ways, as I learned recently at an event where I was the one who was supposed to be doling out ideas.

The forum was a “meet the author” event at a bookstore in our neighborhood on the West Side of Columbus, Ohio, during which I talked about my writing journey, followed by Q&A and a book signing.

After my presentation, rather than ask a question, an audience member related his own experience writing many years ago. A supervisor had asked him to draft a press release, striking terror in this non-writer’s heart.

“How do I do that?” he asked.

The supervisor responded: “Well, think about what you want to say, then say it.”

The story elicited a chuckle from audience members. But the more I thought about it, the more I realized how sound the advice was, and how succinctly it encapsulated a writing philosophy to live by.

Here are three things the remark brought to mind:

First off, unbeknownst to the person relating this anecdote, he waded perfectly into the plotter vs. pantser debate. As someone who has tried both pure pantsing and extensive plotting, and now straddles the line between the two approaches, I value the idea of thinking about what I’m going to write before I pen a single word. In my case, the “thinking” that comes before beginning a new book involves an outline that covers around 75% of what I expect to happen, leaving me plenty of wiggle room as unexpected characters and plot twists emerge during the “say it” portion of writing.

While not an outliner, crime novelist Karin Slaughter, in a 2023 interview, captured what I consider an ideal way to think about plotting and writing:

Before I start a book, I think about it a lot, and I get some idea of the story. Then I sit down with my editor, and we talk it through. And she’s like, ‘Okay, this sounds good’ or ‘Well, you’ve killed everybody in the first chapter.’ And I’ll be like, ‘Oh, maybe I should kill someone in the fifth chapter.’ That kind of thing. We don’t outline. It’s more like this happens, this happens, this happens. And that’s a good scaffolding for me to follow.

Secondly, the “first this, then that” structure of the audience member’s advice is a reminder that, having conceived of an idea, it’s important to get the work done. As crime writer Susan Isaacs has noted, “Writing may be an art. It is certainly a craft. But also it’s a job. You have to put in regular hours and go to work whether you feel like it or not.” Similarly, you can’t just think about what you want to say. At some point, you also have to say it however you best work: pen on paper, fingers on keyboard, dictation app primed and ready to go.

Finally, the audience member provided a valuable lesson in how we define writers. One of my least favorite words is the adjective-turned-noun “creative,” as in, “Of course he’s a good writer—he’s a ‘creative’.” A creative, the implication being, as opposed to the rest of us mere mortals. I couldn’t disagree more. Everyone is a creative in some form or fashion, whether they’re a gifted artist, baker, or car mechanic. And within the context of this essay, everyone has the ability to write, especially when called into service, whether to pen a novel or an important press release. As novelist Phoenicia Rogerson has said:

It’s quite common, I think, to have this idea of what a real writer is, and to go chasing after that, rather than letting yourself be who you are. If you write, you’re a real writer, and there’s no superiority in writing one genre over another.

“Think about what you want to say, then say it.”

I couldn’t have put it better myself.

issues.title: Lacquered wood, slips found in Han, Qin graves
issues.summary: An excavation of the Laohudun cemetery in Yunmeng County, Hubei Province, China, has uncovered more than 600 bamboo slips from the Qin Dynasty and another 600+ pieces of lacquered wood objects. Some of the lacquered artifacts are of shapes and decorative motifs that have never been seen before. The cemetery was in use from the … Read the full post → "Lacquered wood, slips found in Han, Qin graves"
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
An excavation of the Laohudun cemetery in Yunmeng County, Hubei Province, China, has uncovered more than 600 bamboo slips from the Qin Dynasty and another 600+ pieces of lacquered wood objects. Some of the lacquered artifacts are of shapes and decorative motifs that have never been seen before.

The cemetery was in use from the late Warring States period (475-221 B.C.) to the early Western Han Dynasty (202 B.C. – 9 A.D.). Excavations began in April, and so far 113 tombs from the Qin and Han dynasties have been uncovered. Forty of them have been waterlogged for centuries, creating anaerobic conditions that preserves organic materials like bamboo and wood.

The bamboo and wood slips are painted with ancient Chinese texts. There are 622 recovered from three toms. Preliminary translations have found texts covering a wide range of topics: a military inventory record noting ten local defenses in the region during the Qin Dynasty, the amount of grain, fodder and copper stored at two of them, details about the dimensions of defensive ditches, the number of soldiers, tools, weapons – the entire system of supplying and defending small garrisons on a daily basis.

There’s also a detailed calendar, information on how to pick auspicious days for events, rituals, prayers and other religious practices. There are slips with medical advice on malaria, toothaches and childbirth, information on silkworm bathing and a complete text on the moral education of women called “Teaching Daughters” or “Exhortations to Woman.”

The other grave goods found include bronze weapons, ceramics, jade objects, silk textile fragments, vividly painted wood objects like a pair of door panels, a pendant and bi set, and lacquerware pieces that are so well-preserved some of them look new. The lacquerware finds include bowls, cups, round boxes, flasks and a spoon with a standing human figure combined with a phoenix as the handle and bowl. One of the lacquer pots had a name inscribed under the bottom.

issues.title: Celtic silver coin hoard found in Hungary

The new substation is being built on a site where archaeological remains have been found in the past, triggering a professional excavation before construction began. Less than 40 cm (16 inches) under the surface, the … Read the full post → "Celtic silver coin ho
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A hoard of more than 200 Celtic silver coins has been discovered during construction of an electrical substation in Szombathely, Hungary. The new substation is being built on a site where archaeological remains have been found in the past, triggering a professional excavation before construction began. Less than 40 cm (16 inches) under the surface, the team from the National Archaeological Institute of the Hungarian National Museum Public Collection Center uncovered a few silver coins that had been scattered by agricultural work. Metal detectors then located the core of the hoard.

They were cached in a pit, some loose, some inside a small earthenware container. The coins are all Velem-type tetradrachms dating from the late 2nd century B.C. to the beginning of the 1st century B.C. On the obverse of the coins is a Celticized head in profile facing right bearing a pearl diadem and necklace. On the reverse is a stylized horse and rider wearing a crested helmet. They were probably minted in the Velem-Szentvid area, less than 10 miles from the find site.

Worth four drachmae a piece (hence “tetradrachms”), the denomination was widely used as trade coin and for state expenses throughout the Greco-Roman world. Their high silver content and large value made them unsuitable as a daily currency for individuals to spend, but perfect for them to store their wealth. The number of tetradrachms found in hoards attest to this usage.

The coin hoard is not the only significant find made in the two years since excavations began. Archaeologists have found material remains and thousands of artifacts covering almost 7,000 years of history. The oldest object is a polished stone axe used to fell trees and work wood. Another stand-out piece is a peacock-eye glass bead from the Early Iron Age (7th-6th century B.C.). From the remains of a Roman building, archaeologists recovered a fragment of a brick with a dog pawprint. It’s a flat tile, perhaps from a pilae stack that raised the floor over a hypocaust heating system.

A selection of the finds from the excavation will be exhibited at the Savaria Museum in Szombathely.

issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A rare medieval copper scepter head has been discovered in Kapan, southeast Armenia. Similar to a modified mace, the scepter is decorated with swirl patterns on the top and eight flattened blades. It was a symbol of royal power from a time when Armenia had vassal kingdoms under the central monarch. It dates to the 10th or 11th century.

The Kapan area was part of the territories of the princely Siunia dynasty. There was a small settlement at the site of what would become Kapan by the 5th century, and a fortress was built nearby in the 4th century. Kapan rose to major prominence in the 10th century when it became the capital of the self-style Kingdom of Kapan. It was a vassal of the Bagratid dynasty rulers of Greater Armenia, and survived a little more than 100 years, from 987 to 1170.

According to Stepanos Orbelian, a medieval Armenian historian, bishop, and a prominent member of the noble Orbelian dynasty, the capital of the Kingdom of Syunik was destroyed in 1126 under the command of Amir Harun as a result of Seljuk invasions, but the kingdom, thanks to the already impregnable fortress of Baghaberd, survived until 1170, being the last independent Armenian kingdom of Greater Armenia.

The first systematic archaeological investigations at the site of Old Kapan an environs began only in 2024. They found evidence of powerful fortifications, double-layered walls and a larger defensive tower near the entrance to the fortress.

Last year’s excavation uncovered the remains of foundations and column bases from a three-aisled basilica dating to the 4th or 5th century. Near the church, archaeologists found a stone oil press four feet in diameter. This year the team uncovered a furnace of polished stone that likely heated the water of a public bath at the site.

The scepter has been transferred to the Kapan Geological Museum for conservation and display.

issues.title: In Search of the Deep Life
issues.summary: Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up ... Read more The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled ​“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”​ As I explained:

“To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote ​several​​more​​essays​ on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I ​launched my podcast​, I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, ​The Deep Life: A Structured Approach​, is now ​available for pre-order​.

The Deep Life brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend ​Oliver Burkeman​, to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

“It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is thekey that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

  • ​Amazon​
  • ​Barnes & Noble​
  • ​Bookshop.org​
  • ​Amazon UK​
  • ​Waterstones ​

You can also pre-order ​a signed copy​ from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. Why not make it deep?

The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: The Good Thing About Hard Things
issues.summary: A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been ... Read more The post The Good Thing About Hard Things appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been attracting attention.

It explores an obvious question: do AI tools negatively affect your ability to think? It does so with a simple experimental design: participants were divided into two groups tasked with solving a series of math problems involving fractions. One group had to find answers on their own, while the other used ChatGPT to help.

At first, the ChatGPT group performed better, which is not surprising because LLMs are good at solving math problems. But then the researchers turned off the chatbot. Not only did the AI group’s accuracy fall below the control group, but many participants in the AI group gave up and started skipping questions altogether.

The researchers repeated the same experiment several more times, including one instance where math problems were replaced with an SAT reading comprehension prompt. They kept finding the same drop-offs in accuracy and persistence.

Here’s how ​a press release​ about the paper summarized these results:

“The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness. When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient.”

Brian Christian, one of the paper’s authors, put it plainly: “You almost couldn’t ask for a clearer story.”

I’ve spent the last decade thinking and writing about how technologies might accidentally degrade our ​cognitive fitness​, and how this might in turn degrade not only our economic productivity, but also the quality of the human experience more generally.

In this sense, these LLM findings aren’t revealing something new.

What is new, however, is the jaw-dropping speed of these impacts. We’re accustomed to slow-moving techno-cognition trends such as the negative effects of ubiquitous smartphone usage, which took years to emerge in the data.

With chatbots, the negative impact is immediate. The high generated by side-stepping mental effort using LLMs is so compelling that, with only a short exposure, hard thinking quickly becomes intolerable.

The good news is that we don’t yet know if these effects are permanent. Presumably, the research participants who struggled immediately after ChatGPT was turned off might do much better on the same type of test if they tried again later in a setting where AI help was clearly not an option.

But we cannot ignore the warnings that these early studies are generating. When it comes to our cognitive fitness, we’re playing with a powerful new force that we don’t yet fully understand.

A key theme of my work in the technology critic space is that a life without serious, sustained, intentional thought is impoverished. Thinking is how we make sense of ourselves and the world, and is how we imagine new horizons and create the key elements of our future. It’s at the heart of philosophy, theology, and human empathy; the ability that separates our species from all other animals.

Silicon Valley is good at creating tools, but terrible at figuring out how we should use them. The latter step is still up to us — but it requires us to care.
