issues.title: It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs
issues.summary: Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior. It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ ... Read more The post It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior.

It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ and reports from OpenAI that try to establish how unnerving and powerful (not to mention ​felonious​) their LLM-powered agent systems have become.

They then handed the baton to Anthropic, whose employees began ​publicly debating​ the exact probability that these technologies would lead to human extinction. They delivered this all with an eerie calmness that conveyed a nihilistic inevitability about their work.

The ground suitably softened, the campaign crescendoed with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodi releasing a letter, titled ​“We Must Pace the Frontier,”​ in which he enumerates all the harms his own company’s research might cause, and then, instead of apologizing and promising to stop, concludes that catastrophe can only be avoided if we “build the technology in the right way,” which involves – surprise, surprise – the government slowing down potential competitors and allowing the labs to take the lead in advancing the relevant tech. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly ​tweeted his support​ for this brave plan.

Internally, these labs have long embraced this style of messianic thinking, casting themselves as humanity’s only hope against the defied powers of superintelligent AI. This summer, in some sense, was their attempt to induct the rest of us into this long-held ideology.

It didn’t work.

Instead of inspiring the masses to stand up and applaud these engineers’ heroic rationalism, it made us instead start to ask, “What the hell is going on over in those labs?”

To that end, last Thursday ​I published an op-ed in TheNew York Times​ calling on Congress to begin a public fact-finding mission to uncover what research projects OpenAI and Anthropic are conducting, how they’re conducting them, and for what purposes.

I suggested three key areas to explore with this questioning:

  1. We must move past vague discussions of “AI” and instead isolate the specific types of systems that are creating problems. The frontier labs want us to think of AI as a singular technology on an inevitable, fixed trajectory. In reality, most of the problems in recent months result from a​ narrow band of incautious experiments​, conducted mainly by the frontier labs. They need to justify why they’re running them.
  2. We must examine the internal safety procedures surrounding these research efforts. ​OpenAI revealed​ a long series of unauthorized hacking attacks by their autonomous agents. Why weren’t these efforts stopped after the first such incident was revealed? Why not pursue criminal liability for them running systems they knew would likely commit crimes?
  3. We have to investigate the role of apocalyptic futurist ideologies in the decisions being made by the frontier labs, both about what research to pursue and how fast to pursue it. I’m increasingly concerned that OpenAI and Anthropic, in particular, are becoming increasingly reckless because they believe collateral damage is justified in a race to redeem humanity. (For more on these beliefs and their connections to the labs, see: ​this​ and ​this​ and ​this​, all published in the Times in just the last several weeks.)

“We need to stop letting a small number of private companies, acting and talking in increasingly erratic ways, dictate how we’re supposed to feel about A.I.,” I concluded. “We’ve heard what they want to say; now it’s Congress’s turn to step in on our behalf to find out what’s really going on.”

The post It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm.
issues.summary: Yesterday, multiple Anthropic employees casually announced online that they thought the types of AI they’re building could kill billions of people. Not in some distant ... Read more The post Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm. appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Yesterday, multiple Anthropic employees casually announced online that they thought the types of AI they’re building could kill billions of people. Not in some distant hypothetical future, but in the next few years. Understandably, this created a tsunami of media attention and anxious discussion.

I added to this debate with a ​brief essay​ of my own. I fear, however, that in the Sturm und Drang of that charged news cycle, some of my conclusions might have been hard to follow. So, I thought it would be useful to publish three short follow-up points that summarize my core claims more directly…

Point #1:Anthropic and OpenAI arenotable to create superintelligent AI.

The Anthropic employees who spoke out yesterday believe the force that might wipe out humanity will be “superintelligent” AI systems that are much too capable for us to control. Let me be clear: We have no idea how to create such machines. We don’t even know if they’re possible. And if they are possible, we are many, many key technical innovations away from getting there. (Simply scaling LLMs won’t be nearly enough.)

The LLM labs attempt to sidestep this reality ​by claiming​ their models will figure this all out on their own, programming better versions of themselves that will be far more capable than anything us measly humans can conceive. But this is just a warmed-over version of the recursive self-improvement trope that Silicon Valley futurists have been peddling ​since the 1960s​; a rhetorical crutch that lets you somberly discuss sci-fi scenarios without actually engaging with relevant technical details.

Point #2:But their obsession with superintelligence can still create real harm.

When you believe,​ as many at OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly do​, that humanity’s fate rests on winning a race to create the most powerful technology ever, you tend to care less about the damage you inflict along the way.

This is what happened with the HuggingFace hacking attacks from this summer. The experiments OpenAI ran were reckless. They took a relatively common technology called an LLM-powered agent, which is used with minimal issues by millions of software developers every day, and ​then added​ a bunch of dangerous features, removed restrictions, and released a whole mess of them into poorly fenced digital wilds. Why? They were desperate to make as much progress as quickly as possible on a hacking test that they felt was an important milestone en route to superintelligence.

This is the equivalent of deploying a fleet of experimental self-driving cars onto the interstate, hoping that at least one will avoid crashing long enough to win a navigation challenge.

In other words, this behavior was negligent. But they likely justified it because it served the far grander goal of summoning a digital God. (Clearly, there may be additional motivations at play here as well. Given OpenAI’s interest in an IPO, for example, there might have been pressure to do well on this particular benchmark to establish their model’s power. But the more I talk to sources connected to these companies, the more I’ve come to believe that their commitment to futurist ideas is what really drives a lot of their more irresponsible behavior.)

Ultimately, I think the HuggingFace attack is a good representation of the types of near-future harm we should actually be fearing if the LLM labs continue to operate as they currently are: that is, more cyber mayhem than catastrophic risk.

But just because these impending harms aren’t nearly as scary as the extinction events touted by the true believers, they’re still plenty worrisome. More importantly, they’re entirely avoidable!

Which brings me to my final point…

Point #3:AI progress does not have to be this scary or dangerous

First things first, it’s important to emphasize something that many media figures and commentators seem to be missing: AI is not the same thing as LLMs. Many of the most impressive AI systems that exist today – including those that beat humans at games, win Nobel prizes for studying proteins, and self-drive cars through crowded city streets – have very little to do with LLMs. Slowing down OpenAI and Anthropic doesn’t mean that you’re stalling AI progress in general. You would only be impacting the subset of AI research that focuses on hyper-scaled LLMs as a central component.

But even when we do focus specifically on LLM-based AI research, none of the harms I described above are unavoidable. They’re instead side effects of reckless experiments motivated by the pursuit of superintelligence.

If the LLM labs simply acted more responsibly, focusing on producing useful products instead of summoning an AI messiah, and following common-sense research safety protocols instead of racing haphazardly toward some imagined utopia, we could be enjoying a steadily advancing AI industry promising tools that excite us, all without having to endure regular doses of dread and fear.

But due to their ideological commitments to superintelligence, these labs seem incapable of such reforms.

This last observation is what’s driving me to advocate for intervention. Those Anthropic employees absurdly implying that they’re willing to risk a digital holocaust to realize their futurist vision was my last straw. They’re far too weird for us to expect them to ever act reasonably.

Please don’t take this as a call for abandoning AI research or somehow ceding AI supremacy to China. Our problem is not with AI progress, but instead with the eccentric way this small group of companies is trying to achieve it. Fix that, and AI innovation can continue, free from all the doom and with much less potential for collateral damage.

The post Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm. appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: Dear SaaStr: What Sucks About Being a CEO?
issues.summary: Dear SaaStr: What Sucks About Being a CEO? A few learnings here: #1. The pressure ebbs and flows, but it never ends. Once you ship, you’re always under the gun. In the earlier days, it’s under the gun to make the cash last. Later, cash doesn’t matter as much as growth. But you always have... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Dear SaaStr: What Sucks About Being a CEO?

A few learnings here:

#1. The pressure ebbs and flows, but it never ends. Once you ship, you’re always under the gun. In the earlier days, it’s under the gun to make the cash last. Later, cash doesn’t matter as much as growth. But you always have to grow. In fact, each year, you often have to add as much in bookings as all the prior years combined.

#2. The others can quit, but you can’t. This isn’t that bad in reality, but it can feel that way in tougher times. That you can’t quit. The rest all can. You always have to be there.

#3. Lack of appreciation . This has weighed on me more and more as the years have gone by. One of the most rewarding parts of being a founder is enabling careers. Its tough when folks don’t appreciate it, or don’t appreciate it much. You can’t say it aloud, but it’s tough.

#4. When the best leave . I know many CEOs and founders say it’s great to see their top folks move on to even bigger and better things, but man it’s tough.

#5. There’s always some CEO that has it a bit easier. OK, this one is subtle, but it’s real. There’s always some hotter startup, growing faster. That finds it easier to raise capital, and recruit. It not that CEOs mostly need to beat folks that aren’t the direct competition. It’s more than it weighs on you. That say Notion or Calendly or whomever is just killing it, seems to be doing with about the same amount of energy as you are putting in. It’s just, they are going even further. You can’t help but sort of wonder, “Man, if only I was CEO of Notion”. At least a little bit.

#6. It never gets easier. Yes, you get better. But it never gets easier. By contrast, a lot of “ordinary” jobs do get easier as you get better and better at them.

#7. Your family probably won’t really understand . They may be there, they may not. They may drift away over time. The intensity of being a CEO, of always being responsible for everything, for always — most folks won’t get it.

What Does — And Doesn’t — Get Easier After $10m ARR

issues.title: 20VC x SaaStr: Jensen Out at Nvidia, Anthropic’s $1.4 Trillion IPO, and HubSpot Brings Back Brian Halligan
issues.summary: Plus: why LPs will now grade VCs on $20B+ outcomes, why SMBs stopped buying software, and what a two-day Microsoft outage says about how fragile everything has become There was more news this week than in almost any week since Harry, Rory and I started doing this together. Nvidia lost its founder. Anthropic got set... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Plus: why LPs will now grade VCs on $20B+ outcomes, why SMBs stopped buying software, and what a two-day Microsoft outage says about how fragile everything has become

There was more news this week than in almost any week since Harry, Rory and I started doing this together. Nvidia lost its founder. Anthropic got set to price the largest IPO ever. HubSpot went back to its founder. Microsoft 365 went down for most of two days. We recorded Monday, before Anthropic priced and before anyone knew whether Jensen would come back. Here are the 11 things that mattered most, followed by the best lines from each of us.

1. Jensen Huang Resigned After 33 Years, and Rory and I Disagree on Whether He Comes Back

What happened: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s president, chief executive and a member of its board, effective immediately, with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. The trigger: Huang admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive, and after the board opened an investigation, a second alleged affair was reported involving a direct report. Separately, Commerce and Justice are looking at chips sold into Southeast Asian data centers that may have served Chinese customers. A petition to bring him back drew around 200,000 signatures, and by Monday Jensen said he’d return if asked.

Rory’s read: Decisions made in haste are usually wrong. He would have pushed for a leave of absence and an interim CEO to buy time. Four or five of these directors have been on the board for 30 years, and Jensen is the most important business relationship of their lives. For them to vote against him, something serious had to be going on. His gut says no return without a board change.

My read: I think there’s a high chance he comes back. The spy story will fade. The export issue is bigger, possibly 20% of revenue counting China, but if Jensen is guilty, so is the CFO who signed the financials. Colette Kress now has to stand behind the guidance she signed as CFO. Her job, more than his, was to know where every GPU went.

Rory’s twist: If he owned 100% of the stock, Jensen is the person he’d most want running Nvidia. But even if he returns, Rory doesn’t think he gets back the freedom to finance the AI ecosystem. The minute he left, everyone started trashing the circular deals they’d cheered for two years.

2. Anthropic Is the Biggest Winner of the Nvidia Mess

What happened: Jensen’s biggest strategic push heading into 2027 was a credible U.S. open-weight alternative, including a pending acquisition of Hugging Face. Reports say some Anthropic people were pleased with how the week went.

Rory’s read: The S-1 says roughly $10B went into training Anthropic’s last model. Nobody but Nvidia had the money and motive to fund a serious U.S. open-weight effort. If that stalls, and China pressure pushes buyers away from Chinese open models, the winner is the closed-weight U.S. provider with pricing power. Anthropic isn’t a big Nvidia customer. OpenAI is.

My read: Nvidia’s remote data centers near China were legal at the time. They no longer are. But if you’re Anthropic watching your models get distilled a few hundred miles from your biggest competitors, that loophole looked like theft. I don’t know that Dario is gloating. It’s still a real boost.

What the Nvidia board should have done

“One of the things I have learned is decisions in haste are often wrong.

Take a leave of absence. We need to figure this out, get to the bottom of it and slow the whole thing down so you can make a better decision.

When I have made dumb… https://t.co/sNw1Sh7qAZpic.twitter.com/BcJiPIsu25

— Harry Stebbings (@HarryStebbings) November 19, 2026

3. Anthropic Will Hit $100B in Revenue With 1/12th the Employees Google Had at the Same Size

What happened: The 825 million-share offering could raise up to $64.4 billion at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, with pricing expected November 18. The IPO was reported six times oversubscribed, and could raise as much as $90.4 billion including a $26 billion private placement. Trading on Nasdaq as ANT was set to start November 19.

My read: The oversubscribed book is the least interesting part. At $100B in revenue, Google had 81,000 employees and Meta had 71,000. Anthropic will get there, likely by Q1 on run-rate, with fewer than 6,000. Yes, $10B goes to compute instead of humans. But that’s 1/12th the headcount, versus the roughly 30% smaller go-to-market teams at AI-native companies like Harvey and Sierra. For jobs, that’s worse than anything we’ve discussed.

Rory’s pushback: This is the extreme case of compute leverage, which is why the people there get paid so much. An old-school consulting firm won’t end up with $5 to $7 of inference per $1 of labor. He thinks it’ll be less grim for jobs than I do.

Harry’s addition: The rumored 40% layoffs at ServiceNow. Unconfirmed, but I think it’s real.

At $100 billion in revenue Anthropic got there with 1/12 the employees that Google had.

“At $100BN in revenue, Google had 81,000 employees. Meta had 71,000. Anthropic will have fewer than 6,000.

The next $100BN company got there with a 12th of the employees of Google and Meta.… https://t.co/sNw1Sh7Yqxpic.twitter.com/MGRWSNjivv

— Harry Stebbings (@HarryStebbings) November 19, 2026

4. LPs Will Now Grade VCs on How Many $20B+ Companies They Own

What happened: Anthropic went from founding to a trillion-dollar listing in about five years. SpaceX took more than two decades. Spark and Menlo led the key early rounds. Sound Ventures turned roughly $435M into about $7B.

Rory’s read: Spark and Menlo will play with house money for years, and everyone else will work just as hard for a tenth or a twentieth of the return. That’s an extreme power law, and it can get in your head. No meaningful venture money got into Anthropic below $5B, and Spark came in from its growth fund while the company was pre-revenue. If only 10 or 20 companies a cycle reach $20B+, the odds of landing one at seed or A go down. That favors the early-plus-growth fund structure.

My read: When I started, one unicorn was enough for LPs to come find you. Now it’s how many $20B+ companies you have, ideally bought below $20B. Carta’s Q3 2026 data shows deal count down 21% and dollars up 2.5x. Fewer rounds, much bigger checks.

Harry’s addition: LPs getting Anthropic distributions will redeploy, and early Anthropic employees are already angel investing in U.K. companies.

5. Every Mega Fund Is Raising Again in Q1 2027

What happened: The mega platforms all raised in Q1 2026. Every one of them is now lining up to raise again starting January 1, roughly 12 months later.

Rory’s read: When you raise money quickly, you usually don’t make as much. The smartest Anthropic checks were written in early 2023 and 2024, when people were scared.

My read: Deployment pace is feeding the markups. Do the best AI companies justify $10B to $20B to $40B in six months? On a spreadsheet, sure. But some of it is the need to deploy justifying itself. If 8x funds compress to 3x or 4x, maybe that’s fine.

6. IC: $200M Into Mercor at $20B, a Pass on Kalshi and Fractile

What happened: Kalshi is in talks to raise fresh capital at a valuation of $65 billion, roughly 62.5% above the $40 billion valuation it locked in only weeks earlier. Mercor, a leader in AI training data, is raising at $20B. Fractile, an inference chip startup competing with Groq and Cerebras, is raising $720M at $7.5B.

My read: A weak lineup after last week’s Zipline, Fal and Revolut. Kalshi at $65B carries too much regulatory and litigation risk. Fractile has no revenue and is the 11,000th inference chip startup. Mercor is a great space because the labs don’t want this work, but I can’t predict the future of the dirty work. I’d pick it because we have to put money to work.

Harry’s read: Bull on all three. Kalshi leads a monster U.S. sports betting market, and states will get too addicted to the revenue to ban it. Mercor could see $10B of spend from the labs. Fractile has a reported $250M order from Anthropic, and chips are specializing.

Rory’s read: At this stage, every company is good. The only question is value relative to TAM. Cerebras is public at roughly $1B of revenue this year, valued in the high $20Bs. Would he buy Fractile over that? He doesn’t know. Mercor has five or ten customers, but each may spend a billion on training data. For Kalshi at around $5B in revenue, the question is the sober TAM: how many bored 25-year-old guys bet on sports?

The decision: $200M into Mercor at $20B.

7. Without Jensen, the Liquidation Preference Got Weaker

What happened: Nvidia’s run of acqui-hires and backstops, including talks around Reflection and the pending Hugging Face deal, is now in doubt. Poolside sold because it couldn’t raise the capital it needed.

My read: For two years, a lot of AI deals carried an unspoken safety net: Nvidia or a friend would buy the team or backstop the round. I don’t think the CFO-turned-CEO is going to buy all these kids for $15B or $17B. If Salesforce also sits out 2027 digesting this year’s deals, it’s a very different year from the “you can’t lose with a liq pref” year of 2026. Will Thinking Machines survive? I don’t know.

Rory’s read: Washington is split, with Commerce and Lutnick in the sell-to-China camp and Rubio in the don’t-sell camp. You’re dealing with a government that’s mad at itself, which could mean two years of regulators kicking back any acquisition. He hopes Hugging Face got a good breakup fee.

Harry’s read: Nearly perfect timing on Hugging Face, assuming it closes.

8. HubSpot Went From 10,000 Net New Customers a Quarter to Guiding Below 5,000

What happened: Co-founder Brian Halligan returned as CEO, replacing Yamini Rangan in an abrupt leadership reset as the company races to reposition around AI agents. Its shares have halved this year, and Adobe’s Karen Burgess will become finance chief. Halligan called it a refounding, with HubSpot as a “customer relationship harness.”

My read: HubSpot added about 10,000 net new customers a quarter like clockwork, even through the 2024 downturn. Then 6,000, then 5,000, and now guiding below that. Monday.com went from roughly 1,200 net new 10-plus-seat customers to under 200. Net new logos were always my lighthouse metric, and price increases can mask the decline for years. Founder energy will help. The question is whether it’s enough, fast enough. And Intercom doesn’t prove what VCs say it does. Eoghan came back and went all-in on agents, and it worked, but it got to roughly $100M of agentic revenue and we never saw the next act.

Rory’s read: No B2B company from the pre-AI era has reaccelerated above 30%. At a billion in revenue, you’re playing to push growth back to 25%, while a Sierra growing 4x gets all the sizzle. Scale backed HubSpot’s Series C in 2010, and he isn’t sure a 100-person HubSpot customer has an opinion on “harnesses.” But when boards’ backs are against the wall, they bring the founder back, and in each recent case it was right.

Harry’s read: He asked Daniel Dines why he’d go back to UiPath. Man loves to struggle, and founders who’ve already made their money come back with an aggression outside CEOs can’t match.

9. SMBs Stopped Buying Software, but They Buy an $800 Receptionist Agent the Same Day

What happened: Net new customer counts at HubSpot and Monday.com have fallen sharply over three quarters, and Ramp data shows newer CRMs like Attio picking up only a small amount of that spend.

My read: This isn’t vibe coding. Your average SMB isn’t building its own CRM. They’re just not buying, running Google Sheets plus ChatGPT another six months rather than spend $40K on HubSpot. Meanwhile, three of my portfolio companies selling $500 to $1,000 a month front-office agents close prospects the same day. The SMB’s P0 is “my receptionist quits every Wednesday,” not a Kanban board.

Rory’s read: The truth is in the middle. Every associate at his firm has built a Claude front end on Salesforce, and nobody logs into Salesforce anymore. Granted, they went to HBS and work in San Francisco.

Harry’s read: Monday’s users are not vibe coding their own CRM.

10. Microsoft 365 Was Down for Two Days, and Fireworks Got Called Out by Its Own Customers

What happened: Microsoft says its Microsoft 365 services are fully operational again after a global outage that ran from November 12 to November 14, 2026. An issue linked to an earlier network-capacity upgrade surfaced after a more recent network change. The FAA also had a nationwide ground stop tied to a contractor’s router problem. Notion, Cursor and Harvey all publicly named Fireworks after a breach, and an Optimizely compromise hit sites including CNN, the BBC and Zoom.

Harry’s read: Air traffic control, Microsoft, the NSA’s internal comms. He’s never seen systems this fragile. The FAA outage was straight out of Die Hard 2.

Rory’s read: These were old-school IT failures, not AI attacks. When DocuSign got big, he brought in a board member with a cyber background who told the team: you’re going to get hacked, here’s what you spend. Mission-critical companies need that seriousness now.

My read: It’s DDoS 2.0. Microsoft’s bug sat in production for four months until load hit a new level. Now anyone can spin up 10,000 agents and probe every network with traffic, load and hacking at once. We want one-person billion-dollar startups, and those products will have close to zero security. I’m not sure you should trust any web analytics plugin, or any new payments startup besides Stripe or Adyen.

Harry’s addition: Fireworks has a world-class engineering team. If it still happened to them, everyone should be worried.

11. OpenAI Bought Adessia, and Horizontal Agents Are Already Locking In

What happened: OpenAI acquired Adessia, a travel-focused personal agent founded by Sonder founder Francis Davidson. Harry’s question: are vertical personal assistants over?

My read: I’m all-in on Muse, Meta’s horizontal agent. It runs our outbound, content editing, clips and attendee analysis, and reranks every inbound venture deal each night. Mine and Amelia’s coordinate with each other without telling us. With 20 or 30 workflows running, a shallow moat has gotten wide. And this is how SMB software gets displaced: you get a $30K HubSpot quote, realize Muse can do more of it than you thought, and push the purchase out.

Harry’s read: He has about 50 automations on Instinct. Switching would be a real pain.

Rory’s read: Power users will gravitate to whoever can give them the most functionality at a tenth of the cost, and that’s Meta. If most users don’t need that much compute, Instinct has a chance. Still scary when a company with 4 to 5 billion users ships something more powerful than yours. It didn’t work for Threads, though.

On the workforce: Harry’s biggest challenge is getting teams to ask “could an agent do this?” first. My view: our agents now do all our collections, replacing a contractor who billed $3,000 to $4,000 a month. You won’t fire people. They’ll leave, and you won’t backfill. We went from 20 people to 3 humans and 21 agents. Rory’s counter: someone then spends 6 to 10 hours a day managing agents.

On SpaceX, briefly: Rory called Starship one of the year’s top five achievements. But launch is under 10% of SpaceX’s market cap, and most of the TAM is compute. You buy SpaceX based on whether Anthropic is buying more compute a year from now.

Quotable Moments

Rory O’Driscoll

  • “If I owned 100% of the stock of this company, the person on the planet I would most want to run this company is Jensen.”
  • “You’re not just dealing with a government that might be mad at you. You’re dealing with a government that might be mad at itself.”
  • “You buy SpaceX the stock entirely on the basis of what you think Anthropic will be paying you one year from now for that compute.”

Jason Lemkin

  • “At $100 billion in revenue, Google had 81,000 employees. Meta had 71,000. Anthropic will have less than 6,000.”
  • “I think the liquidation preference has been weakened by the Nvidia drama.”
  • “You know what my P0 is? My receptionist quits every Wednesday. That’s what people want to buy. Not Kanban crap.”

Harry Stebbings

  • “Every single fund is queuing up out the door for Jan 1. We have to get the bag.”
  • “Man loves to struggle.”
  • “Right now the clips that you make, we can’t do with AI. In a year we will be able to. You need to get better or you will be replaced.”

issues.title: The Top 10 Metrics From Anthropic’s IPO for B2B Execs: $33 Billion in Nine Months, 900% NRR, and 12x More $100K Customers in a Year

Then it did $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. No B2B company is going to copy that growth rate. But we can still learn from Anthropic.... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Anthropic’s revenue went from $41M in 2023 to $386M in 2024 to $4.585B in 2025. Then it did $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year.

No B2B company is going to copy that growth rate. But we can still learn from Anthropic. Most of the operating metrics apply to any B2B + AI company at $10M or $100M in ARR.

My Top 10 Learnings for B2B Folks:

#1. Net Revenue Retention of ~900%, Excluding Flat-Fee Plans

Anthropic reports roughly 900% net revenue retention: existing customers collectively generated about nine times as much revenue in the September quarter as they did a year earlier. Snowflake was at 158% when it filed and GitLab was at 152%, and people thought those were crazy.

The definition in the filing matters here. The number reflects how much a year-old cohort now spends, excluding Pro and Max subscribers. All of that 900% comes from metered accounts. The flat-fee subscriptions aren’t in it.

A seat-priced product tops out somewhere around 120-130% NRR, because a customer can only add so many seats. The 900% happens when the bill grows with the work the product does.

#2. $100K+ Customers Went From 950 to 11,900 in One Year

As of Sept 30, more than 11,900 customers were at $100K+ in trailing-12-month revenue, up from more than 950 a year earlier. Further up: 1,900+ above $1M and about 250 above $10M.

The filing also discloses about 40 million customers below $100K. Anthropic leads with the $100K count because that’s the number that shows enterprise traction. If you’re selling to the enterprise, that cohort belongs at the top of your board deck too.

#3. Gross Margin of 85.5%, Up From 29.4% a Year Earlier

The amended prospectus puts cost of revenue at $4,812 million against $33,242 million of revenue for the first nine months of 2026, an 85.5% gross margin by FourWeekMBA’s arithmetic, up from 29.4% a year earlier.

Two caveats. Anthropic moved gross margin off the income statement, so this is derived from the footnotes. And per The Information, the ~85% excludes the cost of developing its models.

Still, a year ago this business kept 29 cents of every revenue dollar after serving customers, and now it keeps about 85. If your AI product runs at 50% gross margins today, that’s where you are now, not where you’ll end up. It’s a bad reason to set prices at cost-plus.

#4. Compute Went From 48% of Revenue in Q2 to 58% in Q3

In the first half, revenue outran compute badly. In Q2 2026, revenue rose 1,368% year over year while compute costs rose 300%.

Then Q3 reversed part of that. Compute as a share of revenue went from 48% in Q2 to 58% in Q3. And Anthropic disclosed purchase commitments of $895.4 billion.

Inference cost per dollar of revenue doesn’t go down every quarter. It moves with model mix, agent workloads, and how much heavier usage gets. Track it quarterly, next to gross margin, so a bad quarter shows up before your board asks about it.

#5. Sales & Marketing at 23% of Revenue (First Half)

First-half 2026 sales and marketing was $3.808B, about 23.4% of revenue. That’s at 1,000%+ growth. Plenty of B2B companies growing 30% spend twice that ratio.

When the product is pulling, S&M grows slower than revenue. If your S&M ratio is flat or rising while you grow, you need to fix the product and the pricing before you add AEs.

#6. 79% of Revenue Is Consumption-Based

In the first nine months of 2026, consumption brought in $26.3 billion, or 79% of revenue, and subscriptions $6.9 billion, or 21%. The Pro, Max, and Team plans everyone sees are the smaller business.

The filing also shows the cost of consumption pricing: customer spending fell about 20% in the two weeks ended Jan 2, 2026, vs. the two weeks ended Dec 19, 2025. Usage revenue drops when customers’ engineers go on vacation. Committed-spend contracts are what keep a usage forecast intact through December.

#7. 48% of Revenue Came Through Cloud Marketplaces (First Half)

48% of H1 2026 revenue came through cloud marketplaces, reported gross. Marketplaces also account for 58% of receivables.

So nearly half of Anthropic’s revenue gets bought through AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, because enterprises have committed cloud spend they need to draw down. If you sell to the enterprise and aren’t listed there, procurement takes longer than it has to.

#8. Under $1 of Every $1,000 in Fortune 500 Spend

Anthropic already counts more than half the Fortune 500 as customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue. Among the publicly traded companies in that group, spending with Anthropic still averages less than one dollar for every thousand dollars of total expenses. The ten largest Fortune 500 customers spend more than 8x the group’s average share of expenses, but still below 1%.

The denominator is total expenses, not the IT budget. Anthropic is going after spend on headcount, services, and operations, not just the software line.

I use this exact test for agentic B2B deals in Fund II. I won’t invest unless the company unlocks budget beyond software, and the proof is deal sizes at least 2x what pre-AI competitors get.

#9. More Than Half of $100K+ Customers Use Two Products, Up From 30%

More than half of $100K+ customers used both Claude Platform and at least one Anthropic application in the September quarter, up from about 30% in Q4 2025.

That’s the second-biggest NRR driver in the filing, after pricing. API customers picked up Claude Code and the apps, and app customers started building on the API. If you have a second product, report its attach rate in your top cohort every quarter.

#10. Customers Outside the Top Five Went From 64% to 79% of Revenue

The top five customers were about 25% of revenue for the first nine months of 2026. But customers outside the top five supplied about 79% of September-quarter revenue, up from about 64% in the March quarter. One customer, “Customer C,” went from 43% of revenue in 2023 to 11% in H1 2026.

The top five didn’t shrink to get there. Each top-five customer hit a revenue record in the September quarter. The rest of the base grew faster. Early concentration is survivable if the trend line looks like this, and that trend line is what to show your board.

5 More Numbers From the Filing

  • Q3 growth slowed, from a very high base: Q3 revenue was $17.0bn, up 46.7% on Q2, after Q2 had grown about 140% on Q1.
  • Operating income moved back and forth: Q3 was a $567M operating loss, after Q2’s $974M operating income.
  • The net loss is mostly accounting: Of the $80.7B first-half GAAP net loss, $72.4B is a fair-value change on convertible notes and SAFEs.
  • Revenue per employee: over $6.6M on a trailing basis. Strong public B2B companies typically land somewhere around $300K-$500K.
  • The most regulated buyers are already in: The customer list includes all ten of the largest banks and nine of the ten largest pharma companies.

Five Numbers to Add to Your Next Board Deck

  • NRR on usage-based accounts, reported separately from seats
  • $100K+ customer count and its year-over-year growth
  • Inference cost as a percentage of revenue, by quarter
  • Second-product attach rate in your top cohort
  • Your spend as a share of your customers’ total expenses, not just their software budget

Anthropic grew 12x in a year while gross margin went from 29% to 85% and S&M stayed under a quarter of revenue. Your numbers will be smaller, but you can track all five of these metrics at your scale.

issues.title: KeyBanc’s 2026 AI x Software Survey: 24% Median ARR Growth, Only 6% at the Rule of 40, and 43% of Vendors Watching Customers Vibe Code Their Product
issues.summary: KeyBanc Capital Markets just published the 17th edition of its private software benchmark. For years it has been one of the better sources of private B2B data. Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
KeyBanc Capital Markets just published the 17th edition of its private software benchmark. For years it has been one of the better sources of private B2B data. This year KeyBanc added a large AI section covering pricing, AI costs, agents, internal adoption, and whether customers are building their own replacements.

The survey ran from July through September 2026. 81 companies took part, and 62 of the answers came from CFOs and CEOs. Median ARR was $22M in 2025, so most of the sample is $10M-$50M B2B companies.

The sample is small. Some of the cuts below rest on 4 to 15 answers, so read the medians as directional.

The top takeaways:

  • The median company grew 24% in 2025, plans 23% in 2026, and plans 40% in 2027. Only 6% met the Rule of 40 in 2025. 62% plan to meet it in 2027.
  • 43% of vendors say customers are already using AI coding tools to rebuild their product or features. At companies under 100 employees, it’s 55%.
  • Only 41% charge for AI. The most common model is bundling it into the core price. Where it is charged, the median premium is 20%.
  • Only 8% report seat compression from AI.
  • 30 of 68 companies are over budget on AI spend, mostly because token usage beat the plan. Companies spending more than 5% of revenue on AI run 66% gross margins. Light spenders run 78%.

1. The Median Plan Goes From 23% Growth in 2026 to 40% in 2027

The median trajectory, using management’s own forecasts:

  • ARR growth: 24% (2025) → 23% (2026E) → 40% (2027E)
  • EBITDA margin: -3% → 1% → 8%
  • Rule of 40: 16% → 20% → 44%
  • Share of companies at Rule of 40: 6% → 18% → 62%

The median company plans to speed growth up by 17 points and add 7 points of EBITDA margin in the same year. That would follow a 2026 with flat growth.

These operators did beat their own plan last year. Last year’s survey forecast 20% growth for 2025, and the actual was 24%. EBITDA was planned at -4% and came in at -3%. A 4-point beat is still a long way from a 17-point acceleration.

The 12 companies with “very high” confidence in their forecast plan about 30% growth for 2027. The companies with “moderately high” or “average” confidence plan 40-41%.

The GTM side of the plan assumes every efficiency metric improves together:

  • New-customer ARR per AE: $411K → $450K → $487K
  • Quota attainment: 70% → 75% → 80%
  • Gross magic number: 0.76 → 0.79 → 0.97
  • CAC payback: 21 → 19 → 17 months

Meanwhile, 84% say AI has had no material effect on how long deals take. 9% say cycles got shorter, and 7% say they got longer. Median cycles are 2 months in SMB, 3 in mid-market and 8.5 in enterprise. KeyBanc titled that slide “Buyer Process, Not Vendor Efficiency, Sets Deal Pace.”

On one of these boards, I’d underwrite the 30% the high-confidence operators plan. Then I’d ask management for a quarter-by-quarter bridge to the other 10 points.

2. 43% of Vendors Say Customers Are Rebuilding Their Product With AI Coding Tools

43% of respondents report customers using AI coding tools to recreate their product or features. Exposure falls with company size:

  • Under 100 employees: 55%
  • 100-249 employees: 40%
  • 250+ employees: 25%

By sector, vertical software is the most exposed at 48%. Horizontal and infrastructure are both at 39%. KeyBanc analyst Jackson Ader noted that 43% is far more than the share of customers building their own versions 5 years ago.

When asked for their single biggest AI threat, respondents ranked:

  1. Incumbent competitors shipping AI features faster (15)
  2. AI reducing the need for the product (12)
  3. Customers vibe coding (11)
  4. AI-native startups (10)
  5. Hyperscalers (5)

AI-native startups ranked fourth, behind customers needing the product less and customers building it themselves.

The churn data points the same way. In 2025, the median company lost 10% of revenue: 7 points from customers leaving entirely and 3 points from downsell. Ader ties part of that full-logo churn to customers trying AI-native alternatives or building their own.

Contract length has the biggest effect on churn in the data. Median gross dollar churn by initial contract term:

  • 12 months: 9%
  • 24 months: 7%
  • 36+ months: 4%

I use Replit every day and have built production apps on it without an engineering background. A decent internal version of a $20K/year point tool takes a weekend now. The vendors that are hard to replace hold proprietary data, run deep inside workflows, or own integrations nobody wants to rebuild. 64% of vendors in the survey build on proprietary or permissioned data. KeyBanc tells investors to focus diligence on “difficulty of replicating core functionality.”

3. Companies Charging for AI Grew 27%. Companies Bundling It Grew 17%.

How AI is monetized today:

  • 41% charge for AI products
  • 29% are testing or piloting monetization
  • 30% don’t charge for AI separately

The main pricing model, out of 69 respondents:

  • Included in core product price: 31
  • Add-on / separate product: 16
  • Hybrid: 12
  • Usage or consumption: 4
  • Outcome-based: 1

The AI price premium has a median of 20%, a 25th percentile of 4%, and a 75th percentile of 26%. KeyBanc’s summary: “customers have not settled on what AI is worth.”

Growth by monetization stage:

  • Charging for AI: 27% growth in 2025, 30% planned for 2026
  • Testing / piloting: 24% → 22%
  • Not charging separately: 17% → 21%

AI-driven ARR shows the same split. Companies with no AI-driven ARR grew 11% in 2025. Companies with up to 25% of ARR from AI grew 31%.

Net retention sits at roughly 100-104% in all three groups, so charging for AI hasn’t moved retention yet. Some of the growth gap is likely selection: companies with AI good enough to charge for probably had stronger products to begin with.

AI-driven ARR was 4% of total ARR in 2025. The plan is 12% in 2026 and 17% in 2027. Planned 2026 growth in AI ARR is 128%, up from 74% in 2025. Only 21 companies answered that question, and KeyBanc tells investors to “diligence how AI-driven ARR is defined.”

4. Only 8% of Companies Report Seat Compression From AI

I’ve argued all year that seat-based pricing is under pressure. This group doesn’t show it yet.

  • 92% report no seat compression from AI. 8% do.
  • Fixed seat-based is the most common model in use (33 of 64 companies). Usage/consumption is close behind at 30.
  • Of the 30 companies moving to usage-based pricing, 53% are piloting, 27% have partially moved, and 20% have fully moved.

Ader again: “‘Consumption’ can be a scary word for a CIO or CFO.”

This is a mid-market group with a $22M median. Seat compression shows up first at large platforms with very large seat counts in support, sales and service, where one agent can replace a team. A $20M ARR vendor selling 40 seats to a mid-market customer hasn’t seen those cuts yet. Most companies are adding usage pricing on top of seats while keeping the seat base.

Companies whose core product is AI lean further toward usage: 38% of their pricing models are usage/consumption, against 25% for companies embedding AI.

5. 30 of 68 Companies Are Over Budget on AI Spend. Only 4 Are Under.

Year-to-date AI spend against budget:

  • More than 20% over: 16
  • 0-20% over: 14
  • Roughly in line: 34
  • Under: 4

Of the 33 companies that explained their overruns, 25 cited higher-than-expected token usage and 16 cited more adoption of AI features. Per-unit inference cost was flat for 47 of 67 companies. The overruns came from volume.

AI spend intensity against the P&L (2025 medians):

AI spend as % of revenue Under 2% 2-5% Over 5% ARR growth 24% 23% 17% Gross margin 78% 72% 66% ARR per FTE $205K $174K $159K Opex per FTE $171K $166K $83K

The over-5% group is only 4 to 7 companies. In 2025, its AI spend showed up as a 12-point gross margin gap without a growth payoff. Those companies also run at half the opex per employee of everyone else, and still produce less ARR per employee.

Companies selling AI as their core product compared with companies embedding AI in a broader product:

  • Growth: 34% vs 22%
  • EBITDA: -12% vs -1%
  • ARR per FTE: $117K vs $201K
  • Spending more than 5% of revenue on AI: 38% vs 17%

Half of the Core AI companies report a last valuation of 16x revenue or more. Under a third of all other companies do.

On gross margin overall, 16 of 56 companies say AI has hurt it, 22 say no effect, and 18 say it improved. We’ve seen the same split in public companies this year. Figma took the AI cost in gross margin. Box, which sells the content layer underneath the AI rather than buying inference, barely moved.

6. 91% Use AI in Engineering. 65% Have Cut Zero Headcount Because of It.

Internal AI use by function:

  • Engineering 91%, customer support 63%, sales 63%, back office 61%, IT 56%, marketing 54%
  • 24 of 40 companies say AI writes half or more of their new code (2 say all of it)
  • 92% say AI has shortened development cycles
  • R&D as a share of revenue is planned to fall from 29% in 2025 to 24% by 2027

65% report no AI-related headcount reduction or reallocation. Planned cuts over the next 12-24 months are concentrated in R&D (45%), customer service (37%) and marketing (21%). 16% expect cuts in sales.

Jason Celino at KeyBanc says companies are putting the engineering savings into shipping faster, and few are taking them to the bottom line.

32% have no formal way of measuring AI productivity, and fewer than a third track any financial metric. Companies running 6+ internal AI use cases had $188K ARR per FTE in 2025, against $141K for companies with 0-5. They plan $295K by 2027.

We run SaaStr with 3 humans and 20+ agents in production, across events, sales, marketing and support. Most of our leverage came from agents outside engineering.

7. Bootstrapped Companies Posted a 36% Rule of 40. VC-Backed Companies Posted -3%.

The bootstrapped group is only 7-9 companies. The 2025 numbers:

VC-backed Bootstrapped ARR $19M $24M ARR growth 25% 24% EBITDA margin -13% 13% Rule of 40 -3% 36% Gross magic number 0.73 1.08

Growth was nearly identical. EBITDA margin differed by 26 points. The bootstrapped companies added about 48% more net new ARR per dollar of sales and marketing.

The financing data is tough. 16 of 38 companies had less than 12 months of runway at their last VC or growth raise, and 27 of 38 had less than 24 months. Recent raises cluster at modest multiples, and much of the 16x+ group still rests on 2021-2022 marks. 27% say they’re open to being acquired. Active acquirers are mostly in the >$50M ARR group.

5 More Interesting Learnings

  • New logos carry the growth plan. New customers were 56% of net new ARR in 2025 and are planned at 63% in 2026. Median NRR is 102%, planned at 101% in 2026.
  • Infrastructure software is accelerating. It grew 33% in 2025 and plans 54% for 2026. Horizontal software went from 19% to a planned 17%. KeyBanc’s Eric Heath credits data-stack and cybersecurity spending pulled along by AI.
  • Customer-facing agents are mostly supervised. 48% of vendors offer semi-autonomous agents, 33% copilots, and 20% fully autonomous agents. 43% require human approval for agent actions.
  • 57% of vendors use multiple models for customer-facing AI. Model strategy made almost no difference to net retention.
  • 8% of vendors report broad, scaled customer deployment of their AI features. ROI uncertainty and data privacy tie as the top adoption barriers (24 each), with budget next (22).

issues.title: DD415 / MBA: school of profit
issues.summary: Issue 415: MBA: school of profit – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
When I finished high school and started exploring my study options back in Germany, I came across the then-new MBA (Master of Business Administration) and found it a bit baffling. I thought you first had to master a craft, then turn it into a business. The MBA seemed to suggest that the craft was not important and you could just learn how to run any business. The course description was thick with English jargon, which didn’t help. I vaguely remember someone describing it as learning how to make more money without producing anything.

That description came back to me while reading a recent opinion piece by Christopher Marquis, who has spent more than 20 years teaching at famous business schools. His verdict on his own industry: business schools can’t be repaired; it’s time to shut them down.

“I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system – they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to ‘fix’ business schools. We need to abolish them.”

Marquis points to research showing that managers with business degrees cut wages, yet didn’t become any more productive. He concludes:

“What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer – value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.”

He also puts into words what I couldn’t as an adolescent:

“A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice – undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they ‘need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.’”

The tension is usually glossed over with the comforting ‘win-win’ story:

“These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of ‘stakeholder capitalism’: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.”

So what should we teach instead? Marquis points to the idea of “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business:

“Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from ‘How do we maximize shareholder value?’ to ‘How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward – and which should we strengthen?’”

“The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.”

To me, this is what rethinking our economic system could look like at its most basic level. An ethics elective won’t do it. The work starts with how we teach people to think about power and capital: how currently both tend to accumulate at the top, while the ecological and social mess gets filed under ‘externalities’ and left for future generations to sort out.

We need people who can read a balance sheet and run a payroll, of course. But we could also teach them to build co-operatives, strengthen communities and organise around shared interests. Extracting value for personal gain is one model of doing business, with a long track record of consequences, but certainly not the only one.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD414 / Organising the discontent
issues.summary: Issue 414: Organising the discontent – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
I can still feel it – the collective exhale. Ann Friedman calls it ‘the great unclenching’, and Rebecca Solnit writes that a win for democracy of this size deserves a proper celebration. Fair enough.

But while the rest of us were glued to swing-state maps, something remarkable was unfolding in a corner of Europe that rarely makes our news feeds.

In Serbia, a movement led by students forced snap elections and then won them outright, ending more than a decade of autocratic rule. It started in 2024, when a train station canopy collapsed and killed 16 people. To many Serbians, it was corruption made visible. Students blockaded their universities and demanded accountability. Within months, farmers, actors, judges and pensioners had joined them, filling city squares in some of the largest protests the country has ever seen.

What’s amazing is that this ideologically mixed movement hasn’t splintered into rival factions. Instead, it has built a shared identity without a single face on the poster. Its electoral list had no leader. The 250 candidates on the ballot papers were nominated, grilled and voted on by student plenums – open assemblies at each university. This produced something that represents a decent slice of the country: a cardiologist, a grammar school teacher, a coal miner, a social worker, a former central bank governor and, for good measure, a retired basketball star.

I’ve been a fan of citizens’ assemblies for years (see DD220). There is lots of evidence that ordinary people, given time, reliable information and a genuine stake in the outcome, can make remarkably good and fair decisions. Serbia’s plenums aren’t a textbook citizens’ assembly – nobody was picked by lottery – but they share the spirit. The power to choose sat with big, messy rooms full of people. And few people have a bigger stake in the outcome than students, who’ll be living with the results long after today’s power brokers have retired to their holiday homes.

It’s hard not to see echoes of Serbia in the Gen Z protests spreading across the world. Of course, some protests turn ugly, and the looting and vandalism deserve condemnation. But the media is often far more interested in pictures of ghouls smashing shop windows than in understanding why so many people took to the streets in the first place, why so many young people can’t see a future worth studying for. Serbia shows what that frustration can build once it gets organised.

The proof is in the pudding, of course. Leaderless movements can be great at opposing and clumsy at governing. Decision-making by committee isn’t pretty. Consensus takes time, patience and a healthy tolerance for disagreement. But there’s something very inspiring about a political movement that started by asking who should represent it, not who should lead it.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD413 / The lost art of having people over
issues.summary: Issue 413: The lost art of having people over – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
As a kid, I loved our big lunch and dinner parties. There are photos of 30-odd people – friends, family, neighbours – squeezed into our apartment on borrowed chairs around tables that didn’t match. It was chaotic, loud and a lot of fun. They didn’t happen nearly often enough, and I sometimes wonder why something we all enjoyed so much was saved for birthdays and other rare occasions.

Over the years, we’ve actually made them rarer still. Derek Thompson has the numbers to prove it:

“In the last 30 years, Americans have seen double-digit declines in practically every measure of socializing. ... The share of Americans who say they host friends or family at their home at least monthly has fallen from 42 percent in 1975 to 12 percent in 2026 – a 70 percent collapse in a half-century.”

These days, the convenience economy has made staying in so easy that inviting people over feels like a self-inflicted chore.

Elizabeth Oldfield went the other way. For more than a decade, she and her husband have hosted shared dinners every other week, first squeezing eight people around a table in a tiny London flat, now feeding up to 16 at a time in their community house. By her count, around 1,500 people have come through the door. The trick, she says, is putting it in the calendar and refusing to renegotiate:

“This bizarre culture of possessive individualism will always give us reasons not to be together, so sometimes it takes a strong container to push back. ... Always keeping our options open and autonomy over our time sounds good but leaves us lonely and disoriented. Make a commitment and your future self will thank you.”

I love how unbothered she is about the state of the house. As her husband puts it, hospitality is ”not the same as entertaining”:

“To be invited into someone else’s imperfect house is, it turns out, a blessing. I do not tend to find very primped, spotless, Instagram-ready homes especially relaxing to be in. If we are going to move towards each other and build real community we have to let go of the desire to impress people.”

I wrote about the radical act of regular open-door dinners a while back (DD331), and Oldfield’s dinners are about the most practical version of that idea I’ve come across. (Do check out her list of tips in the essay.)

So why don’t more of us do it? Thompson has a pretty good theory:

“Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. ... Compared to TikTok, a dinner party is a terrible leisure technology. It requires matching schedules, cleaning the house, buying food, accommodating children and allergies, tolerating awkwardness, and taking the risk that the evening is mediocre. By contrast, what does television ask of us? Nothing. TikTok? Even less.”

When I look at those old photos and my mum’s kitchen, I notice who’s doing the cooking. Those parties ran on a lot of unpaid labour, mostly by women, and Thompson points out that the social calendar frayed when they took on paid work and the men didn’t pick up the slack. Today’s cost-of-living pressures and two exhausted working parents make the couch and screens combo look very appealing.

Oldfield offers us a way back that doesn’t require a kitchen full of women doing all the work and stressing about being a perfect host. Her dinners run on cheap dahl and wine from Lidl. Guests chop, set the table and stay for the clean-up. Nobody performs, nobody keeps score, and somehow everyone leaves a little less alone.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD412 / Breaking up with Gmail
issues.summary: Issue 412: Breaking up with Gmail – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
On a visit to Google’s HQ in Mountain View in 2007, I watched people run almost their entire working lives out of a browser. Gmail was still new-ish, and the Googlers I met were doing clever things with labels, aliases and filters that made my Outlook setup look like an old filing cabinet.

When Google started offering a paid Gmail version with custom domains, I made the move and Gmail slowly became the app I spent most of my days in. Docs, Sheets and Google Maps followed.

By the time I started feeling uneasy about Google, I was thoroughly entangled. The thought of dragging hundreds of thousands of emails somewhere else, and giving up some of Gmail’s then-unique features, sat in the too-hard basket for almost a decade.

But earlier this month, a friend reminded me of the EFF’s Opt Out October, and that finally gave me the nudge. I know plenty of you are in the same boat, so here’s a quick rundown of how it went.

My emails turned out to be the easy part, which is annoying given how long I spent dreading it. My shortlist came down to Proton, Fastmail* and iCloud. I liked Proton a lot when I trialled it, but its (admirable) emphasis on security means calendars and contacts won’t sync with the native apps on my iPhone. iCloud now supports custom domains, and since I’m already deep inside Apple’s walled garden, it would have been the path of least resistance. It would also have meant handing more money to a different Big Tech company.

So I went with Fastmail, a small Melbourne company (represent!) with a solid reputation. Its migration tool pulled everything across via IMAP in a few hours and mirrored my Gmail labels. On my laptop I use the web interface and don’t miss a single feature. On my iPhone, I can still use the native Calendar and Contacts apps, and Fastmail’s own app for email (it’s good). When I made a mistake during my custom domain setup, an actual human replied to my support request within a day with an answer that helped. I’d forgotten that was possible.

Google itself isn’t disappearing from my life any time soon, though. Too many clients and collaborators live in Docs and Sheets. But, I learned that once you remove your custom domain from Google Workspace, it takes Google about 20 days to ‘release’ it, after which you can sign up for a free Google account with that same custom email address.

What you can’t do is bring your other stuff with you. Ugh. Drive files have to be exported and re-uploaded into the new account. Maps and YouTube have no migration path at all, so I’m rebuilding those from scratch, one saved café at a time. Google Maps’ reviews are hard to beat, sorry Apple.

So yeah, Google does remain a fixture for a handful of ‘free’ apps. But the elephant in the room – my big fat inbox – walked out the door far more willingly than I’d expected. All up, it took a few hours over a couple of weekends. Years of dread, overcome by two weekends of mild admin. Shoulda done it ages ago. (And yet, I was just in time.)

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers
issues.summary: There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like. But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years.... issues.author: Matthew Kepnes
issues.content_html:
There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

What are Holafly Plans?


Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas. You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic eSIMs vs Plans


Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. Plus, you can get a phone number, unlimited data, and a hotspot. In the US, if you were to get T-Mobile’s plan, which caps data and is the closest thing we have to “affordable” international plans, you’re going to spend over $100 USD a month (I know because I used to use this plan!). Holafly Plans costs less and gives you more.

Here’s how it compares:

Feature / CostHolafly Plans (Unlimited)US Major Carrier Roaming PassBuying Local SIMs / Single eSIMsMonthly Cost ~$55–$65 / month
depending on monthly, quarterly, or annual payment plan $100–$300 / month ($10/day add-ons) $60–$120 / month (varies by region) Data Allowance Unlimited Capped at high speeds, then throttled Varies (usually 5GB–10GB packages) Hassle FactorZero. Set it up once, works in 160+ destinations. Low, but extremely expensive. High. Re-buying, swapping QR codes, line drops at borders. Hotspotting Included (multiple devices) Often restricted or throttled Varies by carrier

What about the Ultra Plan?

Holafly also recently launched a new tier called The Ultra Plan by Holafly, and it’s a bit different from anything else in the eSIM world.

Basically, it takes everything in the Unlimited Plan (unlimited data, hotspot, phone number, 160+ destinations) and adds a a small travel insurance component that ib:

  • Luggage protection – If the airline loses or delays your checked bag, you get €150 within 24 hours of filing your claim. No receipts needed for what was in the bag. They’ll also help you recover up to €1,900 from the airline. (Amounts are also available in USD. Check the plan terms for the details.)
  • Flight claims – If your flight is delayed, cancelled or overbooked, they’ll review your case and handle the claim for you. You keep 100% of what’s recovered. No commission. (Heads up: this mainly applies to flights covered by EU and UK passenger rights rules, plus Brazil, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Most flights within the Americas and Asia aren’t covered.)
  • 24/7 doctor and pedriatics chat – You can chat with a real doctor or pediatrics (for those traveling with children) in English any time, day or night. This is great for figuring out whether that fever or stomach bug needs a hospital or just rest and water.
  • Unlimited video sessions with psychologists, nutritionists and personal trainers – Usually booked within 48 hours. If you’ve been on the road for months, you know loneliness and burnout are real. This is a nice thing to have in your back pocket.
  • Virtual Locations and an ad blocker (coming soon) – Safer browsing on hostel and café Wi-Fi.
  • Always On – Like the other Plans, you still get 1GB of free backup data every month for emergencies.

    • How much does it cost?
    Ultra is $90.95 a month if you pay monthly, $82.65 a month on the quarterly plan, or $73.41 a month if you pay yearly.
    For comparison, Unlimited is $64.90 monthly, $58.65 quarterly, or $52.41 yearly. Quarterly saves you about 10%, and yearly about 20%. (Use my code NOMADICMATT or MATTK gets you another 10% off on top of whichever plan you choose.)

    So, is the upgrade worth it? Ultra costs about $26 a month more than Unlimited if you pay monthly, $24 more on quarterly, and $21 more on yearly. Here’s how I think about it: one lost bag gets you $150, which covers roughly six months of the difference, whichever way you pay. A single doctor visit abroad, or one session with a psychologist, nutritionist, or personal trainer, can easily cost more than that. And that’s before you even factor in the language barrier and the stress of figuring out where to go. With Ultra, you get unlimited access to all that support included in your plan.

    If you’re heading out for a few months, quarterly is the sweet spot. You get the savings without committing to a full year. If you’re taking a two-week vacation, skip it and stick with a standard Holafly eSIM.

    Just to be clear, this doesn’t replace travel insurance. It won’t cover hospital bills, theft, or emergency situations, so you’ll still need proper travel insurance for all of that but if you want small trip related coverage, this can be a cheaper option.

    How Plans Work and How to Subscribe

    Getting set up takes a couple of minutes, not a couple of hours:

    1. Check compatibility – Most modern smartphones support eSIM, but it’s worth confirming yours does before you buy.
    2. Choose your plan – Head to the Holafly Plans page, pick Unlimited or Light, choose monthly, quarterly, or yearly billing, and complete your purchase. Heads up: your billing cycle starts the moment you pay, not the moment you land somewhere, so if you’re buying ahead of a trip, time it close to departure.
    3. Install the eSIM – You’ll get a QR code and an email guide, or you can install it directly through the Holafly app, which walks you through the whole thing in about two minutes.
    4. Turn on data roaming – when you land, activate the eSIM, and you’re connected. No local SIM shop, no border-crossing scramble.

    If anything goes sideways during setup, real people are on the other end of support 24/7.

    Who are Holafly Plans Actually For

    Holafly Plans isn’t for everyone. If you’re taking a single two-week vacation, a classic destination eSIM will cost you less. However, if you’re a frequent traveler who is in and out of multiple countries within a given month or a digital nomad who needs reliable, ongoing connectivity for work, not just casual browsing, then get Holafly Plans. It’s easier and will save you money in the long run.

    Pros and Cons

    Pros:

    • One eSIM covers 160+ destinations, no swapping at borders
    • True unlimited data and hotspot on the top tier, no throttling
    • Always On gives you free backup data for life, even after you cancel
    • Cancel anytime, no lock-in contract
    • Monthly, quarterly, or yearly billing, with real savings if you go yearly
    • No hidden fees, a 6-month refund policy, and real humans answering support
    • Setup takes about two minutes

    Cons:

    • Not the cheapest option if you’re staying in one country for a long stretch
    • The local phone number is Unlimited-only, not included on Light
    • Data plan costs vary by currency/region, so you’ll want to double-check pricing on Holafly’s site before buying

    **** Holafly plans make life easier if you’re a long-term traveler. You don’t have to swap SIM cards, you get unlimited data, and you get a phone number. It’s the closest thing to a traditional phone plan that is out there but without any huge costs or data caps.

    And, as someone who roams the world a lot and uses a lot of data, especially to stream video and use my phone as a hotspot, these plans save me a ton of money!

    If you’re roaming the world and plan to be out of your home country for a while, this is the product to get!

    Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

    FAQ

    Is Holafly Plans different from a regular Holafly eSIM? Yes. Regular Holafly eSIMs are one-off purchases for a single trip or destination (200+ available). Holafly Plans is an ongoing global subscription for people who are more or less always traveling.

    Does Always On cost extra? No. It’s included automatically with every Holafly Plans subscription and keeps giving you 1GB of backup data a month across 150+ destinations even after you cancel.

    Can I switch between Light and Unlimited? You’d need to cancel your current plan and purchase the other tier — there’s no in-place upgrade yet.

    What if I don’t like it? Holafly backs Plans with a 6-month refund policy, which is more generous than most eSIM companies offer.

    How to Travel the World on $75 a Day

    My New York Times best-selling book to travel will teach you how to master the art of travel so that you’ll get off save money, always find deals, and have a deeper travel experience. It’s your A to Z planning guide that the BBC called the “bible for budget travelers.”

    Click here to learn more and start reading it today!

    Book Your Trip: Logistical Tips and Tricks

    Book Your Flight
    Find a cheap flight by using Skyscanner. It’s my favorite search engine because it searches websites and airlines around the globe so you always know no stone is being left unturned.

    Book Your Accommodation
    You can book your hostel with Hostelworld. If you want to stay somewhere other than a hostel, use Booking.com as it consistently returns the cheapest rates for guesthouses and hotels.

    Don’t Forget Travel Insurance
    Travel insurance will protect you against illness, injury, theft, and cancellations. It’s comprehensive protection in case anything goes wrong. I never go on a trip without it as I’ve had to use it many times in the past. My favorite companies that offer the best service and value are:

    • SafetyWing (best for budget travelers)
    • World Nomads (best for mid-range travelers)

    Want to Travel for Free?
    Travel credit cards allow you to earn points that can be redeemed for free flights and accommodation — all without any extra spending. Check out my guide to picking the right card and my current favorites to get started and see the latest best deals.

issues.title: Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs
issues.summary: If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a...
